design_detail: Laboratory test-accuracy study of three portable drug-checking devices against GC/MS, on drug samples rather than people. Filed as test-accuracy (METHODS §5.3, version 0.3.1): the units are seized drug samples tested in a laboratory, and QUADAS-2 is used because the study compares index tests with a reference standard. Two forensic laboratories (Baltimore Police Department Forensic Laboratory; Rhode Island Department of Health Drug Chemistry Laboratory, Providence), September to October 2017. Phase 1: limits of detection with fentanyl reference standards in ethanol, serially diluted and tested in triplicate, then 7 replicates at the estimated limit. Phase 2: 210 police-seized personal-quantity samples (106 fentanyl-positive and 104 fentanyl-negative by earlier GC/MS) tested blind with BTNX Rapid Response fentanyl test strips (both sites), a TruNarc hand-held Raman spectrometer (both sites; direct scan and SERS kit) and a Bruker Alpha FTIR (Providence only, 106 samples); plus an exploratory set of 4 samples with fentanyl analogues.
can_establish: How often one brand of fentanyl test strip, a hand-held Raman device and a desktop FTIR agreed with earlier GC/MS on whether fentanyl was present in 210 police-seized samples from two US cities in 2017, and the lowest fentanyl concentration each detected with reference standards.
cannot_establish: Accuracy for other strip brands or lots, for fentanyl analogues beyond two found in four exploratory samples, for nitazenes or other opioids, for samples with less fentanyl than the GC/MS reference could detect, for samples prepared and read by people at home (the amount dissolved and water volume are not reported; trained chemists did all testing), or in drug markets with other mixtures; nor whether strip use changes behaviour or overdose.

sample.recruitment: Samples, not people: powders and pills seized by the Baltimore and Providence police in cases with personal quantities (exhibits of 1 g or less, small-scale distribution under 50 bags, or one sample from larger exhibits), already analysed by GC/MS; chosen by staff not involved in testing to give about equal numbers of fentanyl-positive and fentanyl-negative samples (Methods › Sensitivity and specificity procedures, 1st paragraph, p. 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Powder and pill samples from the partner police departments; fentanyl-positive samples were fentanyl alone or with other drugs. Cutting agents not classed as controlled substances were not reported (Results › Characteristics of seized drug samples; Table 2, p. 4).
sample.demographics: Not applicable (samples).
sample.attrition: Not reported. The Raman limit of detection was usable only from Providence after software library changes (Table 1 footnote). Several printed percentages cannot be formed from 52 negatives (FTIR specificity 90.2%, Providence SERS specificity 91.5%), which implies some samples were not analysed in some arms, without explanation (editors' calculation).
sample.selection_effects: Samples were selected on known GC/MS status at about 1:1 (a two-gate selection), which fixes prevalence near 50% and can make accuracy look better than in consecutive samples. Police seizures from two US East Coast cities in 2017 may differ from what people bring to drug checking: the Baltimore set held more heroin–fentanyl mixtures and heroin-only negatives, the Providence set more fentanyl alone, cocaine mixtures and other drugs (Table 2; Discussion, 5th paragraph, p. 5).

exposure.measurement: Index tests (Methods › Devices tested, pp. 2–3; Table 3 footnotes, p. 4): BTNX Rapid Response fentanyl test strip (immunoassay approved in Canada, not the US, for urine; drug-checking use off-label; package-insert urine sensitivity 96.8% and specificity 100%; result within five minutes; presence only), with samples dissolved in tap water (Baltimore) or deionized water (Providence); TruNarc Raman (manufacturer's lowest detection limit 2% by weight; up to three direct scans then three SERS-kit scans; positive if any reading showed 'fentanyl', 'fentanyl/methamphetamine' or 'heroin/fentanyl/methamphetamine'; three inconclusive readings in a row coded as fails); Bruker Alpha FTIR with 11 libraries for DEA-controlled substances and cutting agents, all analyses by the first author. Chemists were blinded to sample content; FTIR and Raman training by the companies (about 1.5 h each), strip training 30 minutes by the study team.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (samples). Fentanyl standards were prepared in ethanol starting at about 10 times each vendor's estimated detection limit and reduced by serial dilution; the amount of street sample dissolved and the water volume for strip testing are not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Table 2 gives the controlled substances in each sample by GC/MS. Fentanyl-positive: fentanyl alone (29 Baltimore, 35 Providence), with heroin (21, 12), with acetyl or furanyl fentanyl, cocaine or 4-ANPP. Fentanyl-negative: cocaine (22, 25), heroin (15, 9), oxycodone (6, 3), clonidine (3, 0), alprazolam (2, 2), clonazepam (0, 2), methamphetamine (0, 3), buprenorphine (1, 1), cathinones (dibutylone, ephylone, 4-chloro-alpha-PPP) and others.

comparison.controls: Reference standard: each laboratory's earlier forensic GC/MS result, extracted from laboratory databases. GC/MS detection limits were 3.1 mcg/mL (Providence) and 100 mcg/mL (Baltimore), both above the strip's 0.100–0.150 mcg/mL (Results › Limit of detection, p. 4; Table 1).
comparison.matching: Protocols, method parameters and acceptance criteria were harmonized between the two laboratories, with weekly teleconferences (Methods, p. 2).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to samples. Not measured or not reported: fentanyl concentration in each sample (so misses cannot be linked to amount), the time between GC/MS and index testing and storage conditions, strip lot, how faint lines were read, and the amount dissolved.

outcomes.instruments: Limit of detection (lowest concentration detected, then confirmed in 7 replicates within ±25%; indeterminate results counted as not detected); sensitivity and specificity for fentanyl against GC/MS; for Raman and FTIR also sensitivity for all substances present.
outcomes.validity_norms: GC/MS is the confirmatory forensic method, but here it was less sensitive than the strip, so strip positives in GC/MS-negative samples may be true fentanyl below GC/MS detection; the authors list GC/MS detection-limit differences and undetected analogues as possible reasons for the between-laboratory differences (Discussion, 5th paragraph, p. 5).
outcomes.operationalization: Fentanyl presence (alone or in a mixture) as reported by GC/MS; the strip does not separate fentanyl from analogues.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive; no confidence intervals or tests).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Chemists running the devices were blinded to sample content; the FTIR analyst ran blinded analyses; GC/MS results predated the study.

analysis.effect_sizes: No confidence intervals are printed. Fentanyl strip (Table 3): sensitivity 100.0% (Baltimore) and 96.3% (Providence), specificity 98.1% and 90.4%. Editors' calculation: 52/52 and 52/54 positives detected; 51/52 and 47/52 negatives correct; pooled sensitivity 104/106 = 98.1% (Wilson 95% CI 93.4–99.5%) and specificity 98/104 = 94.2% (88.0–97.3%); pooled false-negative 1.9% and false-positive 5.8%. Raman direct scan: sensitivity 3.8% and 3.7%, specificity 98.1% and 100.0%; SERS kit: 38.5% and 61.1%, specificity 92.3% and 91.5%. FTIR (Providence): sensitivity 83.3%, specificity 90.2%. Detection limits: strip 0.100 and 0.150 mcg/mL; Raman 25 mcg/mL; FTIR 3–4% by weight; GC/MS 3.1 and 100 mcg/mL.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All devices and both sites are reported, and the exploratory analogue set in full. Not reported: what the Baltimore strip false positive contained (the five described match Providence), the denominators behind the FTIR and SERS specificities, strip lots, and the rule for faint lines.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation. 106 positives and 104 negatives give intervals of several percentage points (editors' calculation above); the exploratory analogue set (n = 4) cannot estimate accuracy.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Against earlier GC/MS on 210 police-seized samples, the strip detected fentanyl in 104 of 106 positives (both misses were fentanyl alone) and read positive in about 6 of 104 negatives (the five described held buprenorphine, heroin, methamphetamine or noscapine only); it was positive in all four exploratory analogue samples. Raman missed most fentanyl samples; FTIR detected 83.3% in Providence and identified other components. The strip detected the lowest fentanyl concentrations of all methods, including GC/MS.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract gives the strip's “false negative (3.7%), and false positive rate (9.6%)” (p. 1), which are the Providence figures only, and concludes that the devices are available and valid. The Discussion then recommends the strip if “at most, a 9.6% false negative and, at most, a 3.7% false positive rate” were acceptable (p. 5), the two rates swapped. 'Valid' is strong for one strip brand, two sites, samples selected on known status and a reference less sensitive than the strip; the abstract's detection of analogues 'in both powder and pill forms' rests on four samples, all tested as powders (Discussion, 4th paragraph).

timeline.event: Data collection in Baltimore and Providence forensic laboratories (September to October).
This study published; cited by Laing et al. (2021) as showing good results for fentanyl strips used on dissolved drug.

Bergh et al. (2021): four strip brands, including this one, on fentanyl, 28 fentanyl analogues and 12 other drugs in water; all detected fentanyl, most analogues only at 1000 ng/mL or more, and carfentanil only at 4000 ng/mL on three brands; no reaction to methamphetamine or heroin at up to 1000 ng/mL. Read in this round (card sc_bergh_2021).

Lockwood et al. (2021): false positives on this strip from solutions of seized methamphetamine and MDMA and retail diphenhydramine at about 1–2.5 mg/mL of material; fentanyl detected down to 25 ng/mL when a faint band was counted as positive. Read in this round (card sc_lockwood_2021).
Park et al. (2022): validation of a lateral flow immunoassay for fentanyl in drug samples, sharing authors with this study; cited by Sisco et al. (2024b) and Kutscher et al. (2024); not read.

Halifax et al. (2024): five lots of this strip; lots obtained in 2017 detected fentanyl in water down to 20 ng/mL and lots obtained in 2021 only down to 200 ng/mL; pure d-methamphetamine, MDMA, lidocaine and diphenhydramine gave false positives at mg/mL concentrations. Read in this round (card sc_halifax_2024).
Sisco et al.: fentanyl strips unchanged after two weeks at 55 °C; strips four years past expiry detected fentanyl only at about ten times their listed cut-off; cross-reactivity not studied.

replication.where_it_stands: The strip's high sensitivity for fentanyl in seized samples has no direct replication on real samples among the papers read; British Columbia drug-checking data, known second-hand through Halifax et al. (2024), are consistent (4 of 173 fentanyl-positive samples missed). Detection of fentanyl at ng/mL concentrations in solutions is replicated by independent laboratories (Bergh et al., 2021; Lockwood et al., 2021; Halifax et al., 2024; Sisco et al., 2024b), with limits from 20 to 500 ng/mL that differ by lot, product and reading rule. False positives with methamphetamine and MDMA at mg/mL concentrations in two of those laboratories make cross-reactivity, not only undetected traces, a possible explanation for this study's methamphetamine-only false positive; the amount dissolved here is not reported.

funding.funder: Bloomberg American Health Initiative, Baltimore, Maryland; the funder had no role in design, conduct, data collection, analysis, interpretation or the manuscript (Funding, p. 6).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflict of interest (Declaration of Competing Interest; repeated in Acknowledgments, p. 6). ThermoFisher Scientific and Bruker Optics lent their devices for the study and had no role in analysis or writing (Acknowledgments, p. 6).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from Brown University and Rhode Island Hospital, Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and School of Medicine, the Baltimore Police Department Forensic Laboratory and one independent author; the police departments supplied the samples. The Raman and FTIR makers lent equipment (each about US$20,000 per the text) and trained staff; no support from the strip maker is mentioned. A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A consecutive series of drug-checking samples (powders, pills and residues as people bring them), each tested on several strip lots and brands prepared as people do at home and read by trained and untrained readers, against a reference method at least as sensitive as the strip (for example LC-MS/MS) with fentanyl measured, so that misses and false positives can be linked to concentration and to other drugs present.

domains.note: Two-gate selection on known GC/MS status (106 positive, 104 negative), not consecutive or random; police seizures of personal quantities from two cities. Applicability to drug-checking samples is uncertain.

Chemists were blinded and followed the makers' instructions, but the amount dissolved, water volume, strip lot and the reading rule for faint lines are not reported, and the water differed between sites (tap or deionized).

GC/MS from earlier casework with detection limits (3.1 and 100 mcg/mL) far above the strip's (0.100–0.150 mcg/mL), so strip positives in GC/MS-negative samples may be true fentanyl; analogues outside the GC/MS methods could be missed.

All samples had GC/MS, but the time between GC/MS and index testing and storage are not reported; FTIR was run at one site only; some percentages imply not every sample was analysed in every arm, without explanation.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: QUADAS-2 is used because the study measures test accuracy against a reference standard (METHODS §5.3, diagnostic accuracy); the design is filed as test-accuracy (METHODS §5.3, version 0.3.1). The overall judgment follows the worst domains (selection on known status; a reference less sensitive than the strip). The reference problem works mainly against the strip's specificity, so the strip's specificity may be understated rather than overstated; its sensitivity in these samples is robust, but only samples with enough fentanyl for GC/MS (3.1 or 100 mcg/mL) could enter the positive group, so sensitivity for samples with little fentanyl is not known and may be lower. Citable for: the strip detected fentanyl in 104 of 106 police-seized samples; it read positive on some fentanyl-negative heroin, methamphetamine, buprenorphine and noscapine samples; it had the lowest detection limit of the devices tested; Raman missed most fentanyl. Not citable for: accuracy with other brands, lots or analogues, accuracy when people test at home, or effects on behaviour or overdose.

key_findings.finding: Two-phase laboratory validation in the Baltimore Police Department Forensic Laboratory and the Rhode Island Department of Health Drug Chemistry Laboratory, September to October 2017: limits of detection with fentanyl standards, then 210 police-seized personal-quantity samples (106 fentanyl-positive, 104 fentanyl-negative by earlier GC/MS; 104 in Baltimore, 106 in Providence) tested blind with fentanyl strips, Raman and (Providence only) FTIR.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Methods, 1st paragraph; Methods › Sensitivity and specificity procedures, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Detection limits: fentanyl strip 0.100 mcg/mL (Providence) and 0.150 mcg/mL (Baltimore), the lowest of all methods; Raman 25 mcg/mL (Providence only; Baltimore results unreliable after a software library change), 250 times the strip's; FTIR 3–4% by weight; GC/MS 3.1 mcg/mL (Providence) and 100 mcg/mL (Baltimore).
key_findings.locator: Results › Limit of detection, 1st paragraph; Table 1 and footnotes

key_findings.finding: Fentanyl strip sensitivity 100.0% (Baltimore) and 96.3% (Providence); specificity 98.1% and 90.4%. Editors' calculation from Table 3: 52/52 and 52/54 positives detected, 51/52 and 47/52 negatives read negative; pooled sensitivity 104/106 = 98.1% (Wilson 95% CI 93.4–99.5%) and specificity 98/104 = 94.2% (88.0–97.3%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Sensitivity and specificity, 1st paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: The two missed fentanyl samples contained fentanyl only (no other drug). Five samples read positive that GC/MS found to contain only buprenorphine (1), heroin (2), methamphetamine (1) or noscapine (1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Sensitivity and specificity, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Table 3's specificities imply six false positives (one Baltimore, five Providence); the text describes five, which match Providence. The Baltimore one is not described.

key_findings.finding: Raman direct scan: fentanyl sensitivity 3.8% (Baltimore) and 3.7% (Providence), specificity 98.1% and 100.0%; SERS kit: sensitivity 38.5% and 61.1%, specificity 92.3% and 91.5%. For all substances present: 25.7% by direct scan (48.1% for non-fentanyl samples) and 53.8% with SERS (57.7%).
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Results › Sensitivity and specificity, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: FTIR (Providence, 106 samples): fentanyl sensitivity 83.3% and specificity 90.2% (false-negative 16.7%, false-positive 9.8%); sensitivity for all substances present 81.9%, and 80.4% for non-fentanyl samples.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (p. 4); Results › Sensitivity and specificity, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: 90.2% cannot be formed from 52 negatives (46/52 = 88.5%, 47/52 = 90.4%); it fits 46/51 (editors' calculation), so one negative was apparently not analysed.

key_findings.finding: Exploratory set of four samples (acetyl fentanyl alone 2, furanyl fentanyl alone 1, furanyl fentanyl with heroin 1): the strip was positive in all four; Raman direct scan was inconclusive in all; SERS detected 3 of 4; FTIR libraries did not identify the analogues but visual comparison with the fentanyl spectrum detected 3 of 4. A counterfeit pill with furanyl fentanyl was missed by both Raman and FTIR.
key_findings.locator: Results › Exploratory analyses, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The strip gives presence only: no concentration, no distinction between fentanyl and its analogues, and no information on quantity, purity, adulterants or fill.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Devices tested, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The strips are approved in Canada (not the US) for urine; drug-checking use is off-label; the package insert gives urine sensitivity 96.8% and specificity 100%. The maker lists 11 analogues the strip detects (editors' count of the list); the authors say the strips' size and portability suit home use.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Devices tested, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Identification by the spectrometers (library matching) was harder with heavily cut mixtures (heroin, cocaine and fentanyl together) and with pills; all samples were tested as powders with chemists blinded to the original form. Raman detected cocaine and other non-opioid drugs well, and, as one hypothesis, the authors attribute the between-laboratory Raman differences to more heroin–fentanyl mixtures and heroin-only controls in Baltimore.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The Discussion recommends the strip as the device of choice for detecting fentanyl presence if “at most, a 9.6% false negative and, at most, a 3.7% false positive rate” were acceptable, and FTIR, or a two-step approach (strip plus another device or GC/MS), when more information is wanted.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph
key_findings.note: The rates are swapped relative to the abstract and Table 3 (Providence: false negatives 3.7%, false positives 9.6%).

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states the strip's rates as at most 9.6% false negatives and 3.7% false positives; the abstract and Table 3 give 3.7% false negatives and 9.6% false positives (Providence).
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim citing the Discussion would reverse the strip's error profile; cite Table 3.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's false-negative (3.7%) and false-positive (9.6%) rates are the Providence figures only, presented as the strip's rates; Baltimore had 0% and about 1.9%, and pooled values are 1.9% and 5.8% (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite site-specific values or the editors' pooled values with their intervals, labelled as such.

reporting_issues.issue: The text describes five false positives; the specificities in Table 3 imply six (one in Baltimore, five in Providence). The Baltimore false positive's content is not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The list of substances that gave false positives may be incomplete.

reporting_issues.issue: FTIR specificity 90.2% and Providence SERS specificity 91.5% cannot be formed from 52 negative samples (editors' calculation: 90.2% fits 46/51; 91.5% fits, for example, 43/47); the denominators are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Some samples were apparently not analysed in some arms; the specificity estimates carry unexplained exclusions.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the strip detected two analogues in both powder and pill forms, but the exploratory set had four samples and the Discussion says all samples were prepared as powder for testing.
reporting_issues.consequence: The analogue finding rests on four samples and says nothing about testing pills as pills.

reporting_issues.issue: The limit-of-detection standards were prepared in ethanol (Methods › Limits of detection procedures, 1st paragraph, p. 3), and the paper does not say whether the strips were dipped in the ethanol solutions or in water dilutions of them; the seized samples were dissolved in tap or deionized water.
reporting_issues.consequence: The strip's 0.100–0.150 mcg/mL limits may not carry over to drug dissolved in water: in another laboratory, organic solvent above about 10% v/v slowed wicking and changed some strip readings (sc_sisco_2024b, AM p. 5).

design_detail: Analysis of community drug-checking programme data, filed as cross-sectional because each sample was analysed once; the second aim (strips and FTIR against laboratory results on the same samples) fits the test-accuracy design added in METHODS 0.3.1, and whether to re-file the card with QUADAS-2 is left to the senior author. Eight harm-reduction sites (supervised consumption and overdose prevention sites) in Vancouver and Surrey, British Columbia, October 2018 to January 2020: samples checked at the point of care by FTIR (Bruker ALPHA or ALPHA-II) and BTNX benzodiazepine test strips (with fentanyl strips), and a convenience subset also tested at confirmatory laboratories (Health Canada Drug Analysis Service: qNMR or GC–MS with LC-QTOF/MS confirmation; BC Provincial Toxicology Centre: GC–MS). Confirmatory samples came from five of the eight sites (three in Vancouver, two in Surrey) (Methods, 5th paragraph, p. 3). Two aims: the number and type of NPS benzodiazepines among confirmed samples, and the false-positive and false-negative rates of the point-of-care methods against confirmatory results.
can_establish: Which NPS benzodiazepines confirmatory laboratories found in 159 (and a further 383) drug-checking samples in the Vancouver area in 2018–2020, and how often the benzodiazepine strip and FTIR agreed with those results in the 153 verified samples without only typical benzodiazepines.
cannot_establish: How common NPS benzodiazepines were in the local drug supply (a convenience subset partly sent because of suspected benzodiazepine overdose), the strips' accuracy for typical benzodiazepines (6 samples), accuracy in the 1209 unverified samples, what made the 20 strip false positives react, or any effect on behaviour or overdose.

sample.recruitment: Samples, not people: drugs brought voluntarily to harm-reduction sites. Confirmatory samples were a convenience subset: drugs discarded or not reclaimed, sent at the client's request, or clinically suspicious for benzodiazepine overdose (for example prolonged unconsciousness unlike opioid toxicity alone); the laboratory was chosen by availability or by site (Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 3; Fig. 1, p. 4).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Samples with both point-of-care tests (strip and FTIR) and a confirmatory result; six confirmed to contain only typical benzodiazepines were removed from the NPS-benzodiazepine accuracy analysis (Table 3 note, p. 5).
sample.demographics: Not collected; data were anonymous (Methods, 5th paragraph, p. 3). Expected drug was reported by the person: fentanyl 90, alprazolam 17, 'down' 12, unknown 13, and others (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Of 1368 samples with both point-of-care tests, 159 (11.6%, editors' calculation) had confirmatory results; the rest are outside the accuracy analysis. Fig. 1 gives 543 confirmatory samples, but 159 + 383 = 542.
sample.selection_effects: Verification was partial and non-random and included samples sent because of suspected benzodiazepine overdose, which can raise the share of positives and bias the strip's apparent sensitivity in either direction; people using voluntary services may differ from the wider market (authors' limitation, p. 7).

exposure.measurement: Point of care (Methods, pp. 2–3): FTIR with the TICTAC, Bruker pharmaceutical, SWGDRUG and an in-house library, then the sample dissolved in water and tested with BTNX Rapid Response single-drug benzodiazepine strips (oxazepam calibrator, cut-off 300 ng/mL, validated by the maker for 22 benzodiazepines in urine) and fentanyl strips; results combined. Confirmatory: PTC GC–MS against a calibration list (Supplemental Table 2, not read); DAS qNMR or GC–MS, with LC-QTOF/MS confirmation of a targeted fentanyl and benzodiazepine method (Supplemental Table 3, not read).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (samples).
exposure.polysubstance: Table 2: of the 24 NPS-benzodiazepine-positive samples, 17 also contained fentanyl (one also carfentanil); others contained methamphetamine (10), caffeine (19), phenacetin (7), 4-ANPP, N-phenylpropanamide and melatonin (editors' count from Table 2).

comparison.controls: Confirmatory result: any NPS benzodiazepine by GC–MS, LC-MS or qNMR at either laboratory (Table 1 footnote). Of 7 NPS-benzodiazepine-positive samples sent to both laboratories, 5 were confirmed at both and 2 at only one (Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 3).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to samples. Not measured or not reported: benzodiazepine amounts, what made the 20 strip false positives react, strip lot, the water volume used to dissolve the 2–3 mg tested (the amount is reported; Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 3), the fentanyl-strip results, and the laboratories' target lists (supplement not read).

outcomes.instruments: False-positive rate (false positives over all confirmed negatives) and false-negative rate (false negatives over all confirmed positives) for strips, FTIR and either method, against confirmatory results for NPS benzodiazepines (Table 3, p. 5).
outcomes.validity_norms: The strips are designed for urine metabolites of common benzodiazepines (oxazepam, nordiazepam), not for NPS benzodiazepines or dissolved drug (Limitations, p. 7). The authors present the accuracy values on the assumption of some ability of the strips to detect NPS benzodiazepines (p. 4).
outcomes.operationalization: Positive = strip or FTIR positive; true positive = confirmed NPS benzodiazepine; samples with only typical benzodiazepines removed.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Who ran and read the strips is not stated. Point-of-care testing was done in two steps, FTIR on 2–3 mg of the sample and then the strip in the dissolved sample, with one combined result recorded, so the strip reading was not blind to the FTIR result (Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 3); point-of-care results were recorded before confirmatory testing.

analysis.effect_sizes: No confidence intervals are printed. Strips: 15 of 24 confirmed NPS-benzodiazepine samples positive (sensitivity 62.5%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 42.7–78.8%), false-negative rate 37.5%; 20 of 129 confirmed negatives positive, false-positive rate 15.5% (10.3–22.7%), specificity 84.5% (editors' calculation); detection 7 of 8 (87.5%) with flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam and 8 of 16 (50.0%; 28.0–72.0%) with etizolam alone. FTIR: 2 of 24 detected (false-negative 91.7%), 5 of 129 false positives (3.9%). Either method: 17 of 24 detected (false-negative 29.2%), 23 of 129 false positives (17.8%) (Results › Point-of-care accuracy & error; Table 3).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; ethics approval from the Providence Health Care/University of British Columbia Research Ethics Board.
analysis.selective_reporting: Fentanyl-strip results from the same testing are not reported. The confirmatory-only subset (383) is described for NPS benzodiazepines only. Supplementary Tables 1–3 (strip insert details, laboratory target lists) were not read.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation; 24 confirmed positives give wide intervals (editors' calculation above), as the authors note for the small subsamples (p. 7).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In a convenience subset of 159 drug-checking samples, 24 (15.1%) contained NPS benzodiazepines, mostly etizolam, none expected by the person; 17 of the 24 also held fentanyl. Strips detected 15 of 24 and read positive in 20 of 129 samples with no benzodiazepine found; FTIR detected 2 of 24. Strips detected typical benzodiazepines in all six samples that had them.
interpretation_gap.claimed: On accuracy the authors are cautious: point-of-care methods showed “substantial false positive and false negative rates” and should be routinely paired with confirmatory testing (Abstract; Conclusions, p. 7), which the results support. The framing of a first sizeable outbreak with 6.3% positivity among confirmatory samples (Discussion, p. 6) describes a non-random, partly overdose-driven subset, not the market, as the authors acknowledge in their limitations.

timeline.event: Benzodiazepine strips added to the Vancouver drug-checking programme in October, after counterfeit alprazolam containing fentanyl but no benzodiazepine was found (Methods, p. 2).

Shapiro et al. (2020), a BC Centre on Substance Use report cited in the Methods: flualprazolam and flubromazolam detected by the strips at concentrations similar to alprazolam, etizolam only at higher concentrations, which the report judged still useful for drug checking; not read.
This study.
Sisco et al.: in water, the same maker's benzodiazepine strip reacted to diazepam, alprazolam, bromazolam and flubromazepam but not to etizolam at any concentration tried (0.01 to 0.5 mg/mL).

replication.where_it_stands: Lower detection of etizolam is supported by the later laboratory study, which found no reaction at all, while the earlier report cited here found similar strips detected etizolam at higher concentrations; that half of the etizolam-only street samples were strip-positive here may reflect other reacting compounds, untargeted benzodiazepines, lots or test conditions, which none of these resolves. The 15.5% false-positive rate has no independent estimate in the papers read.

funding.funder: Health Canada Substance Use and Addictions Program grant to the BC Centre on Substance Use to implement and evaluate a drug-checking pilot (Arrangement 1718-HQ-000024); M.E.S. held a Michael Smith Foundation for Health Research/St Paul's Foundation Scholar Award and L.T. a Michael Smith Foundation for Health Research Scholar Award; the granting agencies had no direct role (Funding, p. 7).
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors declare no conflicts of interest (p. 7). Health Canada DAS and the Provincial Toxicology Centre provided confirmatory testing; the authors state the findings are not an endorsement of the point-of-care technologies (Acknowledgements, p. 7).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of British Columbia, the BC Centre on Substance Use, Vancouver Coastal Health, the Provincial Toxicology Centre and Health Canada's Drug Analysis Service, the two laboratories that supplied the reference results; the programme evaluated is the authors' own Health Canada-funded pilot. A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Confirmatory testing of all, or a random sample, of the strip-tested samples with a broad (untargeted) and quantitative method, on several strip lots, so that detection of each NPS benzodiazepine, the causes of strip false positives and the effect of dissolution could be estimated without verification bias.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Drug-checking samples at harm-reduction sites are a fair frame for what service clients bring, not for the drug market (authors' limitation).
A convenience subset (discarded, unclaimed or client-requested samples) plus samples sent because of suspected benzodiazepine overdose.
159 confirmed samples with 24 positives; the 95% interval around the strips' 62.5% sensitivity runs from about 43% to 79% (editors' calculation).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Sites, period, expected drug, laboratory methods and a flow diagram are given.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Only 159 of 1368 point-of-care-tested samples (11.6%) were verified; one confirmatory sample is unaccounted for between Fig. 1 and the text.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Forensic and toxicology laboratories with GC–MS, LC-QTOF/MS and qNMR, but targeted methods may miss the newest compounds (authors), and the target lists are in an unread supplement.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Two laboratories with different methods, chosen by availability or site; 2 of 7 positive samples tested at both were positive at only one.
Rate formulas are correct and re-derive from Table 3, but no intervals are given and one percentage is misprinted (70.1% for 17 of 24).

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Samples, not respondents; partial verification is covered under items 2 and 5.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence fits the first aim (the number and type of NPS benzodiazepines among confirmed samples) and the cross-sectional design. Judged as a test-accuracy analysis, the same problems — partial, non-random verification (159 of 1368), selection partly on suspected benzodiazepine overdose, a targeted two-laboratory reference that disagreed on 2 of 7 duplicate samples, and 24 confirmed positives — put the false-positive and false-negative rates at high risk of bias in directions that cannot be predicted. Citable for: strips and FTIR missed a substantial share of NPS benzodiazepines, especially etizolam; strips read positive in samples with no benzodiazepine found; strips detected typical benzodiazepines in six samples; etizolam was the commonest NPS benzodiazepine in this setting. Not citable for: precise accuracy figures, prevalence in the market, or accuracy elsewhere or with other strip lots.

key_findings.finding: Flow: 6156 samples submitted; 1379 tested by benzodiazepine strips and 1368 also by FTIR; 543 sent for confirmatory testing; 159 had both point-of-care and confirmatory results (120 to Health Canada DAS, 65 to the Provincial Toxicology Centre, 26 to both); 383 confirmatory-only samples had no strip test.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1 (counts read from the figure image); Results › NPS benzodiazepines in confirmatory-only subsample
key_findings.note: 159 + 383 = 542, one fewer than the 543 in Fig. 1 and the text; the gap is not explained.

key_findings.finding: 24 of 159 samples (15.1%) contained at least one NPS benzodiazepine: etizolam 18, flualprazolam 4, flubromazolam 3, flubromazepam 1 (two samples held two). None was expected by the person to be an NPS benzodiazepine; they were expected to be fentanyl (15), alprazolam (5), an unknown opioid (2), heroin (1) or unknown (1).
key_findings.locator: Results › NPS benzodiazepines in primary sample, 1st paragraph; Tables 1–2

key_findings.finding: Of 114 samples expected to be opioids, 18 (15.8%) contained an NPS benzodiazepine and 16 (14.0%) both an NPS benzodiazepine and an opioid, always fentanyl; of all 24 positives, 17 contained fentanyl (one also carfentanil).
key_findings.locator: Results › NPS benzodiazepines and opioids, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Printed as 17 (70.1%); 17/24 is 70.8% (editors' calculation). Repeated in the Discussion (p. 6).

key_findings.finding: Six of the 159 samples (3.8%) contained only typical benzodiazepines (alprazolam, temazepam), all detected by the strips; they were removed from the NPS-benzodiazepine accuracy analysis, leaving 153.
key_findings.locator: Results › Point-of-care accuracy & error, 1st paragraph; Table 3 note

key_findings.finding: Strips: 15 of 24 confirmed NPS-benzodiazepine samples positive (62.5%), false-negative rate 37.5%; 20 of 129 confirmed negatives positive, false-positive rate 15.5%. Detection 87.5% (7 of 8) when flualprazolam, flubromazolam or flubromazepam was present and 50.0% (8 of 16) with etizolam alone.
key_findings.locator: Results › Point-of-care accuracy & error, 3rd paragraph; Table 3 (p. 5)
key_findings.note: The 129 confirmed negatives are the editors' sum of Table 3 counts (20 + 109); the paper gives the rates and the counts, not the total.

key_findings.finding: FTIR: 2 of 24 detected (false-negative rate 91.7%); 5 of 129 negatives positive (false-positive rate 3.9%); the two detections were etizolam samples that were negative on strips.
key_findings.locator: Results › Point-of-care accuracy & error, 4th paragraph; Table 3 (p. 5)
key_findings.note: 129 negatives = 5 + 124 in Table 3 (editors' sum).

key_findings.finding: Either method positive: 17 of 24 detected (false-negative rate 29.2%); 23 of 129 negatives positive (false-positive rate 17.8%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Point-of-care accuracy & error, 2nd paragraph; Table 3 (p. 5)
key_findings.note: 129 negatives = 23 + 106 in Table 3 (editors' sum).

key_findings.finding: Confirmatory-only subset: 10 of 383 (2.6%) contained NPS benzodiazepines (9 etizolam, 1 etizolam with flualprazolam), all with a high-potency opioid (fentanyl 3, carfentanil 4, both 2, fentanyl with furanyl UF-17 1); FTIR was negative for NPS benzodiazepines in all ten. In all, 34 of 543 confirmatory samples (6.3%) contained NPS benzodiazepines.
key_findings.locator: Results › NPS benzodiazepines in confirmatory-only subsample, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Of 7 NPS-benzodiazepine-positive samples sent to both confirmatory laboratories, 5 (71.4%) were confirmed at both and 2 (28.6%) at only one.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Editors' count from Table 2 (the 24 positive samples): FTIR listed caffeine in all 19 samples in which the laboratory found caffeine, but fentanyl (or fentanyl or analogue) in 3 of 17 with fentanyl, methamphetamine in 1 of 10, phenacetin in none of 7, and an NPS benzodiazepine in 2 of 24.
key_findings.locator: Table 2
key_findings.note: A selected set of samples; FTIR results for fentanyl in the whole programme are not reported.

key_findings.finding: Strip used: BTNX Rapid Response single-drug benzodiazepine strip, oxazepam calibrator, cut-off 300 ng/mL, validated by the maker for 22 benzodiazepines in urine; added to the programme in October 2018 after counterfeit alprazolam containing fentanyl but no benzodiazepine was found. A BCCSU report (Shapiro et al., 2020) found flualprazolam and flubromazolam detected at concentrations similar to alprazolam, etizolam at higher concentrations, which it judged still within the range useful for drug checking (p. 3), and no cross-reaction with fentanyl; the authors cite this report as recent evidence of cross-reactivity supporting point-of-care use (p. 4).
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph; Results › Point-of-care accuracy & error, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Authors' limitations: voluntary service may not represent the market; small subsamples may misestimate the rates; strips are designed for urine metabolites of common benzodiazepines (oxazepam, nordiazepam) and not for NPS benzodiazepines or dissolved drug; etizolam is reportedly insoluble in water; FTIR has difficulty with small quantities in mixtures; targeted confirmatory assays may miss the newest compounds.
key_findings.locator: Limitations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that the substantial false-positive and false-negative rates call for cautious use of combined point-of-care methods routinely paired with confirmatory drug checking.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Conclusions; Conclusions

reporting_issues.issue: 17 of the 24 NPS-benzodiazepine-positive samples are reported as 70.1%; 17/24 is 70.8%. The same figure is repeated in the Discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite 17 of 24.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 1 and the text give 543 confirmatory samples, but the two subsets reported (159 with point-of-care results and 383 without strip testing) add to 542.
reporting_issues.consequence: One sample is unaccounted for; the 6.3% overall positivity (34 of 543) is unaffected in practice.

reporting_issues.issue: Fentanyl strips were part of the point-of-care testing (Abstract › Methods; Methods), but no fentanyl-strip results are reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Selective reporting relative to the testing done; the paper cannot be cited for fentanyl-strip performance.

reporting_issues.issue: The 20 strip false positives are defined against NPS benzodiazepines only (samples with only typical benzodiazepines removed), and what they contained, or what made them react, is not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The false-positive rate cannot be linked to any cross-reacting compound.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 3 the 'Either' column under negative results (n = 151) counts samples negative on at least one method, while the combined false-negative rate in the text uses the 'Both' negative column (n = 113).
reporting_issues.consequence: Easy to misread; the combined false-negative rate is 7 of 24 (29.2%).
