design_detail: Narrative review of chemical colour (spot) tests for presumptive identification of illicit drugs, written for law enforcement, border and forensic laboratory settings. It covers history, the reaction chemistry of 15 common reagents (Table 1; Figures 1–4), commercial kits (Table 2), harm-reduction and NPS uses, false positives, validation guidance (selectivity, limit of detection, precision, stability) and newer methods (digital image analysis, sensor arrays, microfluidic and solid sensors). 134 references; no search strategy, criteria or synthesis. Read from the accepted manuscript (35 PDF pages without printed page numbers; 'AM p.' gives the PDF page).
can_establish: Which reagents forensic guidance and the cited studies use for which drug classes, the colours and known false positives the cited sources report for some reagent–drug pairs, what influences results (temperature, light, reader, mixtures, dyes), and which questions (reaction mechanisms, detection limits, reactions of new psychoactive substances) were open as of 2017.
cannot_establish: How accurate any colour test or home kit is in drug checking (no pooled or appraised accuracy data), whether the false positives cited are typical, or how the tests perform with drugs that appeared after 2017.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The abstract mentions a search of the scientific literature, but no databases, dates, terms or criteria are given.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated; sources chosen by the authors.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Selection by the authors for a forensic readership; harm-reduction use takes two paragraphs. Several limitations rest on news reports (a New York Times Magazine article, tabloid stories on doughnut crumbs, baking soda and Epsom salts) and an advocacy report (Marijuana Policy Project) alongside validation studies.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable; colours, detection limits and false positives are as reported by cited sources (mainly Kovar, O'Neal et al., UNODC manuals, Toole et al., Cuypers et al.).
exposure.polysubstance: The review notes that results can be changed by more than one drug in a sample and by colouring agents in tablets (Limitations, 2nd paragraph, AM p. 10).

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Colour reactions read by eye; selectivity, limit of detection, precision and stability as validation parameters (UNODC, SWGDRUG and NIJ guidance as cited).
outcomes.validity_norms: UNODC guidance as cited: the operational detection limit is the lowest concentration positive in five replicates multiplied by ten, and at least ten replicates should give no more than 20% false negatives (Limit of detection; Precision, AM p. 12).
outcomes.operationalization: Presumptive identification, a category C (low discriminating power) technique in SWGDRUG's scheme, like immunoassays (Introduction, AM p. 2).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates. Figures as cited: typical detection limits of 1–50 μg for 36 reagent–drug pairs (O'Neal); d-methamphetamine HCl detected from 100 μg with Mandelin's and 10 μg with Simon's; Zimmerman changed colour at once with 13 of 16 cathinones and with all but bupropion within 5 minutes (UNODC); Scott's sensitivity doubled when cooler and halved above 40 °C; Duquenois-Levine five times slower at 3 °C; of 42 non-cannabis substances on two kits, patchouli, spearmint and eucalyptus tested positive; over 600 NPS had emerged.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection; colours are given for only some reagent–drug pairs, and Table 1 lists target classes, not colours. Counter-evidence on the usefulness of colour tests for harm reduction is limited to one evaluation (Murray et al.) and one review (Harper et al.).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The review documents that colour tests are presumptive, react with many non-target substances (aspirin, sugar, baking soda, lidocaine, ketamine, some cathinones, plant materials), depend on temperature, lighting and the reader, lack specificity for new psychoactive substances, and that reaction mechanisms are unknown for several reagents.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Conclusions are measured; the Conclusions call it “A common misnomer is that color tests provide binary outcomes” (AM p. 15) and stress awareness of false positives. Some limitations rest on news reports presented in the same register as studies, and home use is discussed briefly, mainly through an evaluation concluding that MDMA kits should not be used by the public.

timeline.event: Scott modifies the cobalt thiocyanate test to make it more specific to cocaine (as described in the review).
O'Neal, Crouch and Fatah validate twelve chemical spot tests (cited for detection limits and Marquis colours; not read).
Cuypers et al. test five colour test kits on more than 40 NPS (cited; not read); a commercial presumptive test specific for fentanyl is released.
This review published (online 2017).
Sisco et al. cite this review among presumptive field methods and study urine immunoassay strips instead of colour reagents.

replication.where_it_stands: The review remains a map of reagents, target classes and documented interferences; it contains no accuracy data from drug-checking settings, and none of the other papers read for this batch evaluates colour tests.

funding.funder: Not reported in the accepted manuscript read (no funding or acknowledgement statement).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported in the accepted manuscript read.
funding.affiliations_note: Two authors; affiliations are not printed in the manuscript read. Three of the 134 references are the authors' own work (Toole et al., with Fu; Philp et al. on piperazine and cathinone colour tests). The published version may carry statements absent from the manuscript.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review with a registered protocol of colour-test accuracy on real drug-checking samples, by reagent and drug, including reader variation, followed by field studies with consecutive samples and laboratory confirmation.

domains.note: A literature search is mentioned in the abstract only; no databases, dates, terms or criteria.
No appraisal; news reports and an advocacy report are used alongside validation studies without distinguishing their weight.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Three of 134 references are the authors' own (colour tests for cathinones and piperazines).
Mostly descriptive and the future-perspectives section is labelled, but anecdotes of wrongful arrests are presented in the same register as study findings.

domains.domain: Balance of forensic and harm-reduction perspectives
domains.note: Written for police and forensic laboratories; home and harm-reduction use is under-represented (two paragraphs), and colours for drugs common in home kits (MDMA, ketamine, LSD) are mostly not given.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The review is a useful map of reagents, their target classes, reaction chemistry and documented false positives, but selection is unsystematic, sources are not appraised and most figures are second-hand. Claims may cite it for which reagent is used for which drug class, the colours it reports, and the kinds of false positives and influences it documents, labelled as second-hand; not for the accuracy of any test.

key_findings.finding: Colour tests are used strictly for presumptive identification, and SWGDRUG places them, with immunoassays and ultraviolet spectroscopy, in its lowest discriminating-power category (C), below infrared, Raman and mass spectrometry (A).
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph; Current situation, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Marquis: originally a test for morphine and other alkaloids (red-violet); purple product with opium alkaloids; orange-brown with amphetamine HCl (an orange carbenium product in Kovar's account), black with MDA HCl and olive-green with 3,4-dimethoxymethamphetamine HCl; it also reacts with aspirin and sugar. No colour is given for MDMA or methamphetamine.
key_findings.locator: Chemistry of common color tests › General screening reagents, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Mandelin's: orange with cocaine, olive with codeine and brown with heroin; the chemistry of these reactions has not been investigated. Froehde's: purple product with morphine. Table 1 lists Mandelin's for amphetamines and anti-depressants and Froehde's for a range of aromatic compounds.
key_findings.locator: General screening reagents, 3rd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Simon's: blue product with secondary amines, particularly methamphetamine and MDMA; Table 1 says it distinguishes primary and secondary amines. It detected d-methamphetamine HCl from 10 μg against 100 μg for Mandelin's (O'Neal, as cited).
key_findings.locator: Functional group selective, 1st paragraph; Limit of detection, 2nd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Zimmerman: recommended by UNODC for synthetic cathinones (immediate colour change with 13 of 16; only bupropion unreacted after 5 minutes) and described for benzodiazepines (Kovar); no colours given. Liebermann's gave intensely yellow products with methcathinone analogues and Marquis identified methylenedioxy cathinones (Toole et al.); 3-fluoromethcathinone reacted with neither.
key_findings.locator: Functional group selective, 2nd paragraph; New Psychoactive Substances (NPS), 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Scott's (cobalt thiocyanate) test for cocaine: a blue organic layer, whose intensity told crack cocaine from 5-MeO-DIPT; Table 1 lists methadone as a further target. False positives: pyrrolidine-type cathinones, the cutting agents dibucaine and ketamine with larger test samples, and lidocaine; the original cobalt thiocyanate test gave many false positives; in image analysis of cut cocaine, false positives rose with sample weight.
key_findings.locator: New Psychoactive Substances (NPS), 6th and 9th paragraphs; Limitations, 2nd paragraph; Selectivity (and specificity), 3rd paragraph; Digital image analysis, 3rd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Duquenois-Levine for cannabis: positive when a purple product moves into the chloroform layer; which cannabinoids it detects is unclear; on two commercial kits, patchouli, spearmint and eucalyptus tested positive and lavender, cypress and oregano were inconclusive among 42 non-cannabis substances; it is unsuitable for synthetic cannabinoids (no THC) and told kratom from cannabis. Fast Blue B or BB salt is the main cannabis test of Brazil's forensic police.
key_findings.locator: Drug class selective, 1st and 6th paragraphs; New Psychoactive Substances (NPS), 3rd and 9th paragraphs; Selectivity (and specificity), 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Ehrlich's reagent detects indoles, specifically LSD and other ergot alkaloids; no colour is given and psilocybin, DMT and 5-MeO-DMT are not named. Mecke reacts with opium alkaloids and has been reported to help distinguish heroin from fentanyl; no colours given.
key_findings.locator: Drug class selective, 2nd and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Synthetic cannabinoids: a research DNP test formed orange-red precipitates (synthetic cathinones did not react); the Van Urk test was ineffective; a commercial kit is labelled with up to six colours, but its specificity is unknown.
key_findings.locator: New Psychoactive Substances (NPS), 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Ketamine: alkaline gold bromide (research) turned deep purple within one minute with no cross-reaction with common ketamine adulterants but reacted with ascorbic acid, mannitol, sucrose and lactose; a cobalt-complex nano-silica kit gave a purple precipitate. Mephedrone: alkaline permanganate turned green after 10 minutes; neocuproine methods needed heating.
key_findings.locator: New Psychoactive Substances (NPS), 7th and 10th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: GHB: a drink-test coaster claimed to detect GHB and ketamine, which one study found true only at high concentrations and depending on the drink; a research colour sensor array detected GHB at sub-millimolar concentrations and told it from GBL, proposed because commercial tests could not detect GHB at low levels capable of causing death.
key_findings.locator: Harm reduction, 1st paragraph; Other colorimetric methods, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: An evaluation of MDMA screening kits (Murray et al., as cited) concluded they should not be used by the public, because pure and adulterated forms cannot be distinguished; a later review found colour tests the best lower-technology option for point-of-care services but recommended handheld infrared or Raman devices.
key_findings.locator: Harm reduction, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Influences on results: more than one drug in a sample and colouring agents in tablets such as ecstasy; reader vision and lighting; temperature (Scott's sensitivity doubled when cooler and halved above 40 °C; at 3 °C many reactions slowed and Duquenois-Levine was five times slower); reagent stability (fresh preparation typically after one month).
key_findings.locator: Limitations, 2nd paragraph; Precision; Stability; Digital image analysis, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: False-positive cases: tablets in Italy presumptively identified as amphetamines by Marquis contained two anabolic steroids and no amphetamine-type substance; news reports describe arrests after positive field tests on doughnut crumbs, baking soda and Epsom salts, and a wrongful conviction after a roadside cocaine test.
key_findings.locator: Limitations, 1st and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Common colour tests lacked specificity for new psychoactive substances, of which over 600 had emerged; the Conclusions call it a misnomer that colour tests give binary outcomes and are easy to interpret.
key_findings.locator: New Psychoactive Substances (NPS), 1st paragraph; Conclusions and future perspectives, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Laboratory alternatives to reading by eye, as cited: colorimetric analysis added to colour tests showed potential for semi-quantitative analysis; RGB values from digital images of Marquis and Simon's reactions with methamphetamine and amphetamine products were semi-quantitative and agreed well with gas chromatography (Choodum et al.); a sol-gel sensor holding Simon's reagent, read by digital colorimetry, gave quantitative results. These are research methods for amphetamine-type substances, not kits read by eye.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph (AM p. 2); Advances in color testing › Digital image analysis, 2nd paragraph (AM p. 13); Solid sensors, 1st paragraph (AM p. 15)

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists Fast Blue B (diazotized o-dianisidine), while Figure 1 and Figure 4g show Fast Blue BB, and the text discusses both salts.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which salt Table 1 means for cannabis screening is ambiguous.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 names the Zimmerman component 2,4-dinitrobenzene, but Figure 3b draws nitro groups in the 1,3 positions; a disubstituted benzene cannot be numbered 2,4 (editors' note).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor naming error in the reagent composition.

reporting_issues.issue: Marquis colours are given for 3,4-dimethoxymethamphetamine HCl, a compound not otherwise discussed, and none for MDMA; whether MDMA was meant cannot be told from the review.
reporting_issues.consequence: The olive-green colour must not be attributed to MDMA.

reporting_issues.issue: Detection limits are given as masses (μg) without solution volumes.
reporting_issues.consequence: They cannot be compared with test-strip limits given as concentrations (μg/mL).

verification.source_read: PDF of the accepted manuscript (35 pages, no printed page numbers; cited as AM p. = PDF page; version of record Drug Testing and Analysis 2018;10:95–108), the project PDF folder DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/Cannabis/Philp_2018_SpotTestsReview.pdf: all text, reference list, Tables 1–2, Figures 1–5 (rendered; reaction schemes and a bar chart, no colours). No funding or interest statement present.

disagreements.first_pass: (not recorded)
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 143 (missed): camera-based RGB analysis of Marquis and Simon's results was semi-quantitative and agreed with gas chromatography, and a sol-gel Simon's sensor with digital colorimetry gave quantitative results; relevant to claims that colour tests show no amount (true for reading by eye).
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after checking AM pp. 2, 13 and 15; added as a key finding. cl_dc_colour_mdma and cl_dc_home_what_tests_miss now limit 'no amount' to reading by eye.

verification.checked_by: AI reader 143 (blind second reading) and AI reader 148 (adjudication)

design_detail: Laboratory study of BTNX urine immunoassay test strips used for drug checking, with standards dissolved in water (acetonitrile added for poorly soluble compounds); no real drug samples. Filed as test-accuracy (METHODS §5.3, version 0.3.1; re-filed in adjudication on 27 October 2026): strip readings are compared with the known content of prepared solutions, and the study is appraised with QUADAS-2, as for sc_bergh_2021. Five sub-studies: approximate limit of detection (10 strips per concentration; the lowest concentration at which all 10 gave a clear positive), reproducibility over four weeks (duplicates at five time points), cross-reactivity (79 analytes at High, 0.5 or 1 mg/mL, and Low, 0.01 mg/mL, two strips each; 14 more analytes for xylazine strips), two weeks' storage of unopened strips at 55 °C (eight strip types, triplicate), and strips more than four years past expiry (cocaine, fentanyl, methamphetamine). Strip types: amphetamine, benzodiazepine, cocaine, methamphetamine, nitazene, opiate and xylazine; fentanyl only in the heat and expiry sub-studies. Read from the NIST author manuscript of Forensic Chemistry 2024;40:100594. The PDF was saved in the project as Sisco_2023_XylazineTestStrips.pdf, but it is this paper (reference sisco_2024b), not the xylazine strip paper (sisco_2024a).
can_establish: Which of 79 drugs, cutting agents and other compounds made seven types of BTNX urine strips read positive or faint in water at two concentrations, the approximate lowest concentration at which each strip detected its target, and whether two weeks' heat or years past expiry changed that, for the lots tested.
cannot_establish: How the strips perform on real street samples or mixtures (none tested, as the authors state), with other brands, lots or antibodies, with compounds outside the panel or at other concentrations, or when read outside a laboratory; nor any sensitivity or specificity in real use.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (laboratory standards). Analytes bought from Cayman Chemical, Cerilliant, Sigma-Aldrich and US Pharmacopeia (Table 2, AM pp. 17–18); strips from BTNX (Pickering, Ontario), with listed cut-offs and expiry dates in Table 1 (AM p. 16).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Panel chosen to represent common drugs, cutting agents, diluents and other compounds found in illicit samples; the authors say it is not exhaustive and that other compounds may matter regionally (Results and Discussion › Cross-Reactivity, 2nd paragraph, AM p. 7).
sample.demographics: Not applicable.
sample.attrition: None reported.
sample.selection_effects: One maker, apparently one lot per strip type (lot numbers not given); a panel of 79 chosen by the authors with only five benzodiazepines and three nitazenes; the xylazine strips carried a different antibody from earlier strips (Table 1 footnote, AM p. 16); expired strips were other lots with other listed cut-offs.

exposure.measurement: Strips were dipped in aqueous solutions of known analyte and concentration and read after 5 to 10 minutes, then photographed. All were competitive immunoassays: a test band meant negative, no test band positive, a test band clearly fainter than the control band 'faint negative' (possibly positive at higher concentration); a control band was needed for a valid test (Materials & Methods, 3rd paragraph, AM p. 3; Figure 1).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Concentrations as study conditions: limit-of-detection series between 1,000 and 0.05 μg/mL; cross-reactivity at High (1 mg/mL, or 0.5 mg/mL where solubility limited) and Low (0.01 mg/mL); positive controls at 1,000 μg/mL (10 μg/mL diazepam for benzodiazepine strips) (Materials & Methods, AM p. 4; Table 1).
exposure.polysubstance: No mixtures were tested (authors' fourth limitation, AM p. 11).

comparison.controls: The positive-control analyte for each strip type (Table 1) and pure water as the negative control.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. Not studied: real samples, mixtures, other lots or brands, longer heat exposure, use at high temperature, new cross-reactions after heating, and readers other than the laboratory staff.

outcomes.instruments: Visual reading (positive, negative, faint negative); approximate limit of detection; reproducibility; persistence of results after heat and expiry.
outcomes.validity_norms: No standard or certification exists for strips used in drug checking (Introduction, 4th paragraph, AM p. 2). The number of readers and whether they knew the analyte are not reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Cross-reactivity = a positive or faint result with a compound other than the strip's positive control (Table 3, AM p. 19).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; readers appear to have known the analyte.

analysis.effect_sizes: No statistics; results by strip. Approximate limits of detection (μg/mL): benzodiazepine 0.1 (diazepam and alprazolam) and 0.25 (bromazolam, flubromazepam); amphetamine 0.5; methamphetamine, nitazene (metonitazene), opiate (heroin) and xylazine 1; nitazene strips 5 for N-piperidinyl etonitazene and protonitazene; cocaine 2.5 against a listed cut-off of 0.2; fentanyl 0.5 heated or not (heat sub-study triplicates only; the ten-strip limit study excluded fentanyl). Heated xylazine strips needed 10 μg/mL. Expired strips: cocaine 2.5, methamphetamine 5 (in-date 1), fentanyl 0.25 (listed cut-off 0.02) (Results and Discussion, AM pp. 6, 9–10; Supplemental Tables not read).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Supplemental Tables 1–7 (solvent shares, full concentration series, reproducibility, extra xylazine analytes, heated and expired results) were not read; the main text summarizes them. Table 3 lists every positive or faint result, so compounds not listed gave clear negatives.
analysis.power: Not applicable; two strips per analyte and concentration in the cross-reactivity study, so strip-to-strip variation is not estimated.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In water, each strip detected its target from about 0.1 to 2.5 μg/mL; every strip type except xylazine reacted (positive or faint) with at least one other compound, mostly of the same class; the benzodiazepine strip never reacted to etizolam; acetonitrile above about 10% made benzodiazepine strips read falsely negative; heat changed little except for the xylazine strips, and expiry reduced sensitivity for methamphetamine and, relative to its label, fentanyl strips.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions say the strips were “reproducible, sensitive, and unaffected by storage in elevated temperatures” and that strips made for urine “generally work for identification of drug products” (AM pp. 10–11), although no drug product or mixture was tested, which the authors list as a limitation, and heated xylazine strips lost about tenfold sensitivity. The abstract says expired strips showed little to no change in sensitivity, while the text reports a fivefold loss for methamphetamine strips and about tenfold, against the label, for fentanyl strips (AM p. 10). Cross-reactivity was largely within drug class, as claimed, with exceptions (cocaine strips with MDA and N,N-dimethylpentylone; methamphetamine strips with phenylephrine).

timeline.event: Philp and Fu's review of colour tests, cited by this paper among presumptive field methods.
Green et al.: fentanyl strips on 210 police-seized samples (cited here among fentanyl-strip studies).
Laing et al.: the same maker's benzodiazepine strips in a drug-checking programme detected 50% of etizolam-only samples and 87.5% of samples with other NPS benzodiazepines.

Sisco et al. on an earlier version of the BTNX xylazine strip (cited here as a ChemRxiv preprint, reference 15; published as Sisco et al., 2024a, read in this round, card sc_sisco_2024a): that version cross-reacted with lidocaine; Shuda and Lam on xylazine strips, not read.
This study: first laboratory data on BTNX amphetamine, benzodiazepine, cocaine, methamphetamine, nitazene and opiate strips used on drug in water.

De Vrieze et al. (2024): two lots of the BTNX nitazene strip detected isotonitazene in all replicates from 2000 and 3000 ng/mL and 24 of 33 analogues, missing most desnitazenes; they relay this study's nitazene limits. Read in this round (card sc_de_vrieze_2024).

replication.where_it_stands: For four of the seven strip types (amphetamine, cocaine, methamphetamine, opiate) this is the only laboratory characterisation among the papers read. The nitazene-strip limits (1 to 5 µg/mL) are of the same order as those of De Vrieze et al. (2024) in another laboratory; the xylazine strip tested here is a later version than the one in Sisco et al. (2024a), from the same team; and the benzodiazepine-strip results on etizolam are consistent in direction with Laing et al. (2021), although a report relayed by Laing et al. found similar strips detected etizolam at higher concentrations. No study of these strips on real samples was available.

funding.funder: Not reported in the author manuscript read (no funding or acknowledgement statement). The first page carries a NIST disclaimer that commercial products are identified only to specify the procedure and that this implies no endorsement.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported in the author manuscript.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (four), the University of Washington and UCLA. The corresponding author also led the earlier xylazine strip study cited as reference 15. The published Forensic Chemistry version may carry statements absent from the manuscript.

what_would_settle_it: Testing of real drug-checking samples (powders, pills, residues and mixtures) on several lots and brands of each strip type against a quantitative laboratory method, read by people outside a laboratory, with a broader panel of new benzodiazepines, nitazenes and cutting agents, documented solvent shares, and longer heat exposure.

domains.note: Pure reference standards at chosen concentrations: a known-positive and known-negative panel of 79 analytes chosen by the authors and not exhaustive (five benzodiazepines, three nitazenes), with no street samples or mixtures (authors' limitation, AM p. 11). Applicability to drug checking is low.

Visual reading by laboratory staff who prepared the solutions and very probably knew analyte and concentration; the number of readers and any blinding are not reported. The positivity rule (no test band) and the limit rule (all strips clearly positive) were pre-specified, but faint-negative calls near the threshold are subjective. Acetonitrile, added to dissolve 30 (text) or 33 (Table 2) analytes, can itself make benzodiazepine strips read negative and slows wicking (AM p. 5), so High-concentration negatives for those compounds are uncertain.

Known content by gravimetric or volumetric preparation from four commercial suppliers, not verified analytically; for the acetonitrile-assisted stocks the effective concentration in the strip solution is less certain.

Every panel analyte was tested at both concentrations, but replicates differ by sub-study (ten strips per limit level, two per cross-reactivity cell, three in the heat and expiry studies); the fentanyl strip had no ten-strip limit study, only heat-study triplicates; expired strips were compared with their labels or another product, not with fresh strips of the same lot; the full results are in supplementary tables not read.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: QUADAS-2 is used because the study compares strip readings with the known content of prepared solutions (METHODS §5.3, test accuracy); the card was re-filed from in-vitro with the editors' adapted checklist in adjudication (27 October 2026), as METHODS §5.6(c) allows. The domain judgments were proposed by AI reader 142 (second reader) and checked against the author manuscript by AI reader 148, who reached the same judgments; the previous checklist's overall judgment was also high. The overall judgment follows the worst domains: an artificial panel of pure standards, and readers who knew the content. Citable for: which compounds made these BTNX strips react in water and at what approximate concentrations; etizolam's non-reaction with the benzodiazepine strip from 0.01 to 0.5 mg/mL; the solvent effect; the faint-negative result type; the risk of trace contamination; heat and expiry effects for the lots tested. Not citable for: accuracy on street samples, other brands or lots, or the statement that strips generally work for identifying drug products.

key_findings.finding: Approximate limits of detection (all ten strips clearly positive): benzodiazepine strip 0.1 μg/mL (diazepam; also alprazolam) and 0.25 μg/mL (bromazolam, flubromazepam); amphetamine 0.5 μg/mL; methamphetamine, nitazene (metonitazene), opiate (heroin) and xylazine 1 μg/mL; nitazene strips 5 μg/mL for N-piperidinyl etonitazene and protonitazene; cocaine 2.5 μg/mL, roughly an order of magnitude above its listed 0.2 μg/mL cut-off. All except cocaine were close to their listed cut-offs.
key_findings.locator: Results and Discussion › Limit of Detection, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1 (AM p. 16)

key_findings.finding: Acetonitrile at or above about 10% v/v made benzodiazepine strips read negative when a positive was expected (not seen with methanol); more than 10% organic solvent slowed wicking, and 2:3 acetonitrile:water stopped control and test bands developing, while methanol mixtures up to 3:2 still worked.
key_findings.locator: Results and Discussion › Effect of Organic Solvents on Test Strip Response, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Figure 2

key_findings.finding: All strip types gave correct positive and negative control results over four weeks and were still positive at their detection limits at the end.
key_findings.locator: Results and Discussion › Reproducibility, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Every strip type except xylazine reacted (positive or faint) with at least one other compound in the 79-compound panel. Amphetamine strips: positive with MDA and phentermine, and with MDMA and methamphetamine at High only; faint with high procaine. Methamphetamine strips: positive with MDMA (both concentrations), amphetamine and phenylephrine (High only).
key_findings.locator: Results and Discussion › Cross-Reactivity, 3rd paragraph; Table 3 (AM p. 19)

key_findings.finding: Benzodiazepine strips: positive with diazepam, alprazolam, bromazolam and flubromazepam (positives at Low only, because the High solutions held acetonitrile); no positive with etizolam at either concentration or at further concentrations from 0.01 to 0.5 mg/mL; faint results with high MDMA, amphetamine and metamizole.
key_findings.locator: Results and Discussion › Cross-Reactivity, 4th paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Cocaine strips: positive with benzoylecgonine (both concentrations) and with MDA and N,N-dimethylpentylone (High only); faint with high eutylone and nicotine. Nitazene strips: positive with all three nitazenes and nothing else. Opiate strips: positive with codeine and 6-monoacetylmorphine (both) and oxycodone (High only); faint with high ibuprofen and phenacetin.
key_findings.locator: Results and Discussion › Cross-Reactivity, 5th to 7th paragraphs; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Xylazine strips (an antibody different from earlier strips that cross-reacted with lidocaine): no positive or faint result with any other compound in the main panel, including lidocaine, levamisole, ketamine and medetomidine; of 14 further compounds, brimonidine, clonidine, romifidine and tizanidine cross-reacted at high concentrations.
key_findings.locator: Results and Discussion › Cross-Reactivity, 8th paragraph; Table 1 footnote (AM p. 16)

key_findings.finding: Compounds that gave clear negatives on all seven strip types (not in Table 3) include 2C-B, ketamine, deschloroketamine, LSD, Δ9-THC, Δ8-THC, cannabidiol, phencyclidine, dextromethorphan, methylphenidate, methadone, buprenorphine, naloxone, tramadol, fentanyl and its analogues, caffeine, lidocaine and levamisole.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (analytes); Table 3 (all positive or faint results)
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of Tables 2–3. For the compounds dissolved with acetonitrile (marked in Table 2), a negative at High concentration is less certain.

key_findings.finding: After two weeks unopened at 55 °C, all strip types gave correct control results; all but the xylazine strips were still positive at their detection limits; heated xylazine strips were faint at 1 μg/mL and needed 10 μg/mL; fentanyl strips detected 0.5 μg/mL heated or not; all known cross-reactions persisted, but new ones after heating were not looked for.
key_findings.locator: Results and Discussion › Effect of Elevated Temperature, 2nd to 6th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The fentanyl strip's 0.5 μg/mL comes only from the heat sub-study's triplicates: the ten-strip limit study excluded fentanyl (AM p. 6), so this limit is less robust than the others.

key_findings.finding: Strips more than four years past expiry gave correct controls; cocaine strips kept their 2.5 μg/mL detection limit; methamphetamine strips needed 5 μg/mL against 1 μg/mL for in-date strips; fentanyl strips needed 0.25 μg/mL, about ten times their listed 0.02 μg/mL cut-off. The expired strips had been stored in laboratory conditions.
key_findings.locator: Results and Discussion › Sensitivity Beyond Expiration, 1st to 5th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The in-date fentanyl strips (listed 0.2 μg/mL) needed 0.5 μg/mL, so the expired strips were not less sensitive in absolute terms (editors' comparison); but the listed cut-offs differ tenfold (0.02 against 0.2 μg/mL), so the two were probably different products or versions, and no in-date strip of the expired product was tested, so neither this comparison nor the authors' 'loss in sensitivity' isolates the effect of age.

key_findings.finding: Because of their sensitivity, trace contamination of a powder or residue in a reused container may give a misleading positive; the authors note a typical US banknote carries about ten times the cocaine strip's detection limit in 1 mL of water. No standard or certification exists for strips used in drug checking.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 4th paragraph; Results and Discussion › Limit of Detection, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Authors' limitations: organic solvents may have affected some results; the cross-reactivity panel is not comprehensive; cross-reactions may occur at higher concentrations than tested; no real samples or mixtures; heat exposure only two weeks. They call for a standard way to evaluate strips for drug checking.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 defines a mark for results seen only at Low concentration but uses it nowhere, although the text says the benzodiazepine-strip positives for alprazolam, bromazolam and flubromazepam occurred only at Low.
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 3 alone overstates those positives as concentration-independent.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 refers to Supplemental Table 3 for the extra xylazine cross-reactivities; the text cites Supplemental Table 4 for them and Supplemental Table 3 for reproducibility.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor cross-referencing error.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 30 compounds needed acetonitrile; Table 2 marks 33 (editors' count from the rendered table).
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of compounds whose High-concentration negatives are less certain is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports little to no change in sensitivity for expired strips, but the text reports a fivefold loss for methamphetamine strips and about tenfold, against the label, for fentanyl strips.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the text values, not the abstract.

reporting_issues.issue: No funding, acknowledgement or conflict-of-interest statement appears in the author manuscript.
reporting_issues.consequence: Funding and interests unknown from this version.

reporting_issues.issue: The authors attribute etizolam's non-reaction possibly to 'the presence of the thiazole ring' (Results and Discussion › Cross-Reactivity, 4th paragraph, AM p. 7); etizolam contains a thiophene ring (a thienotriazolodiazepine, as the authors also call it a thienodiazepine).
reporting_issues.consequence: The structural explanation is misstated; the etizolam result itself stands.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives a 2:3 acetonitrile:water mixture as the one in which wicking was incomplete and no bands developed (Results and Discussion › Effect of Organic Solvents on Test Strip Response, 2nd paragraph, AM p. 5), while the Figure 2 caption names the 1:1 and 3:2 ratios (AM p. 15).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the threshold at which acetonitrile stops strips working is uncertain within this range.

verification.source_read: PDF of the NIST author manuscript (pages 1–19, cited as AM p.), Forensic Chemistry 2024;40:100594, doi 10.1016/j.forc.2024.100594, saved as the project PDF folder DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/Cannabis/Sisco_2023_XylazineTestStrips.pdf: all text, Tables 1–3 (rendered to check marks), Figure 1–2 captions, reference list. The file name suggests sisco_2024a, but the content is sisco_2024b. Supplemental Tables 1–7 (PubMed Central web version) were not read.

disagreements.first_pass: in-vitro
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 142 (missed; risk of bias partly-agree): under METHODS §5.3 (0.3.1) this is a test-accuracy study against known concentrations; re-file it and appraise with QUADAS-2, as for sc_bergh_2021, with the reader's own domain judgments (sample selection high, index test high, reference standard low, flow and timing unclear; overall high).
disagreements.resolution: Re-filed as test-accuracy, as METHODS §5.3 requires for a test compared with known content and §5.6(c) allows for a re-appraisal with a different instrument. The adjudicator judged each QUADAS-2 domain from the author manuscript (AM pp. 3–11, 16–19) and reached the same judgments as AI reader 142; the overall judgment (high) is the same as the first reader's checklist rating. Because the adjudicator saw reader 142's judgments before checking them, the blind check that §5.6(c) asks for is listed for the senior author.

disagreements.first_pass: The schema has no design for an analytical study of test devices; 'in-vitro' is the nearest.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 142: as for design.
disagreements.resolution: Follows the re-filing.

disagreements.first_pass: Instrument none-applicable; domains: Strip and lot sampling (some-concerns): One maker, apparently one lot per type, lot numbers not given; expired strips were other lots with other listed cut-offs, so expiry effects are compared with labels rather than with same-lot fresh strips.; Analyte panel and preparation (high): Panel not exhaustive (five benzodiazepines, three nitazenes). Acetonitrile was added to 30 (text) or 33 (Table 2 marks) stock solutions; the paper's own side study shows it can make benzodiazepine strips read falsely negative and slow wicking, so negatives at High concentration for those compounds are uncertain; solvent shares are only in the supplement.; Reading and recording of results (some-concerns): Visual reading with a faint-negative category; number of readers and blinding not reported; strips were photographed.; Limit-of-detection and reproducibility design (low): Ten strips per level with an explicit all-ten-positive rule; positive and negative controls at five time points over four weeks.; Relevance to real samples (high): No street samples or mixtures (authors' limitation), so field accuracy cannot be inferred.; Reporting consistency and interpretation (some-concerns): Table 3 defines a Low-only mark it never uses; it cites Supplemental Table 3 where the text cites Supplemental Table 4; 30 against 33 acetonitrile compounds; the abstract and Conclusions say more than the results on expiry and on use with drug products; no funding or interest statement in the manuscript.; overall high; reasoning: No validated instrument exists for an analytical laboratory study of test devices (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used with domains adapted to this design, and the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. Citable for: which compounds made these BTNX strips react in water and at what approximate concentrations; etizolam's non-reaction with the benzodiazepine strip; the solvent effect; the faint-negative result type; trace-contamination risk; heat and expiry effects for the lots tested. Not citable for: accuracy on street samples, other brands or lots, or the claim that strips generally work for identifying drug products.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 142: re-appraise with QUADAS-2; own judgments: sample selection high, index test high, reference standard low (unclear for the acetonitrile-assisted and suspension stocks), flow and timing unclear; overall high, with high applicability concerns.
disagreements.resolution: Re-appraised with QUADAS-2 (METHODS §5.6(c)). The previous editors' checklist domains, kept here in first_pass, map onto the four QUADAS-2 domains; each was judged from the manuscript: sample selection high, index test high, reference standard low, flow and timing unclear, overall high, the same as AI reader 142. No overall judgment changed.

disagreements.first_pass: fentanyl and its analogues (on the opiate, nitazene, methamphetamine and xylazine strips),
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 142 (key finding 7, confirmed with a correction): per Table 3, fentanyl and its analogues reacted with none of the seven strip types, so the parenthetical restriction to four strip types is unnecessary.

verification.checked_by: AI reader 142 (blind second reading) and AI reader 148 (adjudication)

design_detail: Laboratory evaluation of one production lot of BTNX xylazine lateral-flow immunoassay strips (originally designed for toxicology, listed cut-off 1 µg/mL; lot number and antibody not given), used for drug checking. Four sub-studies: reproducibility (20 strips each on a 5000 µg/mL xylazine solution and on water, two per day over six weeks); approximate limit of detection (13 concentrations from 5000 to 0 µg/mL, 15 strips per concentration over four days); cross-reactivity (77 compounds including xylazine, each at 100 µg/mL in water, two strips each); and 100 drug residue samples swabbed from used paraphernalia in Maryland and Nevada, each tested with two strips against GC-MS/MS quantitation of xylazine, with DART-MS for the other contents. Filed as test-accuracy (METHODS §5.3, version 0.3.1): the units are standards and drug residues tested in a laboratory, and QUADAS-2 is used for the residue-sample accuracy component because it compares the strip with a reference standard (as for sc_green_2020). Read from the journal version (Drug Testing and Analysis, 2024, 16(9), 942–947, a short communication) and checked against the ChemRxiv preprint (version 2, posted 15 June 2023), in which no count or headline figure differs. The online supporting information was also read: Table S1 (all 100 samples) and the GC-MS/MS method with Tables S2–S3; the example photographs (Figure S1) were not read.
can_establish: For the one lot of BTNX xylazine strips tested: whether strong positive and negative controls gave consistent results, the approximate lowest xylazine concentration in water giving a consistent positive, which of 76 other compounds at 100 µg/mL made the strip read positive, and how often the strip agreed with GC-MS/MS on 100 residue samples from used drug paraphernalia.
cannot_establish: Performance on powders, pills or mixtures dissolved as in harm-reduction practice (higher concentrations, which the authors say could change cross-reactivity); other lots, brands or later versions of the strip (the authors cite one other lot of the same brand with similar results, not read; sc_sisco_2024b reports a newer BTNX antibody with a different cross-reaction pattern); cross-reactivity at other concentrations (only 100 µg/mL was tested here; the authors cite a prior study, not read, in which lidocaine also reacted at 10 but not at 1 µg/mL) or faint results caused by other compounds (not reported); whether lidocaine or medetomidine on its own changes strip results in real samples (in Table S1 both appear only in samples that also held xylazine); accuracy when people read strips outside a laboratory; any effect on behaviour or harm.

sample.recruitment: Samples, not people: 100 drug residue samples wiped with cotton swabs from used drug paraphernalia (syringes, plastic bags, wax bags and pill bottles) obtained in Maryland and Nevada as part of another project, and mailed to the laboratory individually in coin envelopes (2.4 Analysis of community-acquired samples, 1st paragraph, p. 943); access was provided by the Maryland Department of Health and the Southern Nevada Health Department (Acknowledgments, p. 946). Standards from Cayman Chemical, LGC Group and Sigma-Aldrich (Table 1, p. 944); strips from BTNX, Pickering, Ontario (2 Materials and methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 943).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: How the 100 residue samples were chosen from the other project (all, consecutive, random or selected) is not reported. Sensitivity and specificity used only samples with xylazine at or above the 1 µg/mL cut-off (n = 38) or none detected (n = 34); the 28 with xylazine detected below 1 µg/mL are presented without classification (2.4 Analysis of community-acquired samples, 2nd paragraph, p. 945).
sample.demographics: Not applicable (samples).
sample.attrition: None reported; all 100 samples appear in Table 2 (38 + 28 + 34, p. 945).
sample.selection_effects: Residues extracted from swabs and redissolved in water may give weaker solutions than powders dissolved as people do in practice, as the authors note (3.5 Limitations, p. 946); samples from two US states only; one production lot from one maker; the cross-reactivity panel was chosen by the authors.

exposure.measurement: Strips were used as the product insert specifies (reference 11) and read and photographed within ten minutes (2 Materials and methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 943). Competitive immunoassay: positive = control band visible and no test band; negative = test band the same colour as with water; 'faint negative' = test band visibly much weaker than with water (p. 943), counted as negative in the accuracy figures (3.4 Analysis of community-acquired samples, p. 946). The example photographs (Figure S1) are only in the online supplement and were not read. Two strips per residue sample; one sample (Sample 65, below 1 µg/mL) with one negative and one faint negative strip was counted negative (Table 2, footnote c, p. 945).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Concentrations as study conditions: reproducibility at 5000 µg/mL xylazine and water (2.1 Reproducibility, p. 943); limit-of-detection series at 5000, 1000, 500, 100, 50, 25, 10, 5, 2.5, 1, 0.5, 0.1 and 0 µg/mL (2.2 Limit of detection, p. 943); every cross-reactivity compound at 100 µg/mL only (2.3 Cross-reactivity, p. 943); residue extracts at whatever xylazine they held, each swab extracted in acetonitrile, dried and redissolved in water for the strips (2.4 Analysis of community-acquired samples, p. 943). GC-MS/MS detection limit 0.1 µg/mL and quantitation limit 0.5 µg/mL for xylazine, with values over 1000 µg/mL reported as '>1000' (Supporting information: GC-MS/MS method; Table S1, notes).
exposure.polysubstance: Standards were tested one at a time; no mixtures of standards. The residue samples held other drugs and cutting agents, identified by DART-MS, and GC-MS/MS also quantified 4-ANPP, cocaine, fentanyl, para-fluorofentanyl, heroin, methamphetamine and tramadol (2.4 Analysis of community-acquired samples, pp. 944–945), with results for every sample in Table S1 of the online supplement. There, DART-MS found fentanyl in 72 of the 100 samples and cocaine in 23; lidocaine appears in 4 samples and medetomidine in 2, all of which also held xylazine, and in none of the 34 xylazine-free samples (editors' count from Table S1). The authors saw no obvious competing compound in samples reading negative and no exceedingly high concentrations of other compounds (3.4 Analysis of community-acquired samples, p. 946).

comparison.controls: Water as negative control and 5000 µg/mL xylazine as positive control (2.1 Reproducibility, p. 943); GC-MS/MS quantitation of xylazine as the reference standard for residue samples, with the strip's listed 1 µg/mL cut-off as the threshold for an expected positive (2.4 Analysis of community-acquired samples, 2nd paragraph, p. 945).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable. Not studied: powders or pills, other lots, brands or versions, panel compounds at other concentrations, faint results from panel compounds, readers outside the laboratory, and the effect of lidocaine on real samples (in Table S1 it appears only in samples that also held xylazine).

outcomes.instruments: Visual reading of strips (positive, faint negative, negative), photographed (2 Materials and methods, p. 943); GC-MS/MS with tetracaine as internal standard for xylazine concentration (2.4 Analysis of community-acquired samples, p. 944), on a Thermo Trace 1310 gas chromatograph with a TSQ8000-evo triple quadrupole and a nine-point calibration from 0 to 500 µg/mL (Supporting information: GC-MS/MS method; Tables S2–S3); DART-MS to identify drugs and cutting agents qualitatively, by a method described in reference 13 (2.4, p. 943).
outcomes.validity_norms: The reference method's detection limit (0.1 µg/mL, signal-to-noise at least 3:1) and its quantitation limit for xylazine (0.5 µg/mL) are below the strip's listed cut-off; calibration curves were linear (R² at least 0.990) and check solutions stayed within ±5% (Supporting information: GC-MS/MS method). No standard for evaluating drug-checking strips is cited. The number of readers and whether they knew the GC-MS/MS results are not reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Expected positive = GC-MS/MS xylazine at or above the 1 µg/mL listed cut-off; sensitivity = share of those samples with a positive strip; specificity = share of xylazine-free samples with a negative or faint strip; approximate limit of detection = lowest concentration at which all 15 strips gave a clear positive; cross-reactivity = a positive with a compound other than xylazine (2.3 Cross-reactivity, p. 943; 2.4 Analysis of community-acquired samples, 2nd paragraph, p. 945; 3.2 Limit of detection, 1st paragraph, p. 945).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Residue samples: sensitivity 0.974 (37/38), specificity 1.00 (34/34), accuracy 0.986 (71/72), excluding the 28 samples with xylazine below 1 µg/mL (3.4 Analysis of community-acquired samples, p. 946; Table 2, p. 945). Editors' calculation (Wilson 95% intervals): sensitivity 0.865–0.995, specificity 0.898–1.000, accuracy 0.925–0.998; across all 66 xylazine-containing samples, 43 read positive (37 + 6; 0.65, 0.53–0.76). Limit of detection: 15/15 positive from 2.5 µg/mL up; 3/15 positive and 12/15 faint at 1 µg/mL; 7/15 positive and 8/15 faint at 0.5 µg/mL; 0/15 positive at 0.1 µg/mL and in water (Table 2, p. 945).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Table S1 (all 100 samples with DART-MS contents, GC-MS/MS concentrations and strip results) is in the online supplement, not in the article PDF; it was read, and its counts match Table 2 (editors' check). Cross-reactivity is reported only as the one positive (lidocaine); faint results with panel compounds, if any, are not reported (3.3 Cross-reactivity, p. 946).
analysis.power: Not applicable; two strips per panel compound and per residue sample, so strip-to-strip variation is estimated only in the limit-of-detection series.

interpretation_gap.results_show: For one lot of BTNX xylazine strips: consistent control results; a consistent positive from 2.5 µg/mL in water, above the listed 1 µg/mL, with mostly faint results at 1 and 0.5 µg/mL; a positive with lidocaine and with none of the other 75 compounds at 100 µg/mL, including the α2-agonists clonidine, detomidine, medetomidine, romifidine and tizanidine; on residues, 37 of 38 samples at or above the cut-off positive, none of 34 xylazine-free samples positive, and 6 of 28 samples with less xylazine positive (43 of 66 overall).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions call the strips "reproducible and sensitive" and cross-reactivity "minimal and limited to lidocaine" (4 Conclusions, p. 946); the abstract reports sensitivity 0.974, specificity 1.00 and overall accuracy 0.986 (p. 942). These rest on one lot, one cross-reactivity concentration with two strips per compound, and residues rather than powders, which the authors acknowledge (3.5 Limitations, p. 946); the headline figures exclude the 28 low-level samples, most of which read negative or faint, and a limit of detection 2.5 times the listed cut-off is called 'slightly higher' (3.2 Limit of detection, p. 945). The authors themselves stress that non-reaction with medetomidine and other α2-agonists could create a false sense of safety and that this highlights a need for comprehensive drug checking services (3.3 Cross-reactivity, p. 946).

timeline.event: Krotulski et al. (CFSRE), 'Evaluation of Xylazine Test Strips (BTNX) for drug checking purposes' (reference 10): an earlier evaluation of the same brand from a different lot, in the laboratory and on a small number of community samples; per the authors it found a lower limit of detection, lidocaine reacting at 10 but not at 1 µg/mL, and results similar to this study's; not read.

This study (ChemRxiv preprint, June 2023; Drug Testing and Analysis, 2024): reproducibility, limit of detection, cross-reactivity with 76 other compounds and 100 residue samples on one lot of the first publicly available xylazine test strips (BTNX).
Sisco and Appley identify the veterinary sedative medetomidine with opioids and xylazine in Maryland (reference 17), the basis of the authors' warning that strips miss it; not read.

Sisco et al., 'Beyond fentanyl test strips': BTNX xylazine strips with a different antibody did not react to lidocaine or medetomidine but reacted to brimonidine, clonidine, romifidine and tizanidine at high concentrations (per sc_sisco_2024b).

replication.where_it_stands: For the first publicly available BTNX xylazine strip this is the only laboratory characterisation among the papers read. The authors cite an earlier, smaller evaluation of the same brand from a different lot (Krotulski et al., 2023, reference 10, not read) that found a lower limit of detection and results similar to theirs, a 'preliminary indication of consistency across lots' (3.2 Limit of detection, p. 945; 3.5 Limitations, p. 946). The later NIST study of a newer version (sisco_2024b) does not replicate this strip: it found no lidocaine reaction but reactions with four other α2-agonist or related compounds at high concentration; both versions missed medetomidine. No study of either version on powders dissolved as in harm-reduction practice was available.

funding.funder: "Nothing declared." (Funding information, p. 942); no funder is named. The Acknowledgments thank the Maryland Department of Health and the Southern Nevada Health Department for access to the residue samples, and a NIST disclaimer says commercial products are named only to specify the procedure, with no endorsement implied (p. 946). The copyright line states that the article was contributed to by U.S. Government employees and is in the public domain in the USA (p. 942).
funding.declared_conflicts: "Dr. Sherman is an expert witness for plaintiffs in opioid litigation." (Conflict of interest, p. 946). No other interests are declared.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from NIST (first and corresponding author), the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health (four), George Washington University and New York University (p. 942). The first author also led sisco_2024b.

what_would_settle_it: Testing several lots and versions of xylazine strips on powders, pills and mixtures dissolved as people do in practice, against quantitative laboratory analysis, with cross-reactivity measured at several concentrations (including high lidocaine and newer sedatives such as medetomidine), faint results reported, and strips read by people outside a laboratory.

domains.note: 100 residue swabs from used paraphernalia (syringes, bags and pill bottles), taken from another project in two states; how they were chosen is not reported. Applicability concern high: residues redissolved in water may be weaker than powder solutions (3.5 Limitations, p. 946), and in Table S1 lidocaine and medetomidine appear only in samples that also held xylazine, so the residue component cannot show false positives from lidocaine or misses of medetomidine on its own.

Strips used per the insert, with reading categories defined in the Methods and results photographed (2 Materials and methods, p. 943); whether readers knew the GC-MS/MS result, and how many read each strip, is not reported; the rule for combining two disagreeing strips is stated for one sample only (Table 2, footnote c, p. 945). One lot of one maker.

GC-MS/MS with tetracaine as internal standard (2.4 Analysis of community-acquired samples, p. 944) and, in the online supplement, a nine-point calibration from 0 to 500 µg/mL (linear, R² at least 0.990), a detection limit of 0.1 µg/mL, a quantitation limit of 0.5 µg/mL for xylazine and check solutions within ±5% (Supporting information: GC-MS/MS method). Presence or absence of xylazine, and placement above or below the 1 µg/mL cut-off, are therefore likely classified correctly. Whether it was run without knowledge of the strip results is not reported, which matters little for an instrumental measurement. Judged unclear while only the article had been read; low again once the supplement was read.

All 100 samples had both tests, but the headline sensitivity, specificity and accuracy exclude the 28 samples with xylazine detected below 1 µg/mL, 22 of which read negative or faint; across all 66 xylazine-containing samples 43 (65%) read positive (editors' calculation from Table 2, p. 945). Swabs were mailed to the laboratory (2.4 Analysis of community-acquired samples, p. 943); time between collection and testing, and storage, are not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: QUADAS-2 is used for the residue-sample component, which compares the strip with a reference standard (METHODS §5.3, diagnostic accuracy); the design is filed as test-accuracy (METHODS §5.3, version 0.3.1). The overall judgment follows the worst domain: the reported accuracy holds only for samples at or above the strip's listed cut-off. The reference-standard domain is judged on the GC-MS/MS method in the online supplement. The analytical sub-studies are outside QUADAS-2: the limit-of-detection series is well designed (15 strips per level over four days), but cross-reactivity was tested at one concentration with two strips per compound, and faint results are not reported. Citable for: this strip version's consistent positive from 2.5 µg/mL in water, above its listed 1 µg/mL; frequent faint results near the cut-off; lidocaine as the only cross-reactant among 76 other compounds at 100 µg/mL; non-reaction with medetomidine and four other α2-agonists; 37 of 38 residue samples at or above the cut-off positive and none of 34 xylazine-free samples positive. Not citable for: powders or pills, other lots or later versions of the strip, cross-reactivity at higher concentrations, reading at home, or effects on behaviour or harm. Read from the journal version and checked against the ChemRxiv preprint: every count and headline figure is the same in both, and Table S1 of the online supplement matches the counts in Table 2.

key_findings.finding: Four sub-studies on one production lot of BTNX xylazine strips (originally designed for toxicology; listed cut-off 1 µg/mL): reproducibility, limit of detection, cross-reactivity with 77 compounds including xylazine, and 100 residue samples swabbed from used paraphernalia in Maryland and Nevada, each tested with two strips against GC-MS/MS.
key_findings.locator: 2 Materials and methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; 2.3 Cross-reactivity; 2.4 Analysis of community-acquired samples, 1st paragraph; single lot: 3.5 Limitations (p. 946)

key_findings.finding: The strip is a competitive immunoassay: a positive shows the control band and no test band; a test band visibly much weaker than with water was recorded as 'faint negative' and counted as negative.
key_findings.locator: 2 Materials and methods, 2nd paragraph; counted as negative: Table 2, footnote c (p. 945) and 3.4 Analysis of community-acquired samples (p. 946); the example photographs (Figure S1) are online only and were not read

key_findings.finding: Reproducibility: 20 strips on a 5000 µg/mL xylazine solution consistently gave clear positives and 20 on water consistently gave clear negatives, two strips per day over six weeks.
key_findings.locator: 2.1 Reproducibility; 3.1 Reproducibility

key_findings.finding: Limit of detection, defined as the lowest level at which all replicates gave a clear positive: all 15 strips were positive at every concentration from 2.5 µg/mL up; at the listed 1 µg/mL cut-off 3 of 15 were positive and 12 faint negative; at 0.5 µg/mL 7 positive and 8 faint negative; at 0.1 µg/mL and in water all 15 negative. The authors put the approximate limit of detection at 2.5 µg/mL, 'slightly higher than the listed cut-off and the LOD found in a previous study'.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Limit of detection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 2
key_findings.note: Editors' observations: 2.5 µg/mL is 2.5 times the listed cut-off; more positives at 0.5 than at 1 µg/mL (7 against 3 of 15) shows that results near the cut-off are inconsistent rather than graded (numbers checked on the rendered table).

key_findings.finding: The authors calculate that, at a dilution recommended for fentanyl strips in harm-reduction settings (reference 12), xylazine could be detected 'down to a level of 0.1% to 0.025% by weight', and say detection below 1% by weight of a powder is obtainable; they cite limited data from Canada and the United States (references 14 and 15, not read) in which xylazine was often at or above 1% by weight of samples. No powder was tested.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Limit of detection, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: at that dilution the 2.5 µg/mL limit corresponds to 0.0625% by weight and the 1 µg/mL cut-off to 0.025%, so the stated range does not follow from the limit of detection (the preprint gave 0.1% and 0.025% for two different dilutions). Reference 12 (Lockwood et al., 2021) is in the reference list.

key_findings.finding: Of 76 compounds other than xylazine, each at 100 µg/mL with two strips, only lidocaine gave a positive. No positive with the α2-agonists clonidine, detomidine, medetomidine, romifidine and tizanidine, the α2-antagonists atipamezole and yohimbine, brimonidine, fentanyl and six fentanyl analogues, 4-ANPP, heroin, 6-monoacetylmorphine, cocaine, benzoylecgonine, methamphetamine, MDMA, ketamine, PCP, LSD, THC, cannabidiol, AB-FUBINACA, eutylone, alprazolam, bromazolam, etizolam, three nitazenes, oxycodone, tramadol, methadone, buprenorphine, naloxone, levamisole, benzocaine, procaine, caffeine or the other cutting agents listed.
key_findings.locator: 2.3 Cross-reactivity; Table 1 (p. 944); 3.3 Cross-reactivity (p. 946)
key_findings.note: Table 1 lists 77 compounds including xylazine (editors' count on the rendered journal table: 9 + 2 + 7 + 34 + 20 + 5). Faint results with panel compounds are not reported.

key_findings.finding: The authors note that lidocaine is a common cutting agent, particularly in cocaine and occasionally in mixtures with fentanyl and other synthetic opioids (reference 16), and may give false positives; they cite a prior study (reference 10) in which lidocaine also reacted at 10 µg/mL but not at 1 µg/mL, and call for research on sample dilutions when lidocaine may be present. Medetomidine and other α2-agonists in the drug supply did not react and would not be detected, which could create a false sense of safety.
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Cross-reactivity

key_findings.finding: Residue samples: 66 of 100 contained xylazine above the GC-MS/MS limit of detection. Of 38 with xylazine at or above 1 µg/mL, 37 read positive and 1 negative (Sample 63, 2 µg/mL); of 34 without xylazine, 33 read negative and 1 faint negative, none positive; of 28 with xylazine below 1 µg/mL, 6 read positive, 10 faint negative and 12 negative. Sensitivity 0.974, specificity 1.00, accuracy 0.986 on the 72 classified samples.
key_findings.locator: 3.4 Analysis of community-acquired samples; Table 2 (p. 945)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: Wilson 95% intervals 0.865–0.995 (sensitivity), 0.898–1.000 (specificity), 0.925–0.998 (accuracy). Across all 66 xylazine-containing samples 43 read positive (37 + 6; Table 2 prints row totals only; 0.65, 0.53–0.76); 22 of the 23 that did not had xylazine below 1 µg/mL. The ≥1 µg/mL row label of Table 2 prints as '³1 μg/ml' (read on the rendered page).

key_findings.finding: The authors saw no obvious difference between residue samples reading positive and negative that would suggest a competing compound, and GC-MS/MS showed no exceedingly high concentrations of other compounds.
key_findings.locator: 3.4 Analysis of community-acquired samples, end of the paragraph

key_findings.finding: Authors' limitations: residues rather than powders dissolved as in harm-reduction practice, which may give higher concentrations and different cross-reactions; one production lot from one maker, with lot-to-lot variation found in other lateral-flow drug tests (reference 18); replication with other lots and makers recommended. They report that another study of the same brand from a different lot (Krotulski et al., 2023, reference 10) gave similar results, a 'preliminary indication of consistency across lots'.
key_findings.locator: 3.5 Limitations

key_findings.finding: The Conclusions say the strips were not responsive to other α2-agonists, so other veterinary sedatives could go undetected with strips alone; in residues they detected xylazine consistently above 2 µg/mL and only sporadically below.
key_findings.locator: 4 Conclusions

key_findings.finding: In Table S1 of the online supplement, lidocaine appears in 4 residue samples and medetomidine in 2, all of which also held xylazine; all 34 xylazine-free samples, which held drugs such as fentanyl, cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine, MDMA or ketamine, read negative (one faint negative). The residue samples therefore could not show whether lidocaine causes false positives, or medetomidine on its own is missed, outside the laboratory.
key_findings.locator: Table S1 (editors' count)
key_findings.note: Table S1 also shows that the two residues holding lidocaine with xylazine below 0.5 µg/mL (samples 6 and 12) read faint negative on both strips, so lidocaine did not turn these residues positive; how much lidocaine they held is unknown, since DART-MS is qualitative.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives '>1 μg/ml' for the 38 samples used for sensitivity (2.4 Analysis of community-acquired samples, p. 945; 3.4, p. 946), although 2.4 also defines an expected positive as 'at or above' the cut-off, and '<1 μg/ml' for those left out; the matching row label of Table 2 prints '³1 μg/ml', evidently ≥1 (read on the rendered page). 3.2 also gives the two lowest levels as '0.1 and 0 mg/ml', which Table 2 lists in µg/mL.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: by the text's signs a sample at exactly 1 µg/mL would fall in neither group; the counts (38, 28, 34) are the same throughout.

reporting_issues.issue: The range '0.1% to 0.025% by weight' does not follow from the 2.5 µg/mL limit at the one dilution cited: there the limit corresponds to 0.0625%, and 0.025% corresponds to the 1 µg/mL cut-off, which the strip did not reach consistently (editors' arithmetic). The preprint gave the two figures for two dilutions.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; detection in powder terms is untested either way, and the lower figure overstates what the tested limit supports.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports cross-reactivity 'against 77 commonly encountered drugs, cutting agents, and other structurally similar compounds', and 2.3 Cross-reactivity a panel of '77 different compounds', but the 77 include xylazine itself (Table 1); 76 other compounds were tested.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite 76 other compounds.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 files etomidate, metamizole and tolazoline under α2-agonists, although they are not usually classed as α2-adrenergic agonists (editors' note); the α2-agonists in the panel are clonidine, detomidine, medetomidine, romifidine and tizanidine, plus brimonidine listed as structurally similar.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; no result changes.

reporting_issues.issue: Cross-reactivity is reported only as positives; whether any compound gave a faint result, as xylazine did near the cut-off, is not stated. The rule for combining two strips that disagreed is given for one residue sample only (Sample 65, Table 2, footnote c).
reporting_issues.consequence: Faint-line effects of cutting agents and the handling of discordant strip pairs are unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The supplement's method text says that concentrations below 1 µg/mL were reported as less than 1 µg/mL, but Table S1 gives xylazine values of 0.5 and below 0.5 µg/mL; its notes give a quantitation limit of 0.5 µg/mL for xylazine and 1 µg/mL for the other compounds (5 µg/mL for heroin). reporting_issues.page: Supporting information: GC-MS/MS method; Table S1
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the split of samples above and below 1 µg/mL is unaffected; the DART-MS lists are qualitative and can miss compounds that GC-MS/MS quantifies.
