design_detail: Short report from the South Atlantic Fentanyl Test Strip Study (SAFTSS): a three-wave prospective cohort of people who inject drugs recruited at two syringe services programmes in rural west-central North Carolina (Appalachian foothills) and north-central West Virginia, baseline June 2021 to March 2022, with follow-up surveys at 6 and 12 months; it extends the baseline report (Zibbell et al., 2024; not read). Outcome: self-reported past-30-day fentanyl test strip (FTS) use at each wave, modelled with mixed-effects logistic regression (subject-specific random intercept) on survey wave, time-invariant covariates and time-varying characteristics, in all 541 baseline participants (1081 observations) and in the 212 who completed both follow-ups (636 observations), with gender-interaction models. FTS use is the outcome here, not an intervention given or compared, so ROBINS-E is used (exposures: witnessing an overdose, housing, drug use, opioid preference) rather than ROBINS-I; the decline across waves is a within-cohort trend, appraised for attrition and for changes over calendar time.
can_establish: Whether self-reported past-30-day fentanyl test strip use changed over 12 months in a cohort of rural people who inject drugs attending two syringe services programmes, recruited in 2021–2022, and which characteristics (witnessing an overdose, being unhoused, heroin use, marital status) were associated with use.
cannot_establish: Why use fell (fentanyl saturation of the market, test-strip supply, contact with services and perceived risk were not measured), whether witnessing an overdose motivates testing (a self-reported association open to confounding by service contact), whether testing changed behaviour or prevented overdose (not studied), or how common use was at each wave (not given in the main text).

sample.recruitment: Community: purposive recruitment by direct intercept of people receiving services at two syringe services programmes, one in North Carolina and one in West Virginia (Olive Branch Ministry and Milan Puskar Health Right, named in the acknowledgements) (Methods, 1st paragraph, p. 2; Acknowledgments, p. 4).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 or older, injected drugs in the past 30 days, proficient in English and willing to share contact information for follow-up (Methods, 1st paragraph, p. 2). No exclusions are reported.
sample.demographics: Full sample at baseline (Table 1, p. 2): mean age 38.8 (SD 9.5); 210 women (38.8%); 98 non-White (18.1%); 168 (31.1%) recruited in West Virginia; 390 (72.1%) with a high school degree; 102 (18.9%) married or living as married; 288 (53.2%) currently unhoused; past-30-day use of methamphetamine 466 (86.1%), heroin 384 (71%) and fentanyl 247 (45.7%). For the complete-case sample the text gives 69% North Carolina, 39% women, 91% non-Hispanic White, 69% at least a high school education and 60% unhoused (Results › Descriptive findings, 1st paragraph), which conflicts with Table 1 on race and education (see reporting issues).
sample.attrition: Of 541, 328 (60.6%) completed at least one follow-up and 212 (39.2%) both; 213 (39.4%) had no follow-up (editors' percentages). Compared with the complete-case sample, the 213 without follow-up had less often witnessed an overdose (56.8% against 69.8%) and less often used FTS (54.3% against 65.1%, lifetime use at baseline), and were less likely to be married (Discussion, 8th paragraph, p. 3); the same phrase also lists being unhoused (read literally, also less likely), without figures. Attrition statistics are in the supplement (not read).
sample.selection_effects: A convenience sample of people already in contact with two rural syringe services programmes; how participants obtained test strips, and whether supply changed during follow-up, is not described. People outside services are not represented. Follow-up retained people more engaged with harm reduction (more lifetime FTS use, more witnessed overdoses), which may bias the trend and the associations. The authors note that findings may not generalise beyond the two programmes or beyond participants who stayed engaged (Discussion, 8th paragraph, p. 3).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported at each survey wave (survey mode not stated in this report): past-6-month witnessing of an overdose and own overdose; current housing; past-30-day use (yes or no) of fentanyl, heroin, methamphetamine, crack and powder cocaine; injections per day; preference for heroin or fentanyl; access to heroin not containing fentanyl; plus sex, age, race/ethnicity, high school degree, marital status, state and enrolment quarter (Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 2; Table 1). No biological verification.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Injection drug use in the past 30 days was an eligibility criterion; mean injections per day at baseline 5.6 (SD 8) in the full sample (Table 1). Reported as study characteristics only.
exposure.polysubstance: Past-30-day use of methamphetamine, heroin, fentanyl, crack and powder cocaine entered the model as separate time-varying covariates; 86.1% reported methamphetamine use at baseline (Table 1). Whether drugs reported as heroin contained fentanyl was not tested; the authors suggest some participants may wrongly believe they use heroin (Discussion, 6th paragraph, p. 3).

comparison.controls: No unexposed control group. Comparisons are between survey waves within the cohort and between participants with and without each characteristic, all entered in one model.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not measured or not reported: how often participants used the syringe services programmes and whether they were given test strips during follow-up; perceived risk of fentanyl and reasons for testing or not testing; social networks; mental health; what participants' drugs contained. The authors' explanations (fentanyl saturation, perceived risk of adulteration) rest on variables that are not in the model.

outcomes.instruments: Self-reported past-30-day FTS use (yes or no) at baseline, 6 and 12 months; lifetime FTS use is also given descriptively for complete cases (Results › Descriptive findings, 3rd paragraph, pp. 2–3).
outcomes.validity_norms: A single self-reported item, not verified; the survey instrument is not described in this report (the baseline paper, not read, describes the survey).
outcomes.operationalization: Any FTS use in the past 30 days. How often people tested, what results they got and what they did after a result were not analysed.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; about 19 coefficients per model in two samples, plus gender-interaction models from which three significant differences are reported.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (self-report).

analysis.effect_sizes: Adjusted odds ratios from mixed-effects logistic regression, full sample then complete cases (Table 1, p. 2): 12-month wave 0.642 (95% CI 0.447–0.923) and 0.557 (0.364–0.853); 6-month wave 0.936 (0.696–1.258) and 0.946 (0.650–1.375); witnessed an overdose in the past 6 months 2.444 (1.784–3.347) and 2.257 (1.529–3.334); currently unhoused 0.679 (0.504–0.913) and 0.611 (0.410–0.909); past-30-day heroin use 1.615 (1.107–2.357) and 1.891 (1.178–3.036); married or living as married 1.521 (1.084–2.134) and 1.608 (1.073–2.410); enrolment quarter 0.793 (0.674–0.932) and 0.825 (0.670–1.015); preferring fentanyl over heroin 0.775 (0.564–1.067) and 0.662 (0.440–0.996); own overdose 0.981 (0.676–1.424) and 0.712 (0.416–1.218). The odds ratios are conditional on the random intercept; no predicted probabilities or wave-specific percentages of past-30-day use are printed in the main text, and the gender-interaction estimates are in the supplement (not read).
analysis.covariates: Survey wave; sex, age, race/ethnicity, high school degree, marital status and state; enrolment quarter (in Table 1, not in the Methods list); time-varying housing, past-30-day use of five drugs, injections per day, own and witnessed overdose, opioid preference and access to heroin without fentanyl, all in one model (Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 2).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or analysis plan is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The prevalence of the primary outcome at each wave, the gender-interaction estimates and the attrition statistics are not in the main text (supplement not read). The Methods say Table 1 shows the direction and significance of the stratified results, which it does not.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation is reported; several intervals in the complete-case sample are wide (for example non-White 0.270–1.337).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 541 rural people who inject drugs, the odds of past-30-day FTS use were lower at 12 months than at baseline (aOR 0.642; complete cases 0.557) but not at 6 months (0.936; 0.946). Witnessing an overdose (2.444; 2.257), heroin use (1.615; 1.891) and being married were associated with higher odds, and being unhoused with lower odds (0.679; 0.611); own overdose, fentanyl use and access to heroin were not associated. Lifetime FTS use among complete cases rose from 65.1% to 79.7%.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes on “declines in FTS use amongst the SAFTSS cohort at six and 12 months” (p. 1), but the 6-month odds ratios are close to 1 with intervals including 1. It calls direct exposure to overdose a key motivator for engaging with harm reduction (p. 1), a causal reading of a self-reported association that could equally reflect contact with services, social networks or reverse ordering. The Discussion describes a decline across all demographic groups (only gender was examined), attributes it to the reduced value of testing for fentanyl in a fentanyl-saturated market rather than to unwillingness, and says FTS use is driven by perceived risk of adulteration (p. 3): reasons for testing and perceived risk were not measured.

timeline.event: Krieger et al.: cited for FTS prompting risk reduction such as using less and not using alone; not read.
Peiper et al., an earlier North Carolina study with the last author: cited for five-fold higher odds of safer use after a positive result; not read.
SAFTSS baseline data collection, June 2021 to March 2022.

Zibbell et al.: SAFTSS baseline findings from the same cohort, cited for fentanyl exposure being broadly presumed; not read. Kutscher et al. (2024), a scoping review read for this batch, relays documented FTS use of 1–80% (median 19%) across studies and more frequent use of drug checking among people who had witnessed an overdose in the past 6 months (one study).
This 12-month follow-up.

replication.where_it_stands: No independent longitudinal estimate of FTS use over time was found among the papers read for this batch; the baseline report comes from the same cohort and authors and is not a replication. The association with witnessing an overdose agrees in direction with the one study relayed by Kutscher et al. (2024).

funding.funder: US National Institutes of Health, National Institute on Drug Abuse: R01DA046444 (Dr. Zibbell, PI) and R01DA047334 (Drs. Zibbell and Feinberg, MPI) (Funding support, p. 4).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest (Declaration of competing interest, p. 4).
funding.affiliations_note: Three authors from RTI International and one from West Virginia University. The analysis extends the authors' own baseline report (Zibbell et al., 2024), and the introduction cites an earlier FTS study with the last author (Peiper et al., 2019) for the benefit of testing. A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A cohort of people who use drugs followed with high retention in markets with different degrees of fentanyl saturation, recording at each wave test-strip supply, contact with services, reasons for testing or not testing and what people did after each result, with overdose as an outcome, would show whether falling use reflects market saturation, supply or disengagement, and whether testing matters for overdose.

domains.note: Many measured characteristics are adjusted for, but likely common causes of witnessing overdoses, housing and FTS use are not measured: how often people used the syringe services programmes, whether they were given strips, social networks and perceived risk. Possible mediators (opioid preference, drug use) are adjusted in the same model. For the decline over waves, changes in test-strip supply or distribution are not described.

Witnessing an overdose, housing and drug use are self-reported over 6- or 30-day windows in the same interview as the outcome; reported heroin use may not mean heroin in a fentanyl-dominated market, as the authors suggest.

Convenience recruitment at two programmes where FTS are presumably obtained; the complete-case analysis keeps only the 212 who completed both follow-ups, who differed from those lost in FTS use and witnessed overdoses.
What the programmes offered after an overdose was witnessed, or during follow-up (strips, naloxone, outreach), is not described; repeated surveys about FTS may themselves prompt use.

213 of 541 (39.4%) had no follow-up and only 212 (39.2%) completed both; those lost had less lifetime FTS use and fewer witnessed overdoses. The full-sample mixed model assumes data missing at random, and the complete-case analysis (described as assumed missing at random) needs stronger assumptions, so neither addresses dropout related to unobserved FTS use; the bias most likely makes the decline look smaller, and its effect on the associations cannot be predicted.
Past-30-day FTS use is self-reported, unverified, by people recruited at services that promote testing, in the same survey as the exposures.

No registration or analysis plan; two analytic samples and interaction models, with three significant gender differences reported among many tests; the wave-specific prevalence of the outcome and the interaction estimates are not in the main text.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E is used because the paper estimates associations of exposures (witnessing an overdose, housing, drug use) and of time with FTS use; no intervention is compared. The overall judgment follows the worst domains (unmeasured confounding by service contact and strip supply; heavy attrition related to the outcome). Citable for: in this rural cohort of people who inject drugs, the odds of past-30-day FTS use were lower at 12 months than at baseline, not at 6 months; FTS use was associated with having witnessed an overdose, heroin use and stable housing; lifetime use kept rising while recent use fell. Not citable for: reasons for the decline, a motivating effect of witnessing overdoses, how many people used FTS at each wave, any effect of testing on behaviour or overdose, or generalisation beyond people in contact with these two programmes.

key_findings.finding: Design and flow: 541 people who inject drugs completed a baseline survey (June 2021 to March 2022) at two rural syringe services programmes in North Carolina and West Virginia; 328 completed at least one follow-up at 6 or 12 months and 212 completed both (complete-case sample); the models used 1081 observations from 541 people and 636 from 212.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Methods; Methods, 1st paragraph; Results › Descriptive findings, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome, past-30-day FTS use: lower at 12 months than at baseline in the full sample (aOR 0.642, 95% CI 0.447–0.923) and in complete cases (0.557, 0.364–0.853); no difference at 6 months (0.936, 0.696–1.258; 0.946, 0.650–1.375).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Table 1 (p. 2); Results › Model results, 1st paragraph (p. 3)
key_findings.note: The proportion of participants using FTS at each wave is not given in the main text (descriptive statistics at all waves are in the unread supplement).

key_findings.finding: Witnessing an overdose in the past 6 months was associated with higher odds of past-30-day FTS use: aOR 2.444 (1.784–3.347) in the full sample and 2.257 (1.529–3.334) in complete cases. Among complete cases, 69.8% reported witnessing an overdose at baseline, 62.3% at 6 months and 65.1% at 12 months.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 2); Results › Descriptive findings, 2nd paragraph (p. 2); Model results, 2nd paragraph (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Being currently unhoused was associated with lower odds of FTS use (aOR 0.679, 0.504–0.913; complete cases 0.611, 0.410–0.909), and being married or living as married with higher odds (1.521, 1.084–2.134; 1.608, 1.073–2.410). Later enrolment was associated with less use in the full sample (aOR per quarter 0.793, 0.674–0.932), not in complete cases (0.825, 0.670–1.015).
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 2); Results › Model results, 1st paragraph (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Past-30-day heroin use was associated with higher odds of FTS use (aOR 1.615, 1.107–2.357; complete cases 1.891, 1.178–3.036). No association with past-30-day fentanyl use (1.332, 0.948–1.872; 1.357, 0.879–2.095), access to heroin not containing fentanyl (0.989, 0.734–1.331; 1.157, 0.778–1.721) or own overdose in the past 6 months (0.981, 0.676–1.424; 0.712, 0.416–1.218). Preferring fentanyl over heroin: 0.775 (0.564–1.067) in the full sample and 0.662 (0.440–0.996) in complete cases. Nor was use associated with methamphetamine use (1.083, 0.712–1.649; 0.951, 0.537–1.684) or injections per day (1.009, 0.991–1.027; 0.979, 0.949–1.010); everyone injected, so only how often could differ.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 2); Results › Model results, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Complete cases over time: own overdose in the prior 6 months reported by 22% at both follow-ups; preference for heroin over fentanyl fell from 58.5% at baseline to 49.1% at 6 months and 40.1% at 12 months, preference for fentanyl over heroin rose from 6.6% to 26.4% at 12 months; lifetime FTS use rose from 65.1% at baseline to 77.8% at 6 months and 79.7% at 12 months.
key_findings.locator: Results › Descriptive findings, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Gender: estimates did not differ by gender except in three respects: women had a greater reduction in FTS use over time than men (p < 0.05 at both follow-up waves); the negative association with fentanyl preference was stronger among men (p < 0.05); and the heroin-use estimate was higher among men (p < 0.01 full sample, p < 0.001 complete cases). The interaction estimates themselves are not printed.
key_findings.locator: Results › Multivariable marginal effects of predictors on FTS use, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Attrition: compared with the complete-case sample, the 213 participants with no follow-up had less often witnessed an overdose (56.8% against 69.8%) and less often used FTS (54.3% against 65.1%), and were less likely to be married; the authors note possible bias if those lost differed systematically and that the convenience sample from two rural programmes may not generalise.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors interpret the decline as reflecting the reduced informational value of testing for fentanyl once its presence is expected, not unwillingness to check drugs; suggest FTS may now serve people dependent on fentanyl to confirm a purchase is fentanyl and avoid withdrawal; and call for strips that detect xylazine and medetomidine and for comprehensive community drug checking. None of these explanations was measured in the study.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd and 7th paragraphs; Conclusion

reporting_issues.issue: For the complete-case sample the text gives 91% non-Hispanic White and 69% with at least a high school education, but Table 1 gives non-White race 38 of 212 (17.9%) and a high school degree for 193 (91%); the text's 91% matches the table's education figure.
reporting_issues.consequence: The race and education make-up of the complete-case sample is uncertain; neither figure should be cited without this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say Table 1 shows baseline descriptive statistics, but several complete-case figures equal the values the text gives for 12 months, not baseline: witnessed an overdose 65.1% (text: 69.8% at baseline, 65.1% at 12 months), preferring fentanyl over heroin 26.4% (text: 6.6% at baseline, 26.4% at 12 months), own overdose 21.7% (text: 22% at follow-up).
reporting_issues.consequence: The complete-case column cannot be read as baseline data; differences between the two columns (for example past-30-day heroin use 71% against 44.8%) may mix survey waves.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's conclusion refers to declines in FTS use at six and 12 months, but the 6-month odds ratios are 0.936 (0.696–1.258) and 0.946 (0.650–1.375).
reporting_issues.consequence: Only the 12-month decline is supported.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say Table 1 displays the direction and significance of the gender-stratified results; it does not, and the interaction estimates are only in the supplement.
reporting_issues.consequence: The three gender differences reported in the Results cannot be checked from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says fentanyl preference was associated with FTS use in the complete-case sample only, without the direction (lower odds, 0.662), and then that opioid preference does not appear to influence adoption of FTS, although the complete-case estimate and the stronger negative association among men point the other way.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement that opioid preference does not matter is not supported by the paper's own estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: Enrolment timing (quarters since Q2 2021) is a covariate in Table 1 but is not in the Methods' list of covariates.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the model specification is incompletely described.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1–4 (journal version, Short Report, International Journal of Drug Policy 154 (2026) 105349, available online 29 May 2026), the project PDF folder DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/Fentanyl-and-analogues/rickson_2026_SouthAtlanticFTSLongitudinal.pdf: all text, Table 1 (checked on the rendered page), funding, CRediT, competing-interest and acknowledgement statements, reference list. The online supplementary material (gender-interaction models, descriptive statistics at all waves, attrition) was not read, nor the baseline paper (Zibbell et al., 2024).

disagreements.first_pass: Past-30-day heroin use was associated with higher odds of FTS use (aOR 1.615, 1.107–2.357; complete cases 1.891, 1.178–3.036). No association with past-30-day fentanyl use (1.332, 0.948–1.872; 1.357, 0.879–2.095), access to heroin not containing fentanyl (0.989, 0.734–1.331; 1.157, 0.778–1.721) or own overdose in the past 6 months (0.981, 0.676–1.424; 0.712, 0.416–1.218). Preferring fentanyl over heroin: 0.775 (0.564–1.067) in the full sample and 0.662 (0.440–0.996) in complete cases.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 145, missed item: injections per day (aOR 1.009, 0.991–1.027; complete cases 0.979) and methamphetamine use (1.083) were not associated with strip use; relevant to the answer on who tests ('more injecting'), which this study does not support.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after checking Table 1 (p. 2): values and intervals as now stated.

verification.checked_by: AI reader 145 (blind second reading) and AI reader 149 (adjudication)

design_detail: Laboratory analytical-performance study of one fentanyl test strip product across five manufacturing lots, on drug standards dissolved in water rather than on drug samples or people. Filed as test-accuracy (METHODS §5.3, version 0.3.1): the units are prepared solutions, and QUADAS-2 is used for appraisal, as for sc_green_2020, because strip readings are compared with known content. One laboratory (Department of Laboratory Medicine, ZSFG Clinical Laboratory, University of California San Francisco). Strips: BTNX Rapid Response fentanyl test strips with a 20 ng/mL urine cut-off (part FLY-1S48-100), a competitive lateral flow immunoassay; lots 082 and 004 obtained and tested in 2017, lots 018, 188 and 196 obtained in 2021 and tested in summer 2022 (lot 196 was the lot community advocates had reported as defective). Experiments: (1) lowest concentration read positive for fentanyl, 13 fentanyl analogues and the non-fentanyl opioid U-47700 spiked into water at nine concentrations from 10 µg/mL to 10 ng/mL (the Methods list; Fig. 1 also has a 50 000 ng/mL row), in duplicate on every lot; (2) cross-reactivity of 11 other drugs and cutting agents at concentrations up to 150 mg/mL where enough standard was available; (3) fentanyl in drug-free urine versus water on the three 2021 lots (1 µg/mL to 20 ng/mL, duplicate). Strips were read by eye by two people and recorded by consensus. No drug samples were tested, so no sensitivity or specificity can be calculated.
can_establish: The lowest concentrations at which five lots of one fentanyl test strip product, obtained in 2017 or 2021, read positive for fentanyl, 13 fentanyl analogues and U-47700 dissolved in water, and the concentrations at which pure d-methamphetamine, MDMA, lidocaine and diphenhydramine solutions gave false positives, in one laboratory.
cannot_establish: How often the strips are right with real drug samples (none were tested), whether the fall in fentanyl sensitivity between the 2017 and 2021 lots comes from manufacturing rather than from the separate testing rounds (2017 and 2022) or from storage, how mixtures, untested analogues, nitazenes or other cutting agents behave, how people prepare and read strips at home, or whether strip use changes behaviour or overdose.

sample.recruitment: Solutions, not people or seized samples: analytical standards bought from Cayman Chemicals or Cerilliant, diluted in analytical-grade water (Fisher Scientific) or drug-free human urine (Golden West Diagnostics) (Methods › Standards, reagents, test strips, 1st paragraph). The number of strips used is not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Opioids: fentanyl, the 13 most cited fentanyl analogues in the authors' description (the 11 that cross-reacted plus sufentanil and alfentanil) and U-47700 (Results › Fentanyl test strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph). Interference panel (editors' count, 11 as the authors state): heroin, 6-acetylcodeine, quinidine, cocaine, ketamine, diphenhydramine, lidocaine, MDMA, l- and d-methamphetamine, levamisole. Upper concentrations were limited to 10, 25 or 50 mg/mL for some substances by the amount of standard that could be bought (Methods › Interferences).
sample.demographics: Not applicable (solutions).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. No invalid strips are reported except several lot-196 strips with no control line at 50 mg/mL diphenhydramine (marked N/A in Fig. 2). No result for a drug-free water blank is reported.
sample.selection_effects: Every solution held one pure analyte at a chosen concentration, so the design is two-gate by construction (known positives, known negatives) and lacks the matrix of real samples: mixtures, several cutting agents together, undissolved powder, pills or residues. The 2017 and 2021 lots were tested in separate rounds (2017 and summer 2022), and the strips were donated through DanceSafe, the organization that had published the community warning about lot performance (reference 49), and by the San Francisco AIDS Foundation, with storage and expiry not reported (Methods › Standards, reagents, test strips, 1st paragraph; Funding).

exposure.measurement: Index test (Methods › Strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 1st paragraph): each strip immersed up to the maximum mark in the test solution for 10 s, laid flat on a clean surface, photographed and interpreted according to the maker's instructions within 5 min by two people independently, the result being recorded by consensus after discussion. The reading rule (which line pattern counts as positive, how faint lines were called) is not stated, nor how discordant duplicates were combined into a limit of detection. Blinding of readers to analyte and concentration is not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (solutions). Study concentrations: opioids at 10 µg/mL, 5 µg/mL, 1 µg/mL, 500, 200, 100, 50, 20 and 10 ng/mL in water; interferents up to 150 mg/mL where available; urine-water comparison at 1 µg/mL, 500, 200, 100, 50 and 20 ng/mL. The authors equate the opioid range to 0.5% down to 0.0005% fentanyl by weight in an assumed 2 mg/mL drug solution (Methods › Strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable: each solution contained a single analyte; no mixture of fentanyl with an interfering substance, and no real drug sample, was tested.

comparison.controls: Reference: the known concentration of purchased analytical standards spiked into water or drug-free urine; prepared concentrations were not verified analytically (for example by LC-MS). Whether the standards were solids or solvent solutions, and the solvent content of the test solutions, are not reported. On-label comparison: fentanyl in drug-free urine on the three 2021 lots, tested alongside water.
comparison.matching: Both rounds were run in the same laboratory space with the principal investigator present to keep methods continuous (Methods › Standards, reagents, test strips, 1st paragraph); whether the readers, standard batches and water were the same in both rounds is not reported.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to solutions. Not measured or not reported: strip storage, expiry dates and age at testing; any side-by-side test of a 2017 lot and a 2021 lot in the same round; individual reader calls (only consensus was kept); the rule for faint lines; how duplicates were combined; the concentration ranges tested for each interferent in the text (Fig. 2 shows that the 2017 lots were tested over narrow ranges only: diphenhydramine 150–50, lidocaine 150–25, MDMA 50–25, methamphetamine 10–2.5 mg/mL).

outcomes.instruments: Lowest concentration read positive (limit of detection) for each opioid and lot; lowest concentration of each other substance that read positive (false-positive threshold) for each lot; limit of detection for fentanyl in urine versus water. Per-lot values are shown in Figs. 1–2 and Additional file 2 (images).
outcomes.validity_norms: The maker's 20 ng/mL cut-off is defined for urine, and the authors show that water and urine differ (Results › Urine and water as test strip eluent comparison). The concentration steps were two- to fivefold apart (for example 200, 100, 50, 20 ng/mL), so each limit is known only to within one step.
outcomes.operationalization: Positive = strip read positive by the consensus of two readers at a given concentration; a limit of detection is the lowest step read positive for an opioid, a false-positive threshold the lowest step read positive for a non-target substance. No sensitivity, specificity or predictive values.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive; no statistical tests or intervals).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: No accuracy statistics and no sample-level counts are given, so the editors could not count true and false results or compute intervals. Text values: fentanyl in water detected down to 20 ng/mL with the 2017 lots and 200 ng/mL with the 2021 lots; in urine, 50 ng/mL (lots 018 and 196) and 100 ng/mL (the third 2021 lot). False-positive thresholds, 2017 lots: d-methamphetamine 5, MDMA 50, diphenhydramine and lidocaine 100 mg/mL; 2021 lots: d-methamphetamine 10, MDMA 2.5–5, lidocaine 2.5, diphenhydramine 0.5–1 mg/mL. Editors' calculation of the change from the 2017 to the 2021 lots: fentanyl limit 10-fold higher; thresholds 10- to 20-fold lower for MDMA, 40-fold lower for lidocaine and 2-fold higher for d-methamphetamine; no change can be computed for diphenhydramine, because the 2017 lots were tested only at 50 mg/mL and above (Fig. 2).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All five lots are reported for the opioids; the 2021 lots were tested only with substances already known to interfere plus levamisole, and only the 2021 lots were tested in urine. Per-lot values for analogues and interferents are given only as figure images. Additional file 3 (Table S1 A–D: estimated strip results for methamphetamine and MDMA samples with and without trace fentanyl at different solution concentrations) is a DOCX download and was not read.
analysis.power: No sample-size reasoning. Duplicate strips per step, consensus reading and no repeatability estimate mean that one-step differences between lots cannot be told apart from test-to-test variation. Two series in Fig. 1 are non-monotone (carfentanil on lot 018; acrylfentanyl on lot 196), so a single consensus reading per step can flip between adjacent concentrations.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In water, two lots obtained in 2017 (tested in 2017) detected fentanyl at 20 ng/mL and three lots obtained in 2021 (tested in 2022) only at 200 ng/mL; the 2021 lots also fell short of the maker's 20 ng/mL cut-off in urine (50–100 ng/mL). All lots detected 11 fentanyl analogues; none detected alfentanil or U-47700, and the 2021 lots missed sufentanil. Pure d-methamphetamine, MDMA, lidocaine and diphenhydramine gave false positives at mg/mL concentrations, at lower concentrations with the 2021 lots except for d-methamphetamine; heroin, 6-acetylcodeine and quinidine were shown negative only up to 10 µg/mL.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports “notable lot-to-lot variability in the sensitivity of the strips for fentanyl” (Abstract › Results), but within each testing round the fentanyl limit was the same for every lot; the tenfold difference lies between strips obtained in 2017 and in 2021 and tested in separate rounds, so lot, storage and round cannot be separated, and the Conclusion's call for distributors to disclose manufacturing changes points to a manufacturing cause that the design cannot establish. The Discussion presents the fall as matching other laboratory results of the period (1st paragraph), but Table 1 gives publication years, not testing years or lots, and limits of 25–200 ng/mL in no time order. It argues that community guidance to dilute stimulant samples to 2 mg/mL now leaves strips open to MDMA false positives (3rd paragraph), although the lowest MDMA concentration that gave a false positive was 2.5 mg/mL (Fig. 2 has no 2 mg/mL step for MDMA; at 2.5 mg/mL only lot 196 read positive and at 1 mg/mL none, so for MDMA the warning extrapolates); for diphenhydramine, whose thresholds (0.5–1 mg/mL) lie below 2 mg/mL, the argument holds. The Conclusion's 10- to 100-fold increase in sensitivity to diphenhydramine is not shown, because the 2017 lots were not tested in the range where the 2021 lots reacted (Fig. 2). The abstract's statement that the strips remain an important overdose prevention tool is not tested here.

timeline.event: Lots 082 and 004 obtained and tested (this study's first round).
Green et al. (2020): strip limit of detection 100 ng/mL, 2 of 2 analogues cross-reacted (as summarized in this paper's Table 1).
McCrae et al. (2020), British Columbia drug checking: strips missed fentanyl in 4 of 173 fentanyl-positive samples, all at 5% fentanyl by weight or less; cited in the Discussion, not read.
Bergh et al. (2021): limit 50 ng/mL, 25 of 28 analogues cross-reacted, no interference among the substances assessed; Wharton et al. (2021): limit 100 ng/mL, 19 of 29 analogues (Table 1); not read.
Lockwood et al. (2021): limit 25 ng/mL; false positives with methamphetamine, MDMA and diphenhydramine (Table 1); read for this batch (card sc_lockwood_2021).
Community notice (DanceSafe, 2021) that a recent batch of strips required different dilutions; lot 196 was the lot reported as defective (Background, 7th paragraph; reference 49); not read.
Park et al. (2022): limit 200 ng/mL, 13 of 17 analogues (Table 1); not read. Lots 018, 188 and 196 tested in summer 2022 (this study's second round).
This study published (18 January 2024).

De Vrieze et al. (2024) cite this study for fentanyl strip lots with limits up to ten times the maker's cut-off and ask for the same lot transparency for nitazene strips; read for this batch (card sc_de_vrieze_2024).

replication.where_it_stands: Fentanyl limits for this strip type range from 25 to 200 ng/mL across the independent evaluations in Table 1, which fits lot or method variation, but no paper read here tested old and new lots side by side in one round. False positives from methamphetamine, MDMA and diphenhydramine appear both here, with pure standards, and in Lockwood et al. (2021), with seized and retail material, at thresholds that differ by lot and method; among the papers read, lidocaine interference with fentanyl strips and the stereospecificity for d-methamphetamine are reported only here.

funding.funder: No specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors (Funding). The competing-interest statement adds that D.C.'s effort was supported by NIH/NIDA grants DA037820 and DA054190. Strips were donated: all lots except DOA2101018 by Emanuel Sferios in partnership with DanceSafe, a peer-based not-for-profit harm-reduction organization; lot DOA2101018 by the San Francisco AIDS Foundation (Funding; Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: J.H., L.L. and K.L. declare nothing to disclose. D.C. is a scientific advisor to Celero Systems and is retained as an expert by Motley-Rice LLC in ongoing opioid litigation (Competing interests).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the UCSF Department of Laboratory Medicine (ZSFG Clinical Laboratory) and Department of Family and Community Medicine. The strips came through DanceSafe, which had published the warning about lot performance, with Emanuel Sferios, who is thanked for his advocacy on lot-to-lot variability, the question tested here, and from the San Francisco AIDS Foundation; no support from the strip maker is mentioned. A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Several current and earlier lots tested side by side in one round with the same analytically verified standards, replicate strips and readers blinded to lot and concentration (with a repeatability estimate), strip age and storage recorded; and, for real-world accuracy, a blinded consecutive series of drug-checking samples, including stimulant samples and mixtures, tested on several lots against a quantitative reference such as LC-MS/MS.

domains.note: Artificial two-gate design: single pure analytes at chosen concentrations as positives and chosen non-target substances as negatives, with no real samples. Applicability to drug checking is low: no mixtures, combined cutting agents, residues or pills.

Two readers and photographs, but only consensus calls were kept; the rule for faint lines and the handling of discordant duplicates are not stated; reader blinding is not reported; high-concentration diphenhydramine strips with faint control lines were read as negative.
Known concentrations of purchased analytical standards, a sound reference for presence and amount, although the prepared concentrations were not verified analytically.

The 2017 and 2021 lots were tested in separate rounds (2017 and summer 2022) with separately prepared solutions and unreported strip storage and age, and not all lots met the same panel: the 2021 lots were tested only with known interferents plus levamisole, and only they were tested in urine.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: QUADAS-2 is used because the study compares strip readings with known content (METHODS §5.3, diagnostic accuracy); the design is filed as test-accuracy (METHODS §5.3, version 0.3.1). The overall judgment follows the worst domains: an artificial two-gate design and a lot comparison confounded with testing round. Within a round, the limits are credible laboratory values for pure analytes in water. Citable for: lots of this strip obtained in 2021 detected fentanyl in water at 200 ng/mL and in urine at 50–100 ng/mL, against 20 ng/mL in water for lots obtained in 2017 (tested in 2017 and 2022 respectively); all lots detected 11 fentanyl analogues, none detected alfentanil or U-47700; pure d-methamphetamine, MDMA, lidocaine and diphenhydramine gave false positives at the stated mg/mL concentrations, with thresholds that differed between lots. Not citable for: accuracy with real samples, a manufacturing cause of the change, heroin or other untested substances not interfering at realistic concentrations, or effects on behaviour or overdose.

preclinical.species_strain_sex: Not applicable: no organisms; the units are drug standards dissolved in water or drug-free urine.
preclinical.dose_route_schedule: Study conditions only: opioid standards at nine concentrations from 10 µg/mL to 10 ng/mL; interferents up to 150 mg/mL where available (some limited to 10, 25 or 50 mg/mL); duplicate strips; one 10-s immersion; reading within 5 min.
preclinical.resembles_human_use: Partly. The strips are the most widely available brand and were used per the maker's instructions, but laboratory staff tested pure single analytes in analytical-grade water; drug checking as described in the Background dissolves drug in water as prepared for injection, rehydrates residues or dissolves a portion of a sample, at concentrations that are unknown and vary (Background, 5th paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Five lots of BTNX Rapid Response fentanyl test strips with a 20 ng/mL urine cut-off (lots D607082, 16120004, DOA2101018, DOA2111188 and DOA2105196, called 082, 004, 018, 188 and 196) were tested in one laboratory: lots 082 and 004 were obtained and evaluated in 2017, lots 018, 188 and 196 obtained in 2021 and evaluated in summer 2022, in the same laboratory space with the principal investigator present at both rounds. Lot 196 was the lot community advocates had reported as defective.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Standards, reagents, test strips, 1st paragraph; Background, 7th paragraph
key_findings.note: Lot 004's number is printed as 16,120,004.

key_findings.finding: Fentanyl, 13 fentanyl analogues and U-47700 were spiked into water at 10 µg/mL, 5 µg/mL, 1 µg/mL, 500, 200, 100, 50, 20 and 10 ng/mL and tested in duplicate on each lot. Each strip was immersed to the maximum mark for 10 s, laid flat, photographed and read within 5 min by two people independently, with the result recorded by consensus. The authors equate these concentrations to 0.5% down to 0.0005% fentanyl by weight in an assumed 2 mg/mL drug solution.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Fentanyl in water: the two 2017 lots read positive down to 20 ng/mL, the maker's urine cut-off; the three 2021 lots only down to 200 ng/mL, ten times higher. Editors' calculation at the authors' assumed 2 mg/mL solution: 0.001% and 0.01% fentanyl by weight.
key_findings.locator: Results › Fentanyl test strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 2nd paragraph; Conclusion, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1 (image)
key_findings.note: Lot and testing round coincide: the 2017 lots were tested in 2017 and the 2021 lots in 2022.

key_findings.finding: All five lots cross-reacted with 11 fentanyl analogues: 3-methylfentanyl, acetyl fentanyl, acrylfentanyl, β-hydroxy-thiofentanyl, butyrylfentanyl, carfentanil, cyclopropylfentanyl, fluorobutyrylfentanyl, furanyl fentanyl, p-fluorofentanyl and tetrahydrofuran fentanyl. The 2017 lots also detected sufentanil and the 2021 lots did not; no lot detected alfentanil or U-47700 at any concentration tested, up to 50 000 ng/mL in Fig. 1 (the Methods list concentrations only up to 10 µg/mL); the 2017 lots detected sufentanil only at 10 000 and 50 000 ng/mL.
key_findings.locator: Results › Fentanyl test strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 1st paragraph; Methods › Strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1 (image)

key_findings.finding: Analogue limits by lot: compared with the 2017 lots, the 2021 lots had limits the authors give as 10 to 50 times lower for acetyl fentanyl, β-hydroxy-thiofentanyl, furanyl fentanyl and p-fluorofentanyl, and poorer sensitivity for acrylfentanyl (except lot 196), butyrylfentanyl and carfentanil (lot 018 better than the other 2021 lots but worse than the 2017 lots); 3-methylfentanyl, fluorobutyrylfentanyl and tetrahydrofuran fentanyl were about the same in all lots. The two 2017 lots did not differ; among the 2021 lots, analogue limits often differed by one to two dilution steps, most for acrylfentanyl, carfentanil and cyclopropylfentanyl.
key_findings.locator: Results › Fentanyl test strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 2nd paragraph; Conclusion, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Per-lot lowest positive concentrations from Fig. 1 (ng/mL; lots 004/082/018/188/196; figure read by AI reader 146 (second reader) on the full-size image and recorded in the saved text; not re-viewed by the adjudicator, as the browser was not available): 3-methylfentanyl 500/500/1000/1000/500; acetyl fentanyl 500/500/100/100/50; acrylfentanyl 100/100/500/500/100; β-hydroxy-thiofentanyl 1000/1000/100/100/100; butyrylfentanyl 100/100/200/500/200; carfentanil 500/500/1000/10 000/10 000; cyclopropylfentanyl 100/100/200/500/100; fluorobutyrylfentanyl 5000 on all; furanyl fentanyl 5000/5000/500/500/200; p-fluorofentanyl 5000/5000/200/200/100; tetrahydrofuran fentanyl 100 on all; sufentanil 10 000/10 000/none/none/none. The 2021 gain is 5- to 10-fold for acetyl fentanyl, 10-fold for β-hydroxy-thiofentanyl, 10- to 25-fold for furanyl fentanyl and 25- to 50-fold for p-fluorofentanyl (editors' calculation), so the authors' range is slightly generous. Two series are non-monotone: carfentanil on lot 018 (positive at 50 000, 10 000 and 1000 ng/mL, negative at 5000 and 500) and acrylfentanyl on lot 196 (positive at 100, negative at 200 ng/mL).

key_findings.finding: Interference, 2017 lots: no cross-reactivity with heroin, 6-acetylcodeine or quinidine at 10 µg/mL, or with cocaine or ketamine at 25 mg/mL; false positives with diphenhydramine and lidocaine at 100 mg/mL, MDMA at 50 mg/mL and d-methamphetamine at 5 mg/mL; l-methamphetamine was negative at 25 mg/mL.
key_findings.locator: Results › Fentanyl test strip interferences, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Heroin, 6-acetylcodeine and quinidine were tested only up to 10 µg/mL as printed, 200 times below the 2 mg/mL solution the authors assume (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Interference, 2021 lots (tested with substances already known to interfere, plus levamisole): lidocaine gave false positives at 2.5 mg/mL and d-methamphetamine at 10 mg/mL in all three lots; MDMA at 5 mg/mL (lots 018 and 188) and 2.5 mg/mL (lot 196); diphenhydramine at 0.5 mg/mL (lots 018 and 188) and 1 mg/mL (lot 196); levamisole showed no cross-reactivity up to 100 mg/mL.
key_findings.locator: Results › Fentanyl test strip interferences, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 2 (image)

key_findings.finding: With the 2021 lots, diphenhydramine at 50 and 100 mg/mL gave unusually faint control lines and extremely faint to invisible test lines, which the readers agreed to call negative; repeating the experiments gave the same result, and several lot-196 strips showed no control line at 50 mg/mL (invalid). The authors call these results paradoxical and unexplained.
key_findings.locator: Results › Fentanyl test strip interferences, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 2 legend; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Fig. 2 differs from the text in one cell: lot 018 is positive at 100 mg/mL, so the consensus negatives are at 50 mg/mL (lots 018 and 188; lot 196 invalid) and at 100 mg/mL on lots 188 and 196 only; at 150 mg/mL all three 2021 lots are positive again (figure read by AI reader 146 (second reader) on the full-size image and recorded in the saved text; not re-viewed by the adjudicator, as the browser was not available).

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculation from the reported thresholds, 2017 to 2021 lots, where both sets were tested at the relevant concentrations: the fentanyl limit rose 10-fold; the false-positive threshold fell 10- to 20-fold for MDMA and 40-fold for lidocaine, and rose 2-fold for d-methamphetamine. For diphenhydramine no change is shown: the 2017 lots were tested only at 150, 100 and 50 mg/mL (Fig. 2), and the 2021 lots also read negative or invalid at 50 mg/mL while positive from 25 down to 0.5–1 mg/mL. The Conclusion describes the change for diphenhydramine, lidocaine and MDMA as a 10-to-100-fold increase in sensitivity.
key_findings.locator: Results › Fentanyl test strip interferences, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Fig. 2 (image); Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Conclusion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Fentanyl in drug-free urine (the on-label matrix), three 2021 lots: positive down to 50 ng/mL (lots 018 and 196) and 100 ng/mL (the third lot, printed 118), better than in water tested at the same time (which reproduced the 200 ng/mL limit) but above the maker's 20 ng/mL urine cut-off; lines were visibly brighter in urine.
key_findings.locator: Results › Urine and water as test strip eluent comparison, 1st paragraph; Methods › Urine and water eluent comparison, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The per-lot results are in Additional file 2 (Fig. S2, a TIFF download), not read.

key_findings.finding: Table 1 summarizes five earlier independent evaluations of the same strip (publication year, fentanyl limit in ng/mL): Green et al. 2020, 100; Bergh et al. 2021, 50; Lockwood et al. 2021, 25; Wharton et al. 2021, 100; Park et al. 2022, 200. Analogue cross-reactivity: 2 of 2, 25 of 28, not assessed, 19 of 29 and 13 of 17 assessed; interferences were assessed only by Bergh et al. (none found) and Lockwood et al. (methamphetamine, MDMA, diphenhydramine).
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (separate HTML table page); Background, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The Discussion cites British Columbia drug-checking data (McCrae et al., 2020) in which the strips missed fentanyl in 4 of 173 (2.3%) fentanyl-positive samples confirmed by qNMR, all with fentanyl at 5% by weight or less, using sample solutions of about 30 µg/mL; 70% of those samples were expected to be opioids and 9% stimulants.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand; not this study's data.

key_findings.finding: The maker claims a 20 ng/mL cut-off for fentanyl and norfentanyl in urine and detection of ten named analogues; three of them (remifentanil, ocfentanil, valeryl fentanyl) were not tested here, and the 2021 lots did not detect a fourth (sufentanil).
key_findings.locator: Background, 5th paragraph; Results › Fentanyl test strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Authors' limitations: only 13 fentanyl analogues and 11 other drugs and adulterants were tested; reading line presence by eye is subjective; only consensus decisions were recorded, so agreement between readers (kappa) cannot be calculated; not all strip results are clearly positive or negative.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that the strips remain useful as part of an overdose-prevention cascade that should include more sophisticated drug checking, and call for independent assessment of each lot and for distributors to disclose changes in reagents and manufacturing.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Discussion; Conclusion, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: In the urine comparison the Results name the third 2021 lot 118; no lot 118 was tested (the 2021 lots are 018, 188 and 196) (Results › Urine and water as test strip eluent comparison, 1st paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the 100 ng/mL urine limit presumably belongs to lot 188.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusion summarizes the 2017-to-2021 change in false-positive thresholds for diphenhydramine, lidocaine and MDMA as 10-to-100-fold; the thresholds in the Results give 10- to 20-fold (MDMA) and 40-fold (lidocaine), while for diphenhydramine no change is shown, because the 2017 lots were not tested below 50 mg/mL (Fig. 2; editors' calculation) (Conclusion, 2nd paragraph; Results › Fentanyl test strip interferences).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the thresholds, not the summary range, and give no 2017 threshold for diphenhydramine.

reporting_issues.issue: Heroin, 6-acetylcodeine and quinidine were tested only up to 10 µg/mL as printed (Results › Fentanyl test strip interferences, 1st paragraph), although the Methods say high upper concentrations (150 mg/mL where available) were chosen, and the substances that interfered did so only from 0.5 mg/mL upward.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either a misprint or a much lower ceiling; either way the paper cannot be cited for heroin not causing false positives at the mg/mL concentrations of drug checking.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports notable lot-to-lot variability in fentanyl sensitivity, but within each round every lot had the same fentanyl limit (20 ng/mL for both 2017 lots, 200 ng/mL for all three 2021 lots); the difference lies between lots obtained in different years and tested in different rounds (Abstract › Results; Results › Fentanyl test strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 2nd paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should describe a difference between lots obtained in 2017 and in 2021 and tested in 2017 and 2022, not variation between lots of one period.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the strips were obtained from BTNX, while the Funding statement says all lots except DOA2101018 were provided by DanceSafe and lot DOA2101018 by the San Francisco AIDS Foundation; storage conditions, expiry dates and time from receipt to testing are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Deterioration in storage cannot be separated from manufacturing differences, which matters most for the 2021 lots, obtained in 2021 and tested in 2022.

reporting_issues.issue: The Funding statement says the work received no specific grant, while the competing-interest statement says one author's effort was supported by two NIH/NIDA grants (DA037820, DA054190).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; both are recorded under funding.

reporting_issues.issue: Testing was in duplicate, but the rule for combining discordant duplicates into a limit, the rule for faint lines and the individual reader calls are not reported (only consensus was kept), and no drug-free water blank result is given (Methods › Strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity; Discussion, 6th paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: Differences of one dilution step between lots may lie within test-to-test variation, which was not measured.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods list nine concentrations, from 10 µg/mL to 10 ng/mL, for the opioid sensitivity series (Methods › Strip sensitivity and cross-reactivity, 1st paragraph), but Fig. 1 shows a tenth row at 50 000 ng/mL.
reporting_issues.consequence: Negatives for alfentanil and U-47700 extend to 50 000 ng/mL in the figure, and sufentanil (2017 lots) and carfentanil (lots 188 and 196) were detected only at 10 000 ng/mL and above.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 2 shows that the 2017 lots were tested with the interferents over narrow ranges only (diphenhydramine 150–50, lidocaine 150–25, MDMA 50–25, methamphetamine 10–2.5 mg/mL), with lower concentrations marked not tested, while the 2021 lots were tested over wider ranges.
reporting_issues.consequence: Every 2017-against-2021 threshold comparison is bounded by these ranges, and the diphenhydramine comparison cannot be made.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the 2021 lots gave consensus negatives with diphenhydramine at 50 and 100 mg/mL (Results › Fentanyl test strip interferences, 2nd paragraph), but Fig. 2 shows lot 018 positive at 100 mg/mL.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the paradoxical negatives hold at 50 mg/mL on two lots (lot 196 invalid) and at 100 mg/mL on two of three lots.
