design_detail: Systematic review with narrative synthesis and no meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42018105366; reporting guided by PRISMA) of studies of drug checking services (DCS) that people who use drugs access voluntarily, across three domains: (a) influence of DCS on behaviour, broadly defined to include intentions and enacted behaviour; (b) monitoring of drug markets by DCS; (c) outcomes related to models of DCS, including barriers and facilitators. Eight databases searched from 1 January 1990 to 26 July 2018, with a full update on 16 October 2019, in any language; peer-reviewed articles, peer-reviewed conference abstracts and, for domain (a) only, grey literature. 90 studies included (54 articles, 19 conference abstracts, 17 grey-literature items), 79 of them cross-sectional or repeated cross-sectional. Risk of bias was scored with National Institutes of Health quality tools for 13 peer-reviewed quantitative articles on domains (a) and (c) only. Read for the senior author's question on whether testing changes what people do; the review does not address the accuracy of any testing method.
can_establish: What studies of drug checking services published from 1990 to October 2019 measured, where and in whom (mostly European services for people in party settings), and the range of reported intentions, self-reported or observed behaviour after results, drug-market findings, and barriers and facilitators to use.
cannot_establish: Whether drug checking or test strips change behaviour, prevent overdose or reduce other harms (no pooled estimate; mostly cross-sectional studies without a comparison group that measured intentions or self-report; 17 of the 31 behaviour studies are unappraised grey literature; one study linked intentions with overdose), the accuracy of any analysis method, test strip or reagent kit (not an outcome), or what happens when people test with kits obtained on their own (excluded by design).

sample.recruitment: Database search (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 1st paragraph): MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews and PsycINFO (all Ovid), Scopus, Web of Science (Science and Social Sciences Citation Indexes, two Conference Proceedings Citation Indexes, Emerging Sources Citation Index) and Dissertations and Theses Global (ProQuest), 1 January 1990 (when services proliferated) to 26 July 2018, full update 16 October 2019, any language. Subject headings and keywords for drug checking (including service names from a 2017 global review), controlled drugs and harm-reduction services, with no outcome terms; strategy developed with a library scientist and peer-reviewed by an outside librarian (PRESS); full strategies in Appendix A (not read). Reference lists of included studies were searched; grey literature on behaviour only, through Google, Google Scholar, service websites and content experts.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included (population, intervention, evaluation): people of any age engaged in non-medical drug use who voluntarily access DCS; studies in which a service was implemented, with no restriction on analysis method; original quantitative or qualitative data on any of the three domains; titles, abstracts and full texts translated as needed. Excluded: analysis of biological specimens; results not offered to clients; clients independently obtaining analysis methods rather than using a service; services not implemented (for example feasibility studies); commentaries, letters, editorials, reviews and unpublished conference abstracts (Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 2nd paragraph). Full-text exclusions: 30 not original research, 19 not drug checking as defined, 17 not on the domains (Results › Study characteristics, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Participants are not summed across studies. Included studies were published 1997–2019 (42 in 2017–19, 22 in 2014–16, 26 before 2014). By country (Table 2): Spain 30 (including 18 of the 19 conference abstracts), the Netherlands 19, Canada 9, United States 9, New Zealand 3, Portugal 3, multi-country 3, Australia, Belgium, France, Italy and the United Kingdom 2 each, Austria, Colombia, Slovenia and Switzerland 1 each. Table 1 lists 24 services, most serving people in party settings ('partygoers' in the studies); seven used fentanyl test strips, five of them US programmes that handed strips out for personal use (organizations in Rhode Island, the Syringe Access Collaborative, syringe services programmes in Boston and New York City, Urban Survivors Union).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level.
sample.selection_effects: 65 of 90 studies are from Europe and most concern services for people in party settings, which the authors say may not generalize to other people who use drugs (Discussion, 1st paragraph); 30 are from Spain, 18 of them conference abstracts. People who use drug checking select themselves: in three European studies DCS clients reported more frequent ecstasy use than people who did not use DCS. Grey literature was sought for the behaviour domain only. The authors name possible publication bias against studies without positive impacts, and the search ended in October 2019, two years before publication; they list 13 later articles (refs. 99–111).

exposure.measurement: The intervention is drug checking as each study implemented it (Table 1): mobile, fixed or postal sample collection; on-site or off-site analysis; or distribution of analysis methods (fentanyl test strips) for personal use. Methods range from reagent colour tests, thin-layer chromatography and fentanyl test strips to FTIR, Raman and UV spectroscopy, GC–MS, LC–MS, HPLC, LC-DAD and NMR. No restriction was placed on analysis methods, and their accuracy is not an outcome of the review.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable at review level. Samples covered MDMA, stimulants, psychedelics, depressants, opioids and NPS; 11 market-monitoring studies concerned MDMA only (Results › Drug market monitoring, 2nd paragraph).

comparison.controls: None at review level, and most included studies had no comparison group. The comparisons reported are within DCS clients (unexpected versus expected result; fentanyl detected versus not detected) or, in three European book-length cross-sectional studies, DCS clients versus people in party settings who did not use DCS (the review does not say they were at the same events).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not addressed in the synthesis: the characteristics that lead people to use a service (caution, risk perception, health literacy, frequency of use, contact with services) may explain both service use and later behaviour. In four studies 70% or more of people in party settings had not used drug-related services before, and 54% of the people who inject drugs in one US study were not syringe-programme clients (Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 8th paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: 55 outcome measures, coded inductively from the studies across the three domains (Figure 2, an image; domain panels 2A–C in a supplement not read). Most common: unexpected substances detected (50 studies), expected substances (44), NPS (40), drugs of concern (32), legal or no drugs (26), source of the sample (17); for behaviour, intent to use the analysed substance (13), influence of results on drug use (10) and disposal (8); for models, facilitators (11) and barriers (7).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not assessed by the review; its appraisal of 13 articles found an absence of clear, valid, reliable and consistently implemented outcome measures (Results › Study quality).
outcomes.operationalization: Behaviour was broadly defined to include behavioural intentions (in response to actual or hypothetical results; 22 studies) and enacted behaviour, observed by staff or self-reported from recall (16 studies). Concordance was coded as detection of the expected substance (alone or with another drug) or of an unexpected substance only (55 studies). Drugs of concern were fentanyl and analogues and other drugs that the included studies identified as causing harm.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: narrative synthesis without statistical tests; 55 is the number of outcome measures the reviewers coded (Results › Outcome measures).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Two independent reviewers screened titles and abstracts and full texts; extraction and risk-of-bias assessment were done in duplicate; conflicts were resolved by consensus with the last author, who triple-checked extraction and quality assessment for 10% of studies (Methods › Screening, data extraction and quality assessment).

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates: narrative synthesis without meta-analysis because of heterogeneity in methods, populations and outcomes. Individual-study estimates quoted in the text: an Australian festival service (n = 83, 2018; grey-literature report, ref. 35), OR 2.63 (95% CI 0.85–8.16) for changing the intention to use when results were unexpected; a US syringe services programme (people who inject drugs, n = 125, 2017; ref. 22), 43% changed behaviour, more likely when fentanyl was detected (aOR 5.08, 2.12–12.17); a Vancouver supervised injection site (n = 1411, 2016–17; ref. 41), intention to use a smaller quantity when fentanyl was detected OR 9.36 (4.25–20.65), and among those intending to use less, overdose OR 0.41 (0.18–0.89) and naloxone administration OR 0.38 (0.15–0.96). Proportions reporting that results affected their drug use: 16% (Netherlands, 1996), 50% (Austria, 1997–99), 87% (New Zealand, n = 47, 2018–19). Disposal: the four rates printed in the text, of eight studies with disposal as an outcome, range from 0% to 10% (refs. 22, 26, 27, 34); none is printed for the UK festival study (ref. 32, Measham, 2019).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable at review level; the covariates behind the one adjusted estimate quoted (aOR 5.08) are not given.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42018105366, registered in 2018 as 'The implementation of drug checking services for people who use drugs: a systematic review' (ref. 16). Declared changes: the drug-market outcome in the protocol was clarified and broadened during screening; outcome measures were not pre-specified but coded inductively; grey literature was reviewed for the primary domain only, and grey literature and qualitative studies were not appraised, for lack of resources. The PROSPERO record was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: Results of individual studies are only in Supplementary Tables S1–S3 (not read); the narrative quotes selected examples, prioritizing findings on behaviour and the commonest outcome measures (Results › Outcome measures). One example cited for a higher likelihood of changing intention has an interval that includes 1 (OR 2.63, 0.85–8.16).
analysis.power: Not applicable (no pooling). The studies quoted range from n = 20 (qualitative) to n = 22,280 (time series); sample sizes are not summed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: 90 mostly cross-sectional studies, 63 on market monitoring. Of the 31 behaviour studies, 17 are grey literature that was not appraised; 22 measured intentions, some in response to hypothetical results, and 16 enacted behaviour, mostly by self-report. Among people using a service, intentions not to use or to use less were more common after unexpected or fentanyl-positive results, and the four disposal rates printed (of eight studies with disposal as an outcome) ranged from 0% to 10%. One study linked intentions with overdose (OR 0.41 among those intending to use less); no study compared health outcomes between people with and without access to drug checking. The 13 appraised articles scored 3 to 7 of 14 points (cross-sectional), and the authors judged all of relatively poor quality.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that DCS “appear to influence behavioural intentions and the behaviour of people who use drugs” (Abstract › Conclusions) without mentioning the result of the quality appraisal, the reliance on intentions and self-report, or the absence of comparison groups. The Discussion says that “Strong evidence exists” that DCS provide a unique form of market monitoring (Discussion, 2nd paragraph), although no market-monitoring study was appraised. The Conclusions section and the limitations are more measured: an emerging evidence base on intentions and, to a lesser extent, enacted behaviour; studies not of high quality; the intention–behaviour gap; possible publication bias (Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Conclusions). The hedged verb and the absence of any claim about overdose or health outcomes keep the gap minor.

timeline.event: Barratt et al. (2018), a global review of drug checking services operating in 2017: 31 services in 20 countries (ref. 5, cited in the Introduction; not read).
Protocol registered in PROSPERO (CRD42018105366); search run to 26 July 2018.

Karamouzian et al. (2018): fentanyl drug checking at a Vancouver supervised injection site, the only included study linking intentions with overdose (ref. 41); read in this batch (card sc_karamouzian_2018).
Search update, 16 October 2019.
Laing et al. (2021), benzodiazepine test strips in community drug checking, named by the authors among articles published after the search (ref. 102).
This review published online on 2 November 2021 (Addiction 117(3), 532–544, March 2022).

Vickers-Smith et al. (2025), outside the review's dates: in a US cohort of 732 clients of strip-distributing harm-reduction sites, baseline strip use went with slightly more self-reported risk-reduction behaviours over four weeks and no clear difference in self-reported nonfatal overdose (adjusted RR 1.20, 0.70–2.06) (read in this batch; card sc_vickers_smith_2025).

replication.where_it_stands: A broad, multilingual systematic map of drug checking research to October 2019, including grey literature on behaviour. Its behaviour findings rest on intentions and self-report from cross-sectional studies, many unappraised, and it says nothing about test accuracy. Karamouzian et al. (2018), Peiper et al. (2019) and Krieger et al. (2018) are inside it, so claims must not count the review and those studies as independent support. Later primary studies are outside it; the one read in this batch, a prospective US cohort (Vickers-Smith et al., 2025), found associations with self-reported behaviour but not with self-reported nonfatal overdose, and like the studies in the review it cannot show an effect.

funding.funder: Support from the Canadian Research Initiative in Substance Misuse (CRISM), a CIHR Vanier Canada Graduate Scholarship (N.M.), a CIHR New Investigator Award (D.W.), a CIHR Fellowship (A.I.S.), an Ontario Ministry of Research, Innovation and Science Early Researcher Award (D.W.) and the St Michael's Hospital Foundation (Acknowledgements; the funding box lists CIHR, CRISM, the Ontario Ministry and the Foundation). The role of the funders is not stated.
funding.declared_conflicts: D.W. is a founder of DoseCheck Technologies, a privately held company seeking to develop drug checking instruments (Declaration of interests). No other interests are declared.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Centre on Drug Policy Evaluation (Li Ka Shing Knowledge Institute, St Michael's Hospital, Toronto), the University of Toronto, Unity Health Toronto library services, the University of California San Diego and Drexel University. The first author led the published protocol of a Toronto drug checking evaluation (ref. 6), the domains were prioritized with content experts and other stakeholders through CRISM, whose drug checking working group is acknowledged, and the corresponding author founded a company developing drug checking instruments. A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A comparative study of access to drug checking, including test strips handed out for personal use, against no access, among people who inject drugs or use opioids (cluster-randomized by site, or a prospective cohort with measured confounders), with enacted behaviour and objectively recorded outcomes (overdoses, naloxone administrations, emergency visits, deaths) rather than intentions.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population, intervention and outcome domains are specified (a population–intervention–evaluation framework), but there is no comparator, consistent with a descriptive question, and the outcome measures were coded inductively rather than defined in advance.

PROSPERO CRD42018105366; one change to the market-monitoring domain is declared and explained, outcome measures were not pre-specified, and grey literature was limited to one domain for lack of resources. The PROSPERO record was not read, so the timing of registration and the planned synthesis were not checked.
All designs reporting original quantitative or qualitative data were eligible; no reason is given for the choice of designs.

Eight databases, strategies in Appendix A (not read), PRESS peer review, any language, a justified 1990 start, reference lists, grey literature and content experts; but grey literature only for the behaviour domain, no trial or study registries, unpublished conference abstracts excluded, and the last search (16 October 2019) about two years before publication.
Two independent reviewers screened titles and abstracts (a record judged relevant by either advanced) and then full texts.
Extraction in duplicate by two reviewers with standardized, pilot-tested forms in DistillerSR; the last author triple-checked 10% of studies.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Counts by reason only (30 not original research, 19 not drug checking as defined, 17 not on the domains; 66 in all, matching 156 − 90). No list of excluded full texts appears in the article, and none of the supplements it describes (Appendices A–C, Tables S1–S3, Figure 2) is said to contain one; the supplements were not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: per-study details are only in Supplementary Tables S1–S3 (not read). The article gives the services' models and methods (Table 1), aggregate characteristics (Table 2), and design, country, year, n and population for the studies it cites.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: NIH quality tools for 13 of 90 studies only (peer-reviewed quantitative articles on behaviour or models), scored by summing the criteria met; none of the 17 grey-literature studies (over half of the 31 behaviour studies), the conference abstracts, the qualitative studies or the market-monitoring studies was appraised.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not extracted; the extraction form is described without funding.
Narrative synthesis without meta-analysis, justified by heterogeneity in methods, populations and outcomes.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No pooled results.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion states that the appraised studies were not of high quality, which may increase uncertainty, and names cross-sectional designs and intention measures (the intention–behaviour gap) as key limitations. A close call: the abstract's conclusion omits this, and the Discussion calls the unappraised market-monitoring evidence strong.

Findings are summarized as ranges, and differences between settings and populations are described (people in party settings versus people who inject drugs; Europe versus North America; use of results before or after use).
No quantitative synthesis; publication bias is named as a limitation (studies without positive impacts may be under-represented).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding is listed and one author's drug checking company is declared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 8 is recorded as no information because study-level details are only in unread supplementary tables; it is not a critical item and cannot change the rating. Two critical items are not met: no list of excluded full texts (item 7), and no risk-of-bias assessment for 77 of the 90 studies, including all 17 grey-literature studies that make up over half of the behaviour evidence (item 9); items 2 and 4 are only partly met, and items 11 and 15 do not apply. This rates how far the review's summary can be trusted as complete and unbiased, not its usefulness: it is a well-searched, multilingual map of drug checking research to 2019. Citable for: what drug checking studies measured and where; that most evidence on behaviour is intentions and self-report from cross-sectional studies without comparison groups; the range of findings (for example the four printed disposal rates, 0–10%); the authors' judgment that the appraised studies were of relatively poor quality; the barriers and facilitators reported. Not citable for: an effect of drug checking on overdose or other health outcomes, the accuracy of any testing method, or testing at home with kits obtained independently.

key_findings.finding: 2463 titles and abstracts and 156 full texts screened; 90 studies included (54 peer-reviewed articles, 19 peer-reviewed conference abstracts, 17 grey-literature items), published 1997–2019. Full-text exclusions: 30 not original research, 19 not drug checking as defined, 17 not on the review's domains.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results; Results › Study characteristics, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 2
key_findings.note: The three exclusion reasons add to 66, matching 156 − 90 (editors' check). The PRISMA diagram (Figure 1) is an image and was not read.

key_findings.finding: 65 of 90 studies (72.2%) were from Europe: Spain 30 (18 of the 19 conference abstracts), the Netherlands 19; Canada and the United States 9 each. Designs: cross-sectional 49 (54.4%), repeated cross-sectional 30 (33.3%), qualitative 7, time-series 2, longitudinal 1, case report 1.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study characteristics, 2nd paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Domains: drug-market monitoring 63 studies (70%), behaviour 31 (34.4%; 14 articles and all 17 grey-literature items), models of DCS 17 (18.9%; all peer-reviewed articles).
key_findings.locator: Results › Study characteristics, 2nd paragraph; Table 2, Domains rows

key_findings.finding: Behaviour outcomes: intent to use the analysed substance (13 studies, 14.4%), influence of results on drug use (10, 11.1%), disposal (8, 8.9%). Enacted behaviour, observed or self-reported from recall, was measured in 16 studies (17.8%); intended behaviour in response to actual or hypothetical results in 22 (24.4%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Refs. 31–37 are counted in both groups: 16 + 22 − 7 = 31 behaviour studies (editors' check).

key_findings.finding: Among people in party settings, a greater intention not to use the analysed substance was consistently reported when results were unexpected (8 studies) or 'questionable'/'suspicious' (3 studies). Example: an Australian festival service (n = 83, 2018; a grey-literature report, ref. 35), OR 2.63 (95% CI 0.85–8.16) for changing the intention to use when results were unexpected; similar findings in two Portuguese studies (n = 310, 2016; n = 100, 2014).
key_findings.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The interval includes 1, so this example on its own does not show a clear difference.

key_findings.finding: Proportions reporting that results affected their drug use: 16% (Netherlands, 1996), 50% (Austria, 1997–99) and 87% (New Zealand, n = 47, 2018–19) among people in party settings; 43% of people who inject drugs at a US syringe services programme (n = 125, 2017; ref. 22), more likely when fentanyl was detected (aOR 5.08, 95% CI 2.12–12.17). Qualitative and longitudinal studies of young adults in the United States (n = 81, 2017; refs. 31, 34) associated fentanyl detection with using less, using with others and other overdose-risk behaviours.
key_findings.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: All self-reported, with no comparison with people who did not test.

key_findings.finding: The only study linking intentions with health outcomes: at a Vancouver supervised injection site (n = 1411, 2016–17; ref. 41, Karamouzian et al., 2018), people who inject drugs more often reported intending to use a smaller quantity when fentanyl was detected (OR 9.36, 95% CI 4.25–20.65); those intending to use less were less likely to overdose (OR 0.41, 0.18–0.89) and to be given naloxone (OR 0.38, 0.15–0.96).
key_findings.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Checked against the primary study (sc_karamouzian_2018): the figures match, but 1411 is the number of drug checks by anonymous clients, not of people; the odds ratios are crude; the 9.36 is limited to checks made before use, while the overdose odds ratio of 0.41 pools checks made before and after use, with 113 of 120 overdoses recorded among post-consumption checks. The review repeats the association without these caveats.

key_findings.finding: Disposal was observed in 5 studies and self-reported in 3, and was more frequent when results were unexpected. Observed disposal among people at Canadian festivals ranged from 4% (n = 2078, 2015) to 7% (n = 2786, 2014); 10% of young adults in the United States disposed of the drug when fentanyl was detected (n = 81, 2017); 0% of people who inject drugs did so in another US study (n = 125, 2017). In qualitative work in Canada (n = 20, 2017–18), people using opioids were less likely than people using stimulants to intend disposal if fentanyl was found.
key_findings.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Selling after a result was measured in one study: 10% of young adults sold the substance after fentanyl was detected (n = 81). 58% of young adults reported giving fentanyl test strips received from a service to others (refs. 31, 34). In 4 of 5 studies most people in party settings intended to share results.
key_findings.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 6th and 7th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: In three European cross-sectional studies (Belgium, n = 486, 2006; the Netherlands, n = 285, 2002; Austria, the Netherlands and Germany, n = 702, 2002), DCS clients reported more frequent ecstasy use than people who did not use DCS; in the multi-country study, frequency of using DCS was negatively correlated with frequency of ecstasy use and unsafe party behaviour. Timing: 77% used DCS before use (Portugal, n = 310) and 49% waited for results before using (Colombia, n = 831); people who inject drugs mostly used DCS before use in two US studies (n = 125, n = 242) and mainly after use in the Vancouver study (n = 1411).
key_findings.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 8th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Market monitoring: concordance between expected and detected contents was reported in 55 studies (61.1%), 11 on MDMA only; European services reported increasing detection of NPS over time. Fentanyl or analogues were detected in 9 studies (Canada, Slovenia and Spain, 2016–19; the Netherlands, 2011), in 6 of them in samples expected to be other drugs, and none reported fentanyl as the expected drug. Other drugs of concern reported in five or more studies: atropine, DOx, levamisole and PMA/PMMA.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug market monitoring, 1st to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Facilitators (11 studies): concern about contents and health effects (the most common motive at a UK festival, n = 230, 2016; more often given in the Netherlands after a shortage of MDMA-like substances, n = 22,280, 2004–10), concern about fentanyl and overdose (US young adults, n = 81; people who use opioids, n = 55), distrust of markets and sellers, results given after use and return of the sample (for structurally vulnerable people who use drugs), central location, accurate and comprehensive results. Barriers (7 studies): lack of concern, trust in sellers, inaccessible location, limits of the results, legal risk under criminalization and anonymity concerns; legal and privacy concerns also deterred drug sellers.
key_findings.locator: Results › Outcomes related to models of DCS, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Study quality (NIH tools, one point per criterion met): 13 articles appraised; 11 cross-sectional studies scored 3 to 7 of 14 (mean 4.8, SD 1.2), one time-series study 5 of 12 and one longitudinal study 4 of 12. The authors judge all of relatively poor quality, with limitations from cross-sectional designs and from the absence of clear, valid, reliable and consistently implemented outcome measures.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study quality; Methods › Screening, data extraction and quality assessment, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Eligibility excluded studies in which people obtained analysis methods independently rather than through a service, results were not offered, biological specimens were analysed, or no service was implemented; test strips handed out by a service for personal use counted as drug checking (Table 1, 'personal use' collection model).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 2nd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Table 1 lists 24 services. Fentanyl test strips were used by seven: two Canadian services testing on site (ANKORS, BCCSU) and five US programmes handing strips out for personal use, to young people who use drugs, street-based people who use drugs, people physically dependent on opioids and people who inject drugs. Other methods were reagent tests, TLC, FTIR, Raman and UV spectroscopy, GC–MS, LC–MS, HPLC, LC-DAD and NMR.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study characteristics, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Authors' limitations: possible publication bias; timing of the search (13 later articles, refs. 99–111); studies of services not implemented were excluded; no meta-analysis because of heterogeneity; grey literature reviewed for the primary domain only; grey literature and qualitative studies not appraised; appraised studies not of high quality; cross-sectional designs and intention measures subject to the intention–behaviour gap; limited research resources and criminalization as barriers to research.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Authors' conclusions: market monitoring by drug checking is well established in Europe and increasingly in North America; there is an emerging evidence base on influence on behavioural intention and, to a lesser extent, enacted behaviour; research is needed on enacted behaviour, on linking behaviour with health outcomes, among people who inject drugs or use opioids, and with more rigorous designs.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions; Abstract › Conclusions

reporting_issues.issue: Drugs of concern: 32 of 90 studies is printed as 36.5% (Abstract › Results; Results › Drug market monitoring, 1st paragraph); 32/90 is 35.6%. Smaller rounding slips: 79 of 90 cross-sectional or repeated cross-sectional studies printed as 87.7% (87.8%) in the abstract, and 3 of 54 Portuguese articles as 5.5% (5.6%) in Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite the counts.

reporting_issues.issue: The Australian example given for partygoers being more likely to change their intention after unexpected results has OR 2.63 with a 95% CI of 0.85–8.16, which includes 1 (Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 2nd paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: The example does not support a difference on its own; the statement of consistency rests on the other cited studies, whose estimates are not given in the text.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract does not report the result of the quality appraisal (the Results judge all 13 appraised studies of relatively poor quality); and the Discussion calls the market-monitoring evidence strong although none of its 63 studies was appraised (Methods › Screening, data extraction and quality assessment, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: Read alone, the abstract and Discussion overstate how well appraised the evidence is; claims should cite the Results › Study quality paragraph alongside any behaviour finding.

reporting_issues.issue: The Vancouver study is described as a study of people who inject drugs with n = 1411, and the lower odds of overdose among those intending to use less is presented as the one link from intentions to health outcomes (Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 4th paragraph). In the primary study 1411 is the number of anonymous drug checks, and the overdose odds ratio is crude and pools checks made before and after use (sc_karamouzian_2018).
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims must not cite the review for an overdose benefit of intending to use less, nor for a sample of 1411 people; cite the primary study with its caveats.
