design_detail: Commentary (journal section Commentary, p. 31) on off-label fentanyl test strips used by people who use drugs outside supervised injection settings, read as a narrative review, as the topic notes direct. It covers fentanyl-related overdose, the licensing of strips and early figures from Vancouver, manufacturer and preliminary laboratory accuracy data, lessons drawn from colour-reagent self-testing of club drugs, open questions on use, effect, acceptability and reach, and a call for qualitative rapid-assessment research. No tables or figures; 64 references, 33 of them websites, news items, press releases, reports, a handbook, databases or a conference presentation (editors' count); no search strategy, criteria or synthesis. Received 30 January 2018, accepted 20 April 2018; open access.
can_establish: What was reported and claimed by early 2018 about off-label fentanyl test strips (licensing in Canada, manufacturer and preliminary laboratory figures, Vancouver programme figures, Health Canada's position), and which practical and ethical uncertainties the authors raise about self-testing outside supervised settings.
cannot_establish: The strips' accuracy (all figures are second-hand and of unstated method), whether self-testing changes behaviour or prevents overdose (no study cited tests this), or how often the harms the authors hypothesize, such as complacency after repeated positives, actually occur.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (commentary). The abstract says the authors review the evidence on off-label sensitivity and specificity, but no search, databases or dates are given.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated; sources chosen by the authors.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Selection by the authors. Every figure on strip accuracy, programme use and behaviour comes from non-peer-reviewed sources (the maker's website, the FORECAST preliminary report, DanceSafe, Health Canada, Vancouver Coastal Health press releases, news reports and a conference presentation), as the authors acknowledge when they note a lack of peer-reviewed evidence (p. 33). The club-drug evidence brought in (Murray et al., 2003; Quest & Horsley, 2007) concerns colour reagents and a drink test, not immunoassay strips.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable; strip characteristics as reported by cited sources (BTNX; FORECAST; DanceSafe; Health Canada).
exposure.polysubstance: The authors note that analogues can occur without fentanyl (O'Donnell et al., 2017, as cited), that strips give no amount, that acidifiers used to prepare brown heroin might affect accuracy (untested), and that contaminated injection equipment could give positives (Testing for fentanyl and fentanyl analogues, 4th paragraph, p. 33; Effect, 2nd paragraph, p. 34).

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable; accuracy figures as cited (accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, detection limit).
outcomes.validity_norms: As described: in Canada the strips are licensed as an in vitro diagnostic device for urinalysis and may be sold only to laboratories or health professionals, while the same strips are sold as a forensic test that needs no licence; drug-checking use is off-label (Testing for fentanyl and fentanyl analogues, 1st paragraph, p. 32).
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates. Figures as cited: the maker reports over 98% accuracy for fentanyl in urine; FORECAST preliminary data give the strips the lowest detection limit of three technologies (printed as 0.13 mg/ml), sensitivity 96% and 100% and specificity 90% and 98% at its two sites, with acetylfentanyl, furanylfentanyl and furanylfentanyl with heroin detected; a preliminary study found 7 of 70 samples gave erroneous or invalid results; at Insite 86% of all samples and 90% of ‘heroin’ samples were positive, 62% of checks were made after use, and on average 4.7 checks a day were made among about 600 daily visitors; press-release figures: people who checked before use and got a positive were 10 times more likely to reduce their dose, and those who reduced it 25% less likely to overdose; in a FORECAST survey of 256, 73% were moderately to highly interested in knowing whether fentanyl was present and 70% said knowing would change their behaviour; a GHB and ketamine drink test was 100% accurate in the laboratory and 65% (sensitivity 50%, specificity 91.6%) in lay hands (Quest & Horsley, 2007). Editors' calculation: 7/70 = 10.0% (Wilson 95% CI 4.9–19.2%); 4.7 checks among 600 visitors is about 0.8% a day.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. Figures favourable to strips (FORECAST, DanceSafe and UCSF, the press-release behaviour figures) are reported and then qualified; the harms hypothesized (complacency, positives being sought, unhelpful responses after a positive, contaminated equipment) are raised without data. The abstract omits the closing endorsement of strip distribution with guidance, naloxone and broader harm-reduction services (p. 35).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: By early 2018 the evidence the authors could cite on off-label fentanyl strips was a maker's claim for urine, one unpublished laboratory study with high sensitivity and specificity, Vancouver programme counts and press releases, and survey interest; none of it tested whether strip use outside supervised settings changes behaviour or prevents overdose. The situated-practice concerns (acidifiers, the two to five minutes a result takes, testing after preparation or on residue, positives being sought, no amount, contaminated equipment, reach) are hypotheses.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and the closing section draw attention to “the weak research evidence informing the use of fentanyl self-testing strips” (pp. 31, 34), which the cited sources bear out. Some statements go beyond their sources: that studies of club-drug self-testing “has demonstrated” limited value outside a package of services rests on one inventory report (EMCDDA, 2001; p. 33); that a considerable proportion of those at risk are less likely to engage with harm reduction is not quantified (p. 34); and evidence from MDMA colour reagents, which in Murray et al. (2003) rests on two testers and eight samples, is carried over to immunoassay strips without that caveat (p. 33). The abstract's statement that using drugs with someone who has naloxone is currently the most practical protection is asserted rather than compared. The paper ends by supporting strip distribution with guidance and naloxone (p. 35), which its title and abstract do not convey.

timeline.event: Winstock, Wolff and Ramsey's critique of ecstasy pill testing, cited here (read for this batch).
The evaluation of an ecstasy colour-reagent kit by Murray et al., cited here for poor accuracy with people unfamiliar with the reagents (read for this batch: two testers, eight samples).
Quest and Horsley's field test of a date-rape drug detection device, cited for the drop in accuracy in lay hands; not read.
Vancouver Coastal Health begins evaluating off-label strip use at the Insite supervised injection site on 7 July (as described).

Health Canada warns about false negatives and limits its endorsement of drug checking to supervised consumption sites; in November British Columbia extends strips to all its supervised injection sites (as described).
FORECAST preliminary report (Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health) cited; this commentary published.
Green et al. publish a laboratory study whose site-level strip sensitivity and specificity match the FORECAST preliminary figures cited here (per the project's first-pass card sc_green_2020).

replication.where_it_stands: The commentary describes the evidence of early 2018. Laboratory accuracy for one strip brand was later published (Green et al., 2020, per the project's card); none of the papers read for this batch tests whether self-testing outside supervised settings changes behaviour or prevents overdose.

funding.funder: Magdalena Harris is funded by the National Institute for Health Research [CDF-2016-09-014]; the views are the authors' and not necessarily those of the NHS, the NIHR or the Department of Health (Funding, p. 35). No other funding is stated.
funding.declared_conflicts: None (Conflicts of interest, p. 35). The Acknowledgements thank Kate Enright (UK-Med) and Shing Kwan Tse (BTNX Inc, the strip maker) for technical advice (p. 35).
funding.affiliations_note: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (McGowan, Harris, Platt, Rhodes), Save the Children UK (McGowan), Liverpool John Moores University (Hope) and the University of New South Wales (Rhodes). Six of 64 references are the authors' own (Harris, Forseth & Rhodes 2015; McGowan, Harris & Rhodes 2013; Rhodes 2009; Rhodes et al. 1999, 2007, 2016); they support the situated-practice argument and the call for qualitative rapid-assessment research, the authors' own field. Technical advice from an employee of the strip maker is acknowledged while conflicts are declared as none. A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective comparative study, ideally randomized by service or area, of fentanyl strip distribution with guidance and naloxone against guidance and naloxone alone among people who use opioids outside supervised settings, measuring what people do after positive and negative results, non-fatal and fatal overdose, and reach among people not in contact with services, with laboratory checking of a sample of tested drugs and qualitative work on how strips are used.

domains.note: The abstract says the authors review the evidence, but no search, sources or criteria are given.

The Insite figures (most checks after use, testing driven by suspicion) and the press-release behaviour figures (a small minority of visitors) are critically appraised, and the lack of peer-reviewed evidence is stated; but the accuracy figures from the maker, a preliminary report and websites are given without methods, and the club-drug studies are generalized without their size.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Six of 64 references are the authors' own; they carry the situated-practice argument, the commentary's distinctive thesis, and the research approach recommended (qualitative rapid assessment) is the authors' own field. The accuracy evidence does not rely on them.

Most mechanisms are hedged (may, unclear, unknown), but some are stated as findings: studies of club-drug self-testing are said to have demonstrated limited value on the strength of one inventory report, and the share of people at risk who avoid services is asserted.

domains.domain: Balance of hypothesized harms and reported benefits of fentanyl self-testing
domains.note: Reported benefits (dose reduction after positives, interest in testing, high laboratory accuracy) are cited and then qualified, while hypothesized harms (complacency, positives being sought, ineffective responses) receive more space without data; the benefits side is under-represented, although the conclusion supports distribution with safeguards.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard instrument applies to a commentary (METHODS §5.3), so the editors' narrative-review checklist is used; the overall judgment follows the unsystematic selection. The commentary is a clear, hedged statement of what was not known in early 2018. Claims may cite it, labelled as second-hand, for: the strips' regulatory status in Canada at the time (urinalysis device; off-label drug-checking use; Health Canada's warning and limited endorsement); the absence of peer-reviewed evidence then on the effectiveness of self-testing; and the uncertainties it lists (preparation practices, timing, no amount, analogues, contaminated equipment, acceptability, reach), labelled as hypotheses. Not citable for: strip accuracy or detection limits (cite the primary studies), behavioural effects, or overdose prevention.

key_findings.finding: Context (as cited): in the United States 19,413 people died in 2016 from unintentional overdoses involving synthetic opioids other than methadone, a twofold increase from 2015; in Canada there were 2,946 opioid-related deaths in 2016 and 2,923 from January to September 2017, 72% of the latter involving fentanyl or its analogues (55% in 2016).
key_findings.locator: Opening section (no heading), 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Analogues (as cited from O'Donnell et al., 2017): in 10 US states, fentanyl analogues were detected in 720 (14%) of 5,152 opioid overdose deaths, including carfentanil in 389 (7.6%), furanylfentanyl in 182 (3.5%) and acetylfentanyl in 147 (2.9%); analogues are not always included in toxicology tests, so surveys may underestimate them.
key_findings.locator: Fentanyl and overdose risk, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Licensing: in Canada the strips are licensed as an in vitro diagnostic device for urinalysis and may be sold only to laboratories or health professionals, but the same strips are sold as a forensic test, which needs no licence and may be sold to anyone, and can be used off-label on dissolved drugs.
key_findings.locator: Testing for fentanyl and fentanyl analogues, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Insite (Vancouver Coastal Health evaluation from 7 July 2016, as cited from press releases): 86% of all drug samples and 90% of ‘heroin’ samples tested positive for fentanyl; the authors suggest this may be an overestimate because 62% of checks were made after consumption and people may test drugs they already suspect. They quote a seller's statement that strips might pick up sub-psychoactive amounts from the air or from handling, and argue that frequent positives without ill effects could breed complacency.
key_findings.locator: Testing for fentanyl and fentanyl analogues, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Health Canada warned that the strips were not designed for direct use by consumers on dissolved drugs, which could lead to false negatives; in November 2017 British Columbia announced strips for all its supervised injection sites; formal promotion of strips appeared limited to supervised facilities.
key_findings.locator: Testing for fentanyl and fentanyl analogues, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Accuracy figures (all second-hand): the maker (BTNX) reports over 98% accuracy for fentanyl in urine and detection of analogues including carfentanil, acetylfentanyl, butyrylfentanyl, 3-methylfentanyl, ocfentanil and sufentanil; FORECAST preliminary data (Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, 2018) give the strips the lowest detection limit of three technologies (0.13 mg/ml as printed), sensitivity 96% and 100% and specificity 90% and 98% at the two sites, and detection of acetylfentanyl, furanylfentanyl and furanylfentanyl with heroin; an evaluation by DanceSafe and UCSF (DanceSafe website) found the strips better than others on the market and able to detect most analogues, including carfentanil at very low concentrations.
key_findings.locator: Testing for fentanyl and fentanyl analogues, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' comparison: the printed 0.13 mg/ml is about a thousand times the 0.100–0.150 mcg/mL recorded on the project's first-pass card for Green et al. (2020), whose site figures match these; the FORECAST report itself was not read (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: A preliminary study found 7 of 70 samples gave erroneous or invalid results, after which Health Canada limited its endorsement of drug checking to approved supervised consumption sites with staff trained in overdose response; the authors note that even the strips' 90% accuracy may be a problem for people with high tolerance who inject up to six times a day.
key_findings.locator: Testing for fentanyl and fentanyl analogues, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The 90% appears to come from the 7 of 70 erroneous or invalid results (63/70, editors' calculation), which counts invalid results as errors. The preliminary study is unnamed and cited through Health Canada (2017) and a CBC news item (Ireland, 2017); McGowan does not say who ran the tests (staff or people who use drugs) or what counted as erroneous, so the figure is not evidence about home use specifically.

key_findings.finding: Situated practice (hypotheses): drug preparation differs by region and heroin type; whether acidifiers used for brown heroin in Europe (citric acid, vitamin C) affect strip accuracy is unknown, though the solution used has been shown to reduce the accuracy of a reagent test (Quest & Horsley, 2007); hurried street injecting and withdrawal may make the two to five minutes a result takes impractical.
key_findings.locator: Testing for fentanyl and fentanyl analogues, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Despite a lack of peer-reviewed evidence on the efficacy and effectiveness of self-testing for preventing fentanyl overdose, strips were being distributed by harm-reduction agencies and sold online for home use.
key_findings.locator: Testing for fentanyl and fentanyl analogues, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Club-drug analogy: Murray et al. (2003) are cited for reduced sensitivity and specificity, and a risk of misreading, when people unfamiliar with reagent tests use them; experts are said to prefer laboratory methods run by trained technicians (EMCDDA, 2001; Murray et al., 2003); a GHB and ketamine drink test was 100% accurate in the laboratory but 65% (sensitivity 50%, specificity 91.6%) in lay hands (Quest & Horsley, 2007); MDMA kits may miss other substances and give no indication of strength (Schneider et al., 2016; Winstock et al., 2001); and self-testing is said to be of limited value outside a package of harm-reduction services (EMCDDA, 2001).
key_findings.locator: Self-testing of club drugs using reagent kits, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Use (the authors' account): strips require the drug to be dissolved in water; only one kit then available included a buffer bottle, so the authors expect most people to test the prepared solution or the residue after use; once the drug is in solution the options are limited, and there are no data on whether taking a smaller amount first works with fentanyl or its analogues.
key_findings.locator: What do we need to know about fentanyl self-testing? › Use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Effect (hypotheses): fentanyl may be desired by some people, so a positive result may be sought or fail to deter use, particularly in withdrawal; strips give no indication of amount; lowering their sensitivity to fentanyl would risk missing samples containing only carfentanil; contaminated equipment such as shared spoons may give positives; repeated non-fatal positives might promote complacency.
key_findings.locator: What do we need to know about fentanyl self-testing? › Effect, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Acceptability: at Insite an average of 4.7 checks a day were made among an average of 600 daily visitors, so press-release figures (people who checked before use and got a positive were 10 times more likely to reduce their dose; those who reduced it were 25% less likely to overdose) concern a small minority; in FORECAST, 73% of 256 participants were moderately to highly interested in knowing whether fentanyl was present and 70% said knowing would change their behaviour, but acceptability of the strips was not reported. Editors' calculation: about 0.8% of daily visitors checked.
key_findings.locator: What do we need to know about fentanyl self-testing? › Acceptability, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Reach: recent US increases in drug use were among groups with historically low heroin use (women, the privately insured, people with higher incomes), who, like people in suburbs and people who use drugs occasionally, are said to have less access to harm-reduction services; the authors doubt that strips would reach those most at risk.
key_findings.locator: What do we need to know about fentanyl self-testing? › Acceptability, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Research called for: qualitative and ethnographic work within a rapid assessment framework on the use, feasibility and acceptability of self-testing, alongside alternatives such as supervised testing and naloxone distribution and including unintended effects; combined with pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic data; and further in vitro and off-label laboratory testing of accuracy and of the range of analogues detected.
key_findings.locator: Do we know enough?, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: the authors support distributing strips with clear guidance on interpreting results, alongside low-threshold naloxone and within broader harm-reduction services, with updated naloxone information, discouragement of visual checks for fentanyl, and encouragement to use only in the company of someone with naloxone; the abstract calls the latter the most practical current way to mitigate fentanyl overdose risk.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Do we know enough?, 3rd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The FORECAST detection limit is printed as 0.13 mg/ml alongside site-level figures of 96% and 100% sensitivity and 90% and 98% specificity. Editors' comparison: these site figures match the project's first-pass card for Green et al. (2020), which records strip detection limits of 0.100 and 0.150 mcg/mL, about a thousand times lower; the FORECAST report itself was not read.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a unit slip; do not cite this commentary for the strips' detection limit, and cite the primary study.

reporting_issues.issue: The strips' 90% accuracy, used to question Health Canada's caution, is not attributed; it appears to derive from the 7 of 70 erroneous or invalid results of a preliminary study, which counts invalid results as inaccurate, while the FORECAST figures in the preceding paragraph are higher.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the underlying counts, not a single accuracy figure; none of these figures is peer-reviewed.

reporting_issues.issue: The behavioural figures (10 times more likely to reduce the dose after a positive; 25% less likely to overdose after reducing it) are quoted from Vancouver Coastal Health press releases without denominators, comparison groups or methods.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not citable as evidence that testing changes behaviour or prevents overdose; the authors themselves note that they concern a small minority of visitors.

reporting_issues.issue: Insite positivity is given as 86% of all samples (from Vancouver Coastal Health), while a cited newspaper item in the reference list is titled with 80%; both are non-peer-reviewed and give no denominators here.
reporting_issues.consequence: Programme positivity figures are second-hand and vary by source and date.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that studies of club-drug self-testing have demonstrated limited value outside a package of harm-reduction services cites only an EMCDDA (2001) inventory of on-site pill-testing interventions.
reporting_issues.consequence: The basis is one inventory report (not read), not studies of outcomes.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that service access is lower among women and people of higher socio-economic status cites Harris et al. (2015); the only 2015 papers with an author Harris in the reference list are a qualitative study of the 2010/2011 UK heroin shortage (Harris, Forseth & Rhodes) and a paper on heroin acidity (Ciccarone & Harris).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the support for this statement cannot be confirmed from the reference list.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 31–36 (journal version, International Journal of Drug Policy 58 (2018) 31–36, open access under CC BY-NC-ND), the project PDF folder DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/_Cross-cutting/McGowan_2018_FentanylSelfTestingCritique.pdf.pdf: all text (all six pages rendered to confirm column order and paragraph breaks), funding, conflict-of-interest and acknowledgement statements, and the reference list (64 entries). The paper has no tables, figures or supplementary material. The FORECAST report and the other grey sources it cites were not read.

disagreements.first_pass: which counts invalid results as errors.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 143 (missed): p. 33: the 7 of 70 result is cited through Health Canada and a CBC news item, and McGowan does not say who ran those tests or what counted as erroneous; this matters because cl_dc_home_vs_service cites it among testing errors.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after checking p. 33 and the reference list (Ireland, 2017, CBC).

verification.checked_by: AI reader 143 (blind second reading) and AI reader 148 (adjudication)

design_detail: Service-evaluation data from the UK's first onsite drug safety testing service open to the public (‘Multi Agency Safety Testing’, MAST), run by the non-profit The Loop over four days in July 2016 at a 25,000-capacity outdoor festival in England (the reference list identifies Secret Garden Party). Filed as a case series because everyone seen received the intervention and outcomes were recorded once, at the end of the consultation; there is no group without testing. Volunteer chemists in an onsite laboratory analysed samples by FTIR, colour reagent tests and mass-loss analysis; results were given in 15–20-minute consultations by healthcare staff with harm-reduction advice and an offer to hand over further substances for police destruction. Outcomes: the result against what the sample was sold as, observed disposals, and stated intentions (an open-ended question coded afterwards), with unadjusted comparisons by result, place of purchase and sex; plus an uncontrolled comparison of the festival's drug-related hospital admissions in 2015 and 2016 from unpublished police reports. Read with ROBINS-I rather than the JBI prevalence checklist because testing with a brief intervention is an intervention and the paper compares groups and infers behavioural and festival-level effects. Not a study of home test kits: chemists did all testing.
can_establish: How often drugs submitted to one onsite festival testing service in England in 2016 were not what they were sold as, how many clients then handed over further substances for police destruction (observed) or stated other intentions, and how disposal differed by result and place of purchase.
cannot_establish: Whether the service changed what people consumed afterwards or reduced harm, hospital admissions or deaths (no comparison group, intentions not followed up, a one-year before–after count from unpublished reports), how accurate its analyses were (no confirmatory testing is reported), or anything about the accuracy or effects of home test kits.

sample.recruitment: Self-referred festival-goers. The service was advertised neither beforehand nor widely onsite and became known mainly by word of mouth through welfare, medical, hospitality and other staff and through artists and management; it was in a welfare area within a police-negotiated ‘tolerance zone’ and open about midday to 8 pm, Thursday to Sunday (Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, p. 104). Data were recorded for one nominated primary client per consultation; clients came in friendship groups of about four, from which the author estimates that advice reached about 900 festival-goers (Methods, 3rd paragraph, p. 104).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Any substance of concern except plant or fungal material, one pill or about 5 mg of powder per sample (p. 104). People judged intoxicated were asked to return later (Pilot limitations, 1st paragraph, p. 106). The 17 samples whose results were not collected are not analysed.
sample.demographics: Primary clients (Results › Sample, p. 104): 66% male, 87% White, mean age 27.6 years (median 26, SD 7.5, range 16–51); women younger than men (25.3 v 28.7 years) and people submitting ketamine younger (24.2) than those submitting MDMA (27.8) or cocaine (27.5); the Welsh postal testing service WEDINOS is cited for comparison (87% male, mean age 32). 5.2% (11 men, 1 woman) had ever had support or treatment for drug or alcohol use; 8.3% had never used the drug submitted (women 11.7%, men 6.5%). 62.9% had already drunk alcohol that day (mean 4.3 UK units) and 43% had used other drugs (p. 106).
sample.attrition: 17 of 247 samples (6.9%, editors' calculation) had no collected result; 19 of 230 consultations (8.3%) have no answer on intentions (Table 3). There was no follow-up after the consultation.
sample.selection_effects: Clients of an unadvertised service chose to come; over four in ten reported concerns about the sample or their own health, including a quarter (25.2%) about that sample, some after adverse effects already experienced at the festival (Methods, 5th paragraph, p. 104). People who seek testing may be more cautious, more worried or more willing to discard than other festival-goers who use drugs. Recording one primary client per group leaves the others out. The reach of about 900 and the ‘one in five’ festival-goers who use drugs are estimates (an assumed group size of four; a national survey figure of 20.9% of festival-goers using illegal drugs), not counts.

exposure.measurement: Intervention (Methods, 2nd–4th paragraphs, p. 104): anonymous drop-off of a sealed sample into a locked amnesty bin; analysis by volunteer postgraduate, mostly postdoctoral, chemists using up to three techniques (FTIR against the TICTAC and Bruker ATR libraries in OPUS 7.5; colorimetric reagent tests for heavily diluted substances or those FTIR might miss; mass-loss analysis for the approximate MDMA content of pills), with results triangulated where appropriate; return of the result about an hour later within a scripted, individually tailored brief intervention by healthcare staff covering medical and drug histories, the sample's expected and actual content, analytical and batch limitations, harm-reduction advice, leaflets, signposting to a local drug service and the disposal offer. Results were also given to all onsite agencies at daily security advisory group meetings and used for targeted site-wide alerts (Meso level impact, 1st paragraph, p. 105).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (no drug was given). One consultation per client, about 15–20 minutes.
exposure.polysubstance: Samples: content identified (cutting agents and pharmaceuticals are named for some samples sold as cocaine); quantities are not reported. Clients: alcohol (62.9%) and other drug use (43%) earlier that day were recorded (p. 106) but not used in any analysis.

comparison.controls: No group without testing. Internal comparisons only: clients whose result did not match what the sample was sold as (45) v matched (164); purchase within the festival (48.3% of 230) v offsite (50%), counts not printed; women v men. For hospital admissions, the festival's 2016 count is compared with its 2015 count.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not measured: what clients intended to do before hearing the result (so stated intentions cannot be compared with prior plans), how much they held and how much they handed over, what they did after leaving (including buying replacements or discarding elsewhere), and, for hospital admissions, changes between 2015 and 2016 in attendance, paramedic practice (the text reports more onsite treatment instead of hospital transfer), recording, and what counted as drug-related.

outcomes.instruments: Consultation records made by healthcare staff at the point of care, matched with the chemists' results and coded in SPSS 22 (p. 104): result ‘matched’ or ‘did not match’ what the sample was sold or given as (Table 2 note: not the client's own expectation); disposal of further substances to the service for police destruction (observed); stated intentions from an open-ended question coded afterwards (Table 3 note). Festival level: drug-related hospital admissions in 2015 and 2016 from unpublished Cambridgeshire Constabulary post-event reports (Ward, 2015, 2016).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validated instruments; the coding frame for the open-ended answers is not described. The author ranks actual disposal immediately after a result as the strongest of four behavioural indicators used in earlier evaluations, and the one that can be corroborated externally (Controversies in drug safety testing, 5th paragraph, p. 103). The accuracy of the onsite analyses was not assessed and no confirmatory analysis is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: ‘Missold’ = analysed content differs from what the sample was sold as; behavioural outcome = disposal (observed) or one coded intention per client (the columns of Table 3 add to their totals); festival-level outcome = count of drug-related hospital admissions.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Three comparisons carry p-values (misselling by place of purchase, disposal by result, disposal by place of purchase), with the test not named; differences by sex are reported without tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: the healthcare staff who gave the result and advice recorded the stated intentions; chemists recorded results.

analysis.effect_sizes: No confidence intervals or effect measures are printed. Editors' calculation (Wilson 95% CI): not as sold 45/230 = 19.6% (15.0–25.2%); disposal 49/230 = 21.3% (16.5–27.0%); disposal after a non-matching result 30/45 = 66.7% (52.1–78.6%) v after a matching result 15/164 = 9.1% (5.6–14.5%), difference 57.5 points (Newcombe 95% CI 42.0–70.0), risk ratio 7.3. Editors' reconstruction of counts from the printed percentages (111 onsite and 115 offsite purchases; 77 women and 153 men, the only split consistent with all the printed sex percentages): not as sold 30/111 v 14/115 (Fisher p = 0.007); disposal 30/111 v 17/115 (p = 0.032); disposal women 19/77 v men 30/153 (p = 0.40); first use of that drug women 9/77 v men 10/153 (p = 0.21).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; ethical approval from the Department of Sociology at Durham University (Acknowledgements, p. 107).
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 3 is titled as listing answers over 1% but includes smaller ones; counts are not printed for the place-of-purchase and sex comparisons; the abstract's ‘one in six moderated their consumption’ is not defined in the Results; how many samples were analysed by each technique is not reported; hospital admissions are given for two years only, with 2015 said to be similar to earlier years.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation; 45 non-matching results; the sex comparisons are too small to detect the differences reported (editors' calculation above).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of 230 samples with results, 45 (19.6%) were not what they were sold as (for example ketamine or cathinones sold as cocaine, n-ethyl pentylone sold as MDMA, plaster-of-Paris pills sold as ecstasy, brown sugar sold as MDMA). After the consultation 49 clients (21.3%) handed over further substances: 30 of 45 (66.7%) after a non-matching result and 15 of 164 (9.1%) after a matching one. 121 (52.6% by editors' calculation; printed 52%) said they would take their usual amount; 22 would take it later or over a longer period, 7 would take a smaller amount, 6 would throw it away, 2 would return it to their dealer and 1 would be more careful about mixing, all stated intentions that were not followed up. Drug-related hospital admissions at the festival were 19 of 59 in 2015 and 1 of 50 in 2016.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says that “another one in six moderated their consumption” (p. 102): these are stated intentions, and the two moderation categories in the Results add to 29 of 230 (12.6%, editors' calculation), one in eight; one in six is reached only by adding throwing away, returning to the dealer and care with mixing (38 of 230, 16.5%). The abstract's “unanticipated feedback loop occurred to some drug suppliers” rests on two clients saying they planned to return drugs to their dealer. Women's higher disposal and first use are stated without tests and are compatible with chance (editors' reconstruction). The Conclusion presents disposals as “reducing harm to the individual and others” (p. 102), which was not measured. The 95% fall in admissions is presented under results; the Discussion concedes that the pilot cannot establish the service's contribution (p. 106), while admissions not related to drugs rose from 40 to 49 (editors' calculation) and paramedics reportedly treated more people onsite.

timeline.event: Sage (2015), ANKORS service data from the Shambhala Music Festival, Canada: cited with Mema (2018) as reports of actual disposal immediately after results; not read.
This pilot: four days in July at one English festival.
Leece (2017), Public Health Ontario evidence brief, cited for disposal rates of 4% to 76% across evaluations of drug checking; not read.
Mema (2018): drug checking at an electronic dance music festival in British Columbia during the public health overdose emergency, cited for actual disposal after results; not read.
This study published (volume 67; copyright 2018).

replication.where_it_stands: Disposal after drug checking has been reported by other services at widely varying rates (4% to 76% in the review cited), so the general observation recurs; the contrast by result and the fall in hospital admissions have no replication or controlled test in the sources read for this card, and later studies were not searched by this reader, so the status is provisional.

funding.funder: The paper was written on research leave funded by Durham University; the pilot's costs were covered by festival and other donations, with staff volunteering their time (Acknowledgements, p. 107).
funding.declared_conflicts: No separate competing-interest statement. The Acknowledgements state that the author is co-founder and co-director of The Loop, the non-profit social enterprise that delivered the pilot (p. 107).
funding.affiliations_note: Single author, Department of Sociology, Durham University, evaluating a service delivered by her own organization, with festival funding and police cooperation; the hospital admission figures come from unpublished police reports. A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A comparison of festivals or event days with and without onsite drug checking (randomized by event, or a stepped introduction), with follow-up of what clients actually consumed, recorded disposals, and independently collected drug-related medical presentations and hospital transfers under fixed definitions, plus confirmatory laboratory analysis of a share of samples to check the onsite results.

domains.note: No group without testing. Disposal is compared by result and by place of purchase without adjustment (onsite purchases were more often missold, so the place-of-purchase difference may be the result difference); the fall in hospital admissions is a one-festival, one-year before–after comparison with other changes that year (more onsite treatment by paramedics) and partner data that varied in quality between years, as the author states.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Self-selected clients of an unadvertised service, many already concerned about their sample; one primary client recorded per group; 17 samples without results excluded.

The matched or non-matching classification rests on FTIR, reagent tests and mass loss with no confirmatory analysis reported, and on what the client said the sample was sold as; 21 samples of unknown origin form a third group.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Consultations were individually tailored and given in non-ideal conditions; 62.9% of clients had drunk alcohol and 43% had used other drugs that day; intoxicated people were asked to return; what each client was told is not recorded.
17 of 247 results not collected; 19 of 230 with no answer on intentions; no data after the consultation; hospital admissions for two years only.

Disposal is observed, but the amount is not recorded and other supplies may have been kept or discarded elsewhere (author); intentions are open-ended answers coded afterwards, recorded by the staff who gave the advice immediately after the result, with no follow-up; hospital admissions come from unpublished reports whose indicators differed between years.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: The abstract's ‘one in six moderated their consumption’ combines categories in a way not defined in the Results; sex differences are reported without tests; Table 3 says it lists answers over 1% but includes smaller ones; the statistical test is not named.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I is used because onsite testing with a brief intervention is an intervention and the paper infers behavioural and festival-level effects (topic instruction; METHODS §5.3). As evidence that the service changed consumption or reduced hospital admissions it is at critical risk of bias: there is no comparison without testing, intentions were not followed up, and the admission figures are an uncontrolled before–after count from unpublished reports. The disposal data are stronger than the stated intentions because they are observed, not self-reported. Citable for: the share of samples not as sold (45 of 230) and the kinds of misselling found, the observed disposal rate (49 of 230) and its difference by result (30 of 45 v 15 of 164), the stated intentions as intentions, and the profile of clients, at one English festival in 2016. Not citable for: effects on consumption, harm, hospital admissions or deaths, the sex differences, or home test kits.

key_findings.finding: Pilot over four days in July 2016 at a 25,000-capacity outdoor festival in England: 247 samples submitted; 230 brief interventions with results (results not collected for 17 samples); clients came in groups of about four, giving an estimated reach of about 900 festival-goers, described as one in five of the festival-goers who use drugs, using a national estimate that 20.9% of festival-goers take illegal drugs.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Controversies in drug safety testing, 6th paragraph (p. 103); Methods, 3rd paragraph (p. 104)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 20.9% of 25,000 is about 5,225, of whom 900 would be 17%; 900 is an estimate from group size, not a count.

key_findings.finding: Procedure: one pill or about 5 mg of powder (no plant or fungal material) was posted into a locked amnesty bin; volunteer chemists analysed it by FTIR (TICTAC and Bruker ATR libraries, OPUS 7.5), colorimetric reagent tests and mass-loss analysis for the MDMA content of pills; the result was returned about an hour later in a scripted 15–20-minute consultation by healthcare staff with harm-reduction advice, leaflets, signposting and an offer to hand over further substances for police destruction.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 2nd–4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: 230 primary clients: 66% male, 87% White, mean age 27.6 years (median 26, SD 7.5, range 16–51); 5.2% (11 men, 1 woman) had ever had support or treatment for drug or alcohol use; 8.3% had never used the drug they submitted (women 11.7%, men 6.5%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Over four in ten clients reported concerns: 25.2% about that sample (including adverse effects such as vomiting already experienced at the festival), 14.8% about past adverse effects of that drug in themselves or friends, 4.3% about how they felt at the time.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: 50% had acquired their substance offsite and 48.3% within the festival. Results (Table 1): MDMA 131 (57%; 37% of samples MDMA crystal or powder and 20% ecstasy pills), ketamine 31 (13.5%), cocaine 23 (10%), cutting agents 16 (7%), cathinone NPS 8 (3.5%), unidentified 6 (2.6%), pill binder (plaster of Paris) 6 (2.6%), other NPS 3 (1.3%), pharmaceuticals 2, LSD 2, amphetamines 2 (0.9% each).
key_findings.locator: Results › Forensic test results, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (p. 105)

key_findings.finding: 45 of 230 samples (19.6%; given as 19.5% in the text) did not match what they were sold as; samples bought within the festival did so more than twice as often as those bought offsite (27% v 12%, p < .01), and those buying within the festival were about two years younger (26.5 v 28.5 years). Misselling included ketamine and cathinones sold as cocaine; cathinones sold as ketamine and MDMA, among them n-ethyl pentylone sold as MDMA; chloroquine, benzocaine, caffeine, ephedrine and paracetamol in samples sold as cocaine; six plaster-of-Paris pills sold as ecstasy; four brown sugar samples sold as MDMA crystal.
key_findings.locator: Results › Forensic test results, 1st paragraph; Tables 2–3 (p. 105)

key_findings.finding: 49 of 230 clients (21.3%) handed over further substances for police destruction: 30 of 45 (66.7%) whose result did not match v 15 of 164 (9.1%) whose result matched (p < .01), and 4 of 21 (19%) with samples of unknown origin; purchases within the festival 27% v offsite 14.8% (p < .05); women 24.7% v men 19.6% (no test).
key_findings.locator: Results › Individual behavioural outcomes, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Stated intentions (open-ended answers coded afterwards, one per client; Table 3): take my usual amount 121 (printed 52%), including 111 of 164 (67.7%) with a matching result and 4 of 45 (8.9%) with a non-matching one; take it later or over a longer period 22 (printed 8%); take a smaller amount 7 (3%); throw it away myself 6 (2.6%); return it to the dealer 2 (0.9%); be more careful about mixing 1; none left 3 (1.3%); no answer 19 (8.3%). By editors' calculation 121 and 22 of 230 are 52.6% and 9.6%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Individual behavioural outcomes, 2nd paragraph; Table 3
key_findings.note: For most of those intending to take it later or in a smaller amount, the result matched what was sold but was stronger than expected (text).

key_findings.finding: Two clients asked for signposting to local drug services, neither previously in contact with one; two planned to return drugs to their dealer to report the contents or ask for a refund, which the author describes as a possible accountability feedback loop.
key_findings.locator: Results › Individual behavioural outcomes, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Results were shared with all onsite agencies at daily security advisory group meetings, and targeted alerts were circulated for chloroquine and ketamine sold as cocaine and for high-MDMA pills. No drug-related deaths occurred at the festival in 2016, a year with six drug-related deaths at UK festivals, the most on record.
key_findings.locator: Meso level impact, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The festival reported 19 drug-related hospital admissions of 59 in total in 2015 (similar to earlier years) and 1 of 50 in 2016, a 95% fall, from unpublished police post-event reports; explanations offered by festival and partner agencies included awareness from alerts, earlier presentation and paramedics' greater confidence in treating drug-related presentations onsite rather than sending people to hospital. The author states that the pilot cannot establish the service's contribution because other variables could not be controlled.
key_findings.locator: Meso level impact, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: admissions not classed as drug-related rose from 40 to 49.

key_findings.finding: The author's limitations: consultations held in non-ideal conditions (62.9% of clients had drunk alcohol, mean 4.3 UK units, and 43% had used other drugs that day); partner-agency data of varying quality, sometimes not separating drug-related from other incidents or alcohol from drug intoxication; possible unintended consequences such as displacement to alcohol not monitored. The author argues, without data, that because clients had already acquired the substances they submitted, drug use is unlikely to rise, and that, given clients' concerns and the misselling found, testing is more likely to deter than to stimulate drug supply and use at the festival.
key_findings.locator: Pilot limitations and future directions, 1st–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The author ranks actual disposal immediately after hearing a result as the strongest of four indicators used in earlier evaluations (intentions after results, recalled behaviour, hypothetical intentions, actual disposal) and cites a review (Leece, 2017) giving disposal rates of 4% to 76%.
key_findings.locator: Controversies in drug safety testing, 4th and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The Introduction relays critics' concerns, without data of its own: field testing at best gives an artificial impression of safety (Winstock et al., 2001); trade-offs between speed, accuracy and portability; dealers using services for quality control; a focus on contaminants rather than risky behaviours such as bingeing and polydrug use; limited evidence that information changes behaviour; reduced deterrence and greater appeal through perceived safety; and normalisation of drug use.
key_findings.locator: Introduction › Controversies in drug safety testing, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: It also relays, second-hand, that two decades of Dutch testing and alerts showed no perverse effect on drug use or drug-related deaths (Brunt, 2012), and that there is no evidence that drug prevalence, initiation or mortality rose in European countries with drug safety testing compared with those without (Benschop et al., 2002; Brunt, 2012; Hungerbuehler et al., 2011): country-level comparisons of services, not of kits.
key_findings.locator: Introduction › Controversies in drug safety testing, 3rd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's ‘another one in six moderated their consumption’ is not defined in the Results. By editors' calculation, taking it later or over a longer period (22) and taking less (7) add to 29 of 230 (12.6%), and one in six requires adding throwing away, returning to the dealer and care with mixing (38 of 230, 16.5%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the Table 3 categories as stated intentions, not as moderated consumption.

reporting_issues.issue: 22 of 230 is printed as 8% in the text and Table 3, 121 of 230 as 52% and 1 of 230 as 0%, and Table 3 is titled as listing answers over 1% while including smaller ones. By editors' calculation the three are 9.6%, 52.6% and 0.4%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite counts.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives 19.5% of samples as not matching what they were sold as; Tables 2–3 give 45 of 230 (19.6%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor.

reporting_issues.issue: Sex differences in disposal (24.7% v 19.6%) and first use of the drug (11.7% v 6.5%) appear in the Results, abstract and Discussion without tests; by editors' reconstruction of the counts from the printed percentages (77 women, 153 men) they give p of about 0.40 and 0.21.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sex differences should not be cited as findings.

reporting_issues.issue: Counts behind the place-of-purchase comparisons are not printed, and no p-value names its test.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparisons can be reconstructed only approximately (editors' reconstruction above).

reporting_issues.issue: The hospital admission figures come from unpublished police reports (Ward, 2015, 2016); total admissions fell only from 59 to 50, so by editors' calculation admissions not classed as drug-related rose from 40 to 49, and the author notes that partner data sometimes failed to separate drug-related from other incidents.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 95% fall may partly reflect classification or referral changes; it cannot be cited as an effect of testing.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Discussion present disposals as reducing harm and say a feedback loop to suppliers occurred; the Results show disposals and two stated plans to return drugs to a dealer, with no measure of harm or of any supplier response.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite disposals and plans as observed or stated, not their consequences.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 102–107 (journal version, International Journal of Drug Policy 67 (2019) 102–107), the project PDF folder DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/_Cross-cutting/Measham_2019_FestivalDrugCheckingDisposals.pdf.pdf: all text, Tables 1–3 (p. 105, rendered and checked against the text extraction; totals and percentages recomputed), acknowledgements (funding, ethics approval and the author's role in The Loop), reference list. No supplementary material is mentioned.
