disagreements.first_pass: case-series, ROBINS-I (critical)
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 145 (risk of bias, agree): the card is filed as a case series, for which METHODS §5.3 lists no instrument, but appraised with ROBINS-I; worth checking against the vocabulary script. For the observed disposal-by-result association, the observed outcome makes the evidence firmer than 'critical' suggests, as the card's reasoning says.
disagreements.resolution: Unchanged: the validator does not check designs without a listed instrument, and re-filing (for example as cross-sectional, since the paper compares results within one service) would be a judgment, not a rule-based correction; referred to the senior author with the same question for two cross-sectional cards (adjudication log). The reasoning already says the disposal data are stronger because they are observed.

verification.checked_by: AI reader 145 (blind second reading) and AI reader 149 (adjudication)

design_detail: Laboratory test-accuracy study of one commercial colour-reagent kit on drug samples, not people. Filed as test-accuracy (METHODS §5.3, version 0.3.1): the units are drug samples tested in a laboratory (as in sc_green_2020), and QUADAS-2 is used because the kit's readings are compared with a reference (GC-MS or known identity). University of Florida, Gainesville; dates of testing not reported. Kit: DanceSafe Complete Adulterant Screening Kit for Ecstasy (Marquis, Mecke and Simon's reagents), two identical kits bought online. Part I: 39 samples sold as MDMA and held as evidence, read by three analysts with the kit's instructions and colour charts (Marquis alone, then all three reagents together), then analysed by GC-MS. Part II: eight blinded samples of seven known drugs (MDMA twice) read by two testers trained in pharmacology and toxicology but new to the kit, given only its labelling. Published in the journal's Research Reports section.
can_establish: Whether, in one laboratory, the kit's reagents read positive for samples that GC-MS showed to contain MDMA and negative for samples without it, whether a positive reading revealed a second drug present alongside MDMA, and how two testers new to the kit classified eight samples of known drugs.
cannot_establish: How accurately people at parties or at home read the kit, how it performs with PMA, MDA, methamphetamine or newer substitutes on their own (none was tested), with current kits or with the mixtures of other markets, any precise accuracy figure for novice readers (two testers, eight samples, four MDMA readings), or whether testing changes behaviour or causes or prevents harm (not measured).

sample.recruitment: Samples, not people. Part I: 39 street samples purported to be MDMA and held as evidence at the Alachua County Sheriff's Office or the University of Florida Forensic Toxicology Laboratory, used because no other tablets were available at the time; the analysts chose samples of different descriptions from the two sources for variety (Methods › Part I Testing, 1st paragraph, p. 1239). Part II: samples of codeine, dextromethorphan, dihydrocodeine, ketamine, MDMA (two samples), morphine and d-norpropoxyphene chosen by the investigators; all but the MDMA are described as legitimate dosage forms of high potency and quality (Methods › Part II Testing, 1st paragraph, pp. 1240–1241; Discussion, 7th paragraph, p. 1243).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated beyond the above. Although described as 39 tablets, the Part I set in Table 2 includes two powders, a capsule containing powder and a fragment in chewed gum (Table 2, p. 1240).
sample.demographics: Not applicable (samples). Readers: three analysts in Part I, called experienced chemists familiar with reagent use in the Table 2 footnote; two testers in Part II, professionals in pharmacology and toxicology inexperienced with the kits (p. 1241). Colour vision, lighting and any training beyond the practice runs are not reported.
sample.attrition: None apparent: all 39 Part I samples appear in Table 2 and all 8 Part II samples in Table 3. Part I results for the Marquis reagent alone are described as similar but not shown (Results › Part I, p. 1241).
sample.selection_effects: Part I samples were police and laboratory evidence picked for variety; the authors note they were almost certain to contain controlled substances, most likely MDMA, which prompted Part II (Methods › Part II Testing, p. 1240). With 35 of 39 MDMA-positive, Part I tests sensitivity far more than specificity (4 negatives). No sample contained PMA or MDA, and in Part I none held methamphetamine or dextromethorphan; the 4 MDMA-negative samples held alprazolam, ephedrine or pseudoephedrine (with guaifenesin or with caffeine) or no identifiable drug. Part II was an investigator-chosen panel weighted to opioids and dextromethorphan (5 of 8 samples) with MDMA in 2 of 8, so its predictive values reflect the panel, not any drug market.

exposure.measurement: Index test (Methods, pp. 1239–1240): two identical DanceSafe kits bought from an Internet source, each with dropper bottles of Marquis reagent, Mecke reagent and the two solutions of Simon's reagent, without lot numbers; Table 1 gives standard reagent compositions from a US Department of Justice standard (ref. 13), not an analysis of the kits. Beforehand the three analysts studied the procedure and colour charts, agreed names for the chart colours and practised on generic pills. Part I: each sample was scraped to 3–5 mg of powder, with roughly equal portions put on white ceramic test plates and into GC-MS vials; four samples were tested per timed 20-second interval; one analyst tested while a second observed, both recording independently, and a third timed; the Marquis reaction was judged alone and then together with Mecke and Simon's; the first and third analysts then swapped roles and repeated the tests with the samples in random order, the second remaining observer. Part II: the two testers had the kit and its labelling and were told only how to record their findings (p. 1241).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (samples).
exposure.polysubstance: GC-MS (Table 2, p. 1240): 7 of the 35 MDMA samples also held ephedrine (2), caffeine (2), amphetamine (1), diazepam (1) or PMMA (1); the text says ephedrine or pseudoephedrine (p. 1241). The four samples without MDMA held alprazolam; ephedrine or pseudoephedrine with guaifenesin; ephedrine or pseudoephedrine with caffeine; or no identifiable drug. Amounts were not measured.

comparison.controls: Reference standards: in Part I, GC-MS in full-scan mode with mepivacaine and ethyl morphine as internal standards, run on separate aliquots after the colour tests (pp. 1239–1240); in Part II, the known identity of the drugs supplied. No amounts or detection limits are reported.
comparison.matching: Not applicable. Part I and Part II differ in readers, samples and reference at the same time, so the contrast between experienced analysts and new testers cannot be separated from the change of sample set.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to samples. Not reported: dates of testing and the interval between the two parts, reagent age and storage, which kit was used in which part, the colours seen, the rule for calling a reading positive, lighting, whether GC-MS was interpreted without knowledge of the colour results, and the source and confirmation of the two Part II MDMA samples.

outcomes.instruments: Part I: positive or negative for MDMA per sample, for Analyst 1 and for Analysts 2 and 3 (one column), with the three reagents together (Table 2); Marquis alone described, not shown. Part II: positive or negative per sample and tester (Table 3), with readings of an MDMA-like substance counted as positive; sensitivity, specificity and positive and negative predictive values pooled over both testers for the three reagents together (Table 3 footnote); Marquis-alone counts in the text.
outcomes.validity_norms: No validated reading protocol: the kit's instructions and colour charts, with colour names agreed beforehand in Part I. The analysts disagreed on the exact colours but generally agreed on whether MDMA was present (Results › Part I, p. 1241).
outcomes.operationalization: Positive = a reading consistent with MDMA on the kit's charts (rule not stated); in Part II a reading of an MDMA-like substance was counted as positive at analysis. Adulterated = MDMA plus another drug by GC-MS. No measure of behaviour or harm was taken; harm induction is the authors' inference.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive; no tests or intervals).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Part I: the analysts knew the samples were sold as MDMA and held as evidence; GC-MS came later; the repeat run was randomized to prevent observer bias, but the same observer watched both runs. Part II: single-blind (the testers did not know which drug each sample was).

analysis.effect_sizes: No confidence intervals are printed. Part I (three reagents): every analyst read all 35 GC-MS-confirmed MDMA samples positive, including the 7 with a second drug; of the 4 without MDMA, Analysts 2 and 3 read all negative and Analyst 1 read 3 negative and 1 weakly positive (the sample with no identifiable drug). Editors' calculation (Wilson 95% intervals): sensitivity 35/35 = 100% (90.1–100%); specificity 4/4 = 100% (51.0–100%), or 3/4 = 75% (30.1–95.4%) for Analyst 1 if the weak reading counts as positive. Part II (three reagents, both testers): sensitivity 50%, specificity 58%, positive predictive value 28%, negative predictive value 77% as printed; editors' recount 2/4 = 50% (15.0–85.0%), 7/12 = 58.3% (32.0–80.7%), 2/7 = 28.6% (8.2–64.1%) and 7/9 = 77.8% (45.3–93.7%). By tester: Novice A detected 0 of 2 MDMA samples and read 5 of 6 others negative; Novice B detected 2 of 2 and read 2 of 6 others negative. Marquis alone (Part II): 10 false positives and 2 false negatives over 16 readings; editors' calculation: specificity 2/12 = 16.7% (4.7–44.8%).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned. Presented in abstract form at the 55th annual meeting of the American Academy of Forensic Sciences, Chicago, February 17–22, 2003 (title-page footnote, p. 1238).
analysis.selective_reporting: Part I Marquis-alone results and all colour readings are not shown, and no reading rule is given. In Part II, readings of an MDMA-like substance are counted as positive by a rule stated only in the Results. Pooled Part II figures are given without per-tester values (these can be derived from Table 3).
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation; the authors call Part I relatively small but all that was available (p. 1243). Part II rests on two testers and four MDMA readings; its sensitivity interval runs from 15% to 85% (editors' calculation).

interpretation_gap.results_show: With experienced analysts, the kit's readings agreed with GC-MS on whether MDMA was present in all 35 MDMA-containing samples and in the 4 without MDMA (one weak positive by one analyst), but a positive looked the same whether or not caffeine, ephedrine, amphetamine, diazepam or PMMA was also present. Two testers new to the kit, reading eight samples of known drugs from the labelling alone, diverged widely: one missed both MDMA samples, the other called four of six non-MDMA drugs (codeine, dihydrocodeine, dextromethorphan, morphine) MDMA or MDMA-like. One tester was slightly injured by a reagent spill.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the reagents “lacked both sensitivity and specificity for the purpose of MDMA identification” with unfamiliar testers and that experienced toxicologists also produced false positives (p. 1238); it does not report Part I's agreement on all 35 MDMA samples, and the experienced false positives amount to one weak reading. The Conclusion states that on no occasion “would our findings have led to avoidance of a contaminated drug” and warns of “harm induction” (p. 1243): the first holds only for the 7 MDMA samples with a second drug, since 4 samples without MDMA read negative in Part I and Novice A read 5 of 6 non-MDMA drugs negative; the second rests on no measure of behaviour or harm. The Discussion's claims that most tablets contain some PMA and that a harm-reduction website overstates the kits' screening for PMA (p. 1242) are untested here: no sample contained PMA. The arguments about MDMA's toxicity (pp. 1242–1243) are outside the study's data.

timeline.event: Murphy (1999), MSc thesis (King's College London): Marquis readings by laboratory staff on 156 amnesty-bin samples compared with GC-MS, known here only as tabulated by Winstock, Wolff and Ramsey (2001); not read.

Winstock, Wolff and Ramsey publish a critique of ecstasy pill testing (cited here as ref. 20); its Table 3 shows purple/blue/black Marquis readings in all 53 amnesty-bin samples with MDMA-like substances and in no others, in laboratory hands (read for this batch).
This study published; presented in abstract form at the American Academy of Forensic Sciences meeting in February 2003.

McGowan et al. cite this study for reduced sensitivity and specificity, and a risk of misreading, when people unfamiliar with reagent tests use them, and for experts' preference for laboratory methods (read for this batch).

A review of colour tests by Philp et al. cites this evaluation as concluding that MDMA kits should not be used by the public (as recorded on the project's card sc_philp_2018; the review was not read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: No later study among the papers read for this batch repeats the novice-reader test. The earlier amnesty-bin comparison tabulated by Winstock et al. (2001) agrees with Part I that a purple/blue/black Marquis reaction tracked MDMA-like substances in laboratory hands; both papers nonetheless conclude against public use. Neither addresses current reagent kits or newer substitutes.

funding.funder: National Institutes of Health grant T35 HL07489 (title-page footnote, p. 1238).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported (no conflict-of-interest statement in the PDF read).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of Florida College of Pharmacy (Department of Pharmacy Practice) and College of Medicine (Department of Pathology, Immunology, and Laboratory Medicine), Gainesville, and the Columbus Regional Drug Information Center, Georgia. Samples came from the Alachua County Sheriff's Office (thanked in the Acknowledgment, p. 1243) and the university's forensic toxicology laboratory; the kits were bought online and no role for the kit's maker is stated. A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A field study of current reagent kits on consecutive samples that people bring for checking, read both by the people themselves following the kit's instructions and by trained staff, against quantitative laboratory analysis, with prespecified reading rules and enough samples of each relevant substitute (for example PMA, PMMA, methamphetamine and cathinones) alone and in mixtures; and, separately, a comparative study of what people do after a kit result.

domains.note: Part I: 39 evidence samples chosen for variety because no others were available, 35 of them MDMA-positive and none containing PMA, MDA, methamphetamine or dextromethorphan; Part II: an eight-sample panel chosen by the investigators. Neither consecutive nor random. Applicability to what people bring to drug checking is uncertain.

Part I readers knew the samples were sold as MDMA; four samples were read every 20 seconds; the observer watched both runs and Analysts 2 and 3 are reported together; no reading rule or colours are reported; reagent age, storage and lot are unknown. Part II's rule counting an MDMA-like reading as positive was applied at analysis. Laboratory plates and staff, not field conditions.

Part I GC-MS in full-scan mode is appropriate for identity but qualitative, does not separate ephedrine from pseudoephedrine, and whether it was read blind to the colour results is not stated. Part II relied on the known identity of the drugs supplied; the source and confirmation of the two MDMA samples are not stated.

All samples received the reference and appear in the tables, but the interval between colour testing and GC-MS, sample storage and the time between the two parts are not reported; the two parts used different reference standards.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: QUADAS-2 is used because the study compares a test's readings with a reference (METHODS §5.3, diagnostic accuracy); the design is filed as test-accuracy (METHODS §5.3, version 0.3.1). The overall judgment follows the worst domains: selected samples, and reading without blinding to the expected drug or a stated rule in Part I, with a rule fixed at analysis in Part II. Part I's four negatives allow no statement about specificity in experienced hands, and Part II is too small to estimate novice accuracy. Citable for: in this laboratory the kit's readings agreed with GC-MS on MDMA presence in all 35 MDMA-containing samples, but a positive reading did not reveal caffeine, ephedrine, amphetamine, diazepam or PMMA present with MDMA; two testers new to the kit misread several samples in both directions, including opioids and dextromethorphan read as MDMA or MDMA-like; a reagent spill caused a minor injury. Not citable for: accuracy when people test at parties or at home, performance with PMA or other substitutes alone, or any effect of testing on behaviour or harm.

preclinical.species_strain_sex: Not applicable: drug samples tested with colour reagents; no cells or animals.
preclinical.resembles_human_use: Not applicable; sample.selection_effects describes how the samples relate to what people buy.

key_findings.finding: Kit and background: the DanceSafe kit contained Marquis, Mecke and Simon's reagents. The authors report that the first kits held only the Marquis reagent, a law-enforcement screening reagent whose interpretation is subjective, and that Mecke and Simon's were added to reduce subjectivity and increase accuracy; harm-reduction groups began promoting such kits partly after media attention to 10 deaths in Orlando and Chicago from PMA mistaken for MDMA, and to other deaths in Europe and Australia. The two kits bought online had no lot numbers.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph; Methods, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Part I procedure: 39 samples sold as MDMA and held as evidence were each scraped to 3–5 mg of powder and tested on ceramic plates, four at a time in timed 20-second intervals, by one analyst while a second observed (both recording) and a third timed; the Marquis reaction was judged alone and then with Mecke and Simon's, using the kit's instructions and colour charts; analysts 1 and 3 then swapped roles and repeated the tests with the samples randomized. Separate aliquots went to GC-MS (full scan; mepivacaine and ethyl morphine as internal standards).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Methods; Methods, 1st paragraph; Methods › Part I Testing, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Part I GC-MS: 35 samples contained MDMA and 4 did not; the 4 held alprazolam, ephedrine or pseudoephedrine with guaifenesin, ephedrine or pseudoephedrine with caffeine, or no identifiable drug. No sample contained PMA. Editors' count of Table 2: 7 of the 35 MDMA samples also held a second drug (ephedrine 2, caffeine 2, amphetamine 1, diazepam 1, PMMA 1) and 28 held MDMA only.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Part I, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Part I readings (three reagents): each analyst recorded 35 positives; all 35 GC-MS-confirmed MDMA samples, including the 7 with a second drug, were read positive by Analyst 1 and by Analysts 2 and 3. Of the 4 samples without MDMA, Analysts 2 and 3 read all 4 negative and Analyst 1 read 3 negative and 1 weakly positive (the sample with no identifiable drug). The analysts disagreed on exact colours but generally agreed on MDMA presence, with Marquis alone and with all three reagents; Marquis-alone results were similar but are not shown. Editors' calculation (Wilson 95% intervals): sensitivity 35/35 = 100% (90.1–100%), specificity 4/4 = 100% (51.0–100%) for Analysts 2 and 3.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 and footnote; Results › Part I, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Part II readings by tester, three reagents together (Table 3): Novice A read only morphine positive (for an MDMA-like substance) and both MDMA samples negative, giving 1 false positive and 2 false negatives; Novice B read only ketamine and d-norpropoxyphene negative, both MDMA samples and codeine positive for MDMA, and dextromethorphan, dihydrocodeine and morphine positive for an MDMA-like substance, giving 4 false positives and no false negatives.
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Results › Part II, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Part II pooled over both testers (three reagents): sensitivity 50%, specificity 58%, positive predictive value 28% and negative predictive value 77%. Editors' recount from Table 3 (Wilson 95% intervals): 2/4 = 50% (15.0–85.0%), 7/12 = 58.3% (32.0–80.7%), 2/7 = 28.6% (8.2–64.1%) and 7/9 = 77.8% (45.3–93.7%); the predictive values depend on the 2 MDMA samples among 8 set by the investigators.
key_findings.locator: Results › Part II, 1st paragraph; Table 3, footnote a
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 2/7 and 7/9 round to 29% and 78%, so the printed 28% and 77% are truncated. The pooled figures treat 16 readings of 8 samples as independent and describe neither tester.

key_findings.finding: Part II, Marquis reagent alone: Novice A read 5 of 8 samples positive for MDMA, with both MDMA samples and ketamine negative (5 false positives, 2 false negatives); Novice B read 7 of 8 positive, all but ketamine (5 false positives, no false negatives). Editors' calculation: specificity over both testers 2/12 = 16.7% (Wilson 95% CI 4.7–44.8%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Part II, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Cross-source context, not a finding of this paper: the Marquis reagent gives violet with codeine, dihydrocodeine and morphine (Winstock et al., 2001, Table 2, p. 1144, from Moffat et al., 1986), so the Part II panel, five of whose eight samples were opioids or dextromethorphan, included known cross-reactants of the Marquis reagent; this bears on any use of Part II's specificity.

key_findings.finding: Safety: one tester was slightly injured after spilling a drop of reagent on his trousers. The Conclusion adds damage to the surroundings, which the Results do not describe.
key_findings.locator: Results › Part II, 1st paragraph; Conclusion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Authors' limitations: possible selection and analyst bias; the seized samples may not all have been sold as pure ecstasy and came from different sources, so consistency could not be compared and the variety chosen may exaggerate product variability; Part I was relatively small (39 samples) but used all that was available; the Part II drugs other than MDMA were legitimate dosage forms that may react differently from clandestine products.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors' conclusions: the kit is inadequate for identifying MDMA in the hands of inexperienced people; on no occasion would the findings have led to avoidance of a contaminated drug; the tests could give a false sense of security; the kits failed to identify several potential contaminants; colour tests may have a place with experienced forensic personnel, but a decision to take a tablet should not rest on them alone; faulty identification can lead to harm induction rather than harm reduction.
key_findings.locator: Conclusion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Discussion: the authors say their results concur with an EMCDDA report that rated the Marquis test unreliable, inaccurate and non-quantifiable and found it gave no information on adulterants, and they note that success depends on the type of testing, the setting and the tester's experience, while kits such as this one are meant for field use by inexperienced people.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Discussion on PMA: a Drug Enforcement Administration brief attributed 10 US deaths to PMA and at least 12 deaths in Australia were attributed to it; the authors cite reports (refs 30–33, including a newspaper article and a teacher resource) suggesting most MDMA tablets contain at least some PMA. In the study's own GC-MS results no sample contained PMA (one held PMMA with MDMA), and no PMA sample was tested with the kit.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Introduction: the authors list dangers they attribute to field testing, without data: people testing are mostly young and inexperienced and may test while intoxicated, the tests may lack precision and accuracy, and because MDMA is regarded as benign there is a temptation to assume a pill is MDMA despite subjective results.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 4th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that the reagents lacked sensitivity and specificity, but this rests on Part II (two testers, eight samples, four MDMA readings); Part I, where the experienced analysts' readings agreed with GC-MS on all 35 MDMA samples and on the 4 without MDMA (one weak positive), is not reported in the abstract.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the two parts separately: the kit's readings tracked MDMA presence in experienced laboratory hands, while the two novice testers' readings did not.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says experienced toxicologists using the unfamiliar procedure generated false-positive results; in Part I the only reading that could be a false positive is one weakly positive reading by Analyst 1 on a sample with no identifiable drug, and the Table 2 footnote calls these analysts familiar with reagent use.
reporting_issues.consequence: False positives in experienced hands rest on one weak reading; whether the abstract instead means the Part II testers (pharmacology and toxicology professionals new to the kit) is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusion states that on no occasion would the findings have led to avoidance of a contaminated drug, yet the 4 Part I samples without MDMA read negative (apart from one weak reading by one analyst), and in Part II Novice A read 5 of 6 non-MDMA drugs negative.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement holds only for the 7 MDMA samples that also held a second drug; it is not citable as a general finding.

reporting_issues.issue: The printed predictive values are truncated: positive predictive value 28% and negative predictive value 77%, where the editors' calculation gives 2/7 = 28.6% and 7/9 = 77.8%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite the counts. The pooled values also merge two testers whose results diverged (sensitivity 0/2 and 2/2; specificity 5/6 and 2/6).

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion cites reports that most MDMA tablets contain at least some PMA and disputes a harm-reduction website's statement about PMA screening, while the study's own GC-MS found PMA in none of its samples and the kit was never tested on PMA; the stated objective includes MDA derivatives, but no MDA sample was tested.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper cannot be cited for PMA prevalence or for how the kit reacts to PMA or MDA.

reporting_issues.issue: The Part I samples are called 39 tablets, but Table 2 lists two powders, a capsule containing powder and a fragment in chewed gum among them.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; describe the set as 39 samples.

reporting_issues.issue: The reading procedure is under-reported: the observer (Analyst 2) watched both runs, Analysts 2 and 3 share one column in Table 2, no colours or reading rule are reported, and Part I Marquis-alone results are not shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: Agreement between readers cannot be quantified, and the Marquis reagent alone cannot be evaluated in experienced hands.

reporting_issues.issue: The source of the two Part II MDMA samples, and whether GC-MS confirmed them, is not stated; the Limitations imply they were not legitimate dosage forms.
reporting_issues.consequence: Novice A's two false negatives cannot be checked against the samples' content.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusion adds damage to the surroundings to the tester's injury; the Results describe only a slight injury from a drop spilled on trousers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite the Results.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1238–1244 (journal version, Pharmacotherapy 2003;23(10):1238–1244), the project PDF folder DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/_Cross-cutting/Murray_2003_EcstasyTestKit.pdf: all text, Tables 1–3 with footnotes (all seven pages rendered; every count checked against the rendered tables), title-page footnotes (affiliations, funding, prior presentation), acknowledgment and reference list. No conflict-of-interest statement and no supplementary material.

editorial_corrections.from: in-vitro
editorial_corrections.to: test-accuracy
editorial_corrections.reason: Rule-based re-filing under METHODS 0.3.1 (decision p-test-accuracy, for the senior author's confirmation): the study compares a test's readings with a reference method or known content, which is the new test-accuracy design; the first reader chose in-vitro as the nearest design the schema then had. The instrument (QUADAS-2) and every judgment are unchanged.

editorial_corrections.reason: Follows the re-filing above; nothing else in the design description changed.

editorial_corrections.from: the design is filed as in-vitro because the units are drug samples.
editorial_corrections.to: the design is filed as test-accuracy (METHODS §5.3, version 0.3.1).
editorial_corrections.reason: Follows the re-filing of 26 October (design in-vitro → test-accuracy, decision p-test-accuracy): the reasoning still named the old design. Found by AI reader 139. No judgment changed.

disagreements.first_pass: (absent)
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 143 (missed): the Marquis reagent gives violet with codeine, dihydrocodeine and morphine (Winstock et al., 2001, Table 2; Philp & Fu, 2018, AM p. 4), so the Part II panel was weighted toward known cross-reactants; worth a line where Part II's specificity is cited.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after checking Winstock et al. (2001), Table 2, p. 1144, and Murray et al.'s Part II panel (Table 3, p. 1241: codeine, dextromethorphan, dihydrocodeine, ketamine, MDMA twice, morphine, d-norpropoxyphene); added as a note on the Marquis-alone finding.

design_detail: Multisite prospective observational cohort (the Stay Safe Study, an ancillary study of the HEALing Communities Study), recruited May to December 2023 at fixed and mobile sites of 14 community harm-reduction organizations that distribute fentanyl test strips (FTS) in Kentucky (5), New York (3) and Ohio (6). Exposure: self-reported FTS use in the 30 days before baseline (yes or no), measured once. Follow-up: four weekly surveys over 28 days (at most 37), using a modified timeline followback to record, for each day with drug use, strip use, drugs used, eight overdose risk-reduction behaviours and nonfatal overdose. Primary outcome: a daily composite score (0–15) of the number and frequency of the eight behaviours; secondary outcomes: the count of behaviours, each behaviour and self-reported nonfatal overdose. Population-averaged generalized estimating equations with prespecified baseline and time-varying covariates; STROBE reporting. Appraised with ROBINS-I because using test strips is an intervention (topic instruction; METHODS §5.3). Strip results were not analysed.
can_establish: Whether people who already used fentanyl test strips, recruited at strip-distributing harm-reduction sites in three US states in 2023, reported more overdose risk-reduction behaviours, and more or fewer nonfatal overdoses, over the next four weeks than people at the same sites who did not, after adjustment for some of the measured differences (not for the baseline level of the same behaviours, which was measured but entered no model).
cannot_establish: Whether using test strips causes people to adopt those behaviours or prevents overdose (strip use was chosen by participants who already reported more risk reduction at baseline, outcomes were self-reported and strip results were not analysed), anything about fatal overdose, or what happens among people outside harm-reduction services.

sample.recruitment: Fixed and mobile harm-reduction sites of 14 community partner organizations distributing FTS in Kentucky, New York and Ohio, May to December 2023 (Methods › Setting; Methods › Study Design, 1st paragraph); written consent on an electronic tablet; compensation up to $250 for screening, baseline and weekly surveys, paid for each survey started (Methods › Study Design, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 or older; self-assessed ability to read and speak English; able to consent; living in Kentucky, New York or Ohio and planning to stay during follow-up; past 30-day use of heroin, fentanyl, cocaine, methamphetamine, or non-prescribed opioids, benzodiazepines or stimulants. Enrolment required starting the baseline survey; the analysed sample required self-reported drug use on at least 1 day and at least 2 completed weekly surveys during follow-up (Methods › Participants).
sample.demographics: Median age 41 (IQR 34–48); 369 male (50.4%); of 722 with race recorded, 587 White (81.3%), 64 Black or African American (8.9%) and 71 other (9.8%); 64 of 724 Hispanic or Latino (8.8%); 391 of 715 unemployed (54.7%); Kentucky 254, New York 162, Ohio 316. Past 30 days: injection 491 (67.1%), fentanyl 489 of 698 (70.1%), heroin 511 of 727 (70.3%), methamphetamine 442 of 725 (61.0%), overdose 168 of 712 (23.6%) (Table 2).
sample.attrition: 424 of 1156 enrolled participants (36.7%) were not analysed because they reported no drug use during follow-up or completed fewer than 2 weekly surveys, a survey counting as completed when any question was answered (editors' calculation; eMethods › Participants, supplement p. 3; reasons in the article's flow diagram, an image not read). eTable 2 (supplement pp. 8–9) compares them with the 732 analysed on demographics only: those not analysed were more often from New York (183 of 424, 43.2%, against 162 of 732, 22.1%) and less often from Kentucky (17.2% against 34.7%; P < .001), more often of other race (17.2% against 9.7%) and Hispanic or Latino (19.5% against 8.7%; each P < .001), more often employed (33.5% against 23.1%; P < .001) and slightly younger (median 40 against 41; P = .03); education did not differ (P = .27). Strip use, drug use, injecting and past overdose are not compared. Editors' calculation: 183 of 345 New York enrollees (53.0%) were not analysed, against 73 of 327 in Kentucky (22.3%) and 168 of 484 in Ohio (34.7%). Within the analysed sample, completion of each weekly survey was similar in the two groups (eTable 1, supplement p. 7: 82.9% to 90.1% of the strip group and 84.0% to 91.8% of the comparison group); 17 (2.3%) were lost to follow-up between the 2nd and 3rd surveys and 67 (9.2%) between the 3rd and 4th (2.7% and 9.7% of the strip group, 1.9% and 8.5% of the comparison group). Adjusted models used 677 to 690 participants (Table 3). Anonymity prevented knowing why people were lost, including whether any fatal overdoses occurred (Strengths and Limitations, 2nd paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Participants were clients of harm-reduction sites that distribute strips, whom the authors call not representative of all people who use drugs (Strengths and Limitations, 2nd paragraph); strip use (56.6%) was far above the median uptake of 19% in the literature cited (Discussion, 2nd paragraph). The exposure is prevalent strip use, not new use. Participants using strips already reported more risk-reduction behaviours at baseline (Results › Baseline Characteristics, 3rd paragraph), were more often from Ohio and White, and more often used fentanyl, heroin, methamphetamine and opioid–stimulant combinations and injected (Table 2). The analysed sample was itself selected from those enrolled by conditions met during follow-up, and differed from the 424 not analysed in state, race, ethnicity and employment (eTable 2, supplement pp. 8–9; see attrition).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported FTS use in the past 30 days, asked once at baseline (whether they had used fentanyl test strips to check their drugs; eTable 1, note 2, supplement p. 7); non-response, 'don't know' and 'prefer not to answer' were classed as no use (Methods › Exposure › Baseline FTS Use; eMethods, supplement p. 4). The number of times strips were used each day during follow-up was recorded as a time-varying characteristic (Methods › Characteristics Varying Over Time) and entered only the overdose model (eMethods, p. 6); the supplement gives no distribution of strip use during follow-up. Strip results were not analysed; the authors defer that to future work (Discussion, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to the exposure. Drug categories and injection were recorded daily and used as covariates.
exposure.polysubstance: Recorded: past 30-day use of eight drug classes at baseline (Table 2) and a daily drug category (opioids only; stimulants only; opioids and stimulants; benzodiazepines; none or unknown), used as a time-varying covariate (Methods › Characteristics Varying Over Time).

comparison.controls: People recruited at the same sites who reported no FTS use in the 30 days before baseline, including those who did not answer (n = 318).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not measured or not adjusted: prior engagement with harm-reduction services (authors' limitation), risk perception, the baseline level of the outcome behaviours (measured, and higher in the strip group: median composite score 8 against 7, eTable 4, supplement p. 12; but in no model, eMethods › Statistical Analysis, supplement p. 6), harm-reduction messaging, which varied by site, and behavioural intent.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: All participants used drugs; the comparison group less often used fentanyl, heroin and methamphetamine and less often injected (Table 2).

outcomes.instruments: Weekly surveys with a modified timeline followback (refs. 17–18). Eight behaviours chosen by the authors from the literature (Table 1): someone else present when using; naloxone nearby; testing the strength of drugs before use; using drugs slowly; asking someone to check on you; using by a non-injection route (smoking, snorting, sniffing, swallowing or anal use); watching someone use the same drugs first; throwing out drugs that were bad or not as expected. Nonfatal overdose: a time in the past week when the participant lost consciousness and someone had to revive them (Methods › Nonfatal Overdose).
outcomes.validity_norms: The composite score is the authors' own; its validity and reliability are not reported in the article or in the eMethods, which state without data that the eight behaviours are independent of one another (supplement p. 3). Behavioural intent was not measured (authors' limitation). Table 1's notes, read in the PubMed Central copy by the second reader, give the scoring (always 2, sometimes 1, never 0; throwing out bad drugs 1 or 0) and define testing the strength of drugs as trying a small amount first, and using slowly as spacing use out over time.
outcomes.operationalization: Daily composite: each behaviour rated always, sometimes or never on each drug-use day and summed across the eight, range 0–15, with discarding counting 0 or 1 because always discarding means no use that day; secondary analyses collapse always and sometimes into yes (Methods › Variables and Measurement › Outcomes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Eleven outcomes (composite score, count, eight behaviours, nonfatal overdose), each unadjusted and adjusted, and 13 interaction tests listed in the eMethods (supplement p. 6; editors' count); the authors call all P values descriptive (Methods › Statistical Analysis; eMethods).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: all outcomes were self-reported by participants who knew their own strip use.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 3, adjusted estimates unless stated. Composite score: difference 0.86 (95% CI 0.34–1.38; n = 684), mean 7.37 (6.63–8.11) in the strip group versus 6.51 (5.83–7.19); unadjusted 0.89 (0.44–1.35; n = 719). Editors' calculation: 0.86 is 5.7% of the 0–15 range and 13% above the comparison group's mean. Behaviour count: RR 1.11 (1.04–1.19). Individual behaviours (RR): naloxone nearby 1.10 (1.04–1.18); testing the strength of drugs before use 1.41 (1.24–1.61); asking someone to check 1.26 (1.10–1.45); throwing out bad or unexpected drugs 1.50 (1.12–2.01; unadjusted 1.27, 0.98–1.66); watching someone use the same drugs first 1.19 (1.04–1.36); someone else present 1.04 (0.99–1.09); using slowly 1.10 (0.99–1.22); non-injection route 0.86 (0.79–0.94). Nonfatal overdose: unadjusted RR 2.06 (1.09–3.89; n = 710), adjusted 1.20 (0.70–2.06; n = 677), mean daily risk 0.02 (0.01–0.03) in both groups; the association was modified by age in adjusted analyses (P = .02) but not in unadjusted ones, the ratio decreasing with age: in eFigure 5 (supplement p. 22) the strip group's modelled daily probability falls with age while the comparison group's stays nearly flat, the lines crossing at about age 42 and the 95% bands overlapping at every age from 19 to 76 (editors' reading of the figure; no age-specific ratios or intervals are printed). Raw daily data (supplement pp. 18–21; editors' reading of the figures): the share of participants reporting a nonfatal overdose on drug-use days was higher in the strip group on 25 of the 28 days, lower on 2 and about equal on the last, averaging about 3.4 against 1.6 in 100 across the daily values, with daily 95% bands that overlap on every day (eFigure 4), in line with the unadjusted ratio; the strip group's daily composite score and count were above the comparison group's on every day, with a gap that neither closed nor widened over the 28 days (eFigures 1 and 2), and the single behaviours ran in the directions of Table 3 (eFigure 3).
analysis.covariates: Prespecified for each outcome (Methods › Covariates). Behaviour models (Table 3, note d): baseline strip use, state, age, race, ethnicity, sex, education, employment, ever having received strip instructions and past 30-day overdose, plus daily drug category, study week and part of the week. Nonfatal-overdose model (note g): baseline strip use, state, age, race, ethnicity and sex, plus daily drug category, study week, part of the week, the composite risk-reduction score and the number of times strips were used. Injecting entered neither as a covariate (notes read in the PubMed Central copy, PMC12076174, by the second reader; the eMethods › Statistical Analysis, supplement p. 6, give the same two sets); daily injection was tested only as a possible modifier of the overdose association. Not adjusted in any model: the baseline level of the outcome behaviours, although it was measured (eTable 4). The covariance structure of each model was chosen by information criteria (best fit).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned in the article or the eMethods; covariates are said to have been prespecified before analysis on the basis of the design and expert opinion. The Stay Safe Study protocol (Pro0006830 in the article's Funding/Support statement; Pro00068304, approved on 16 March 2023, in the eMethods, supplement p. 2) and the parent HEALing Communities Study protocol were approved by Advarra; the parent study's protocol is published (refs. 15–16).
analysis.selective_reporting: All eight behaviours and the overdose outcome are reported, unadjusted and adjusted. The eMethods (supplement p. 6) name the modifiers tested: state, age, race, ethnicity, sex and study week for the composite score and for nonfatal overdose, and daily injection for overdose only (13 interaction tests, editors' count); only the age interaction for overdose is reported, so the results of the other 12 are not given. The analysis by strip result is announced as future work.
analysis.power: The authors state the sample was powered for the primary objective; no calculation is shown in the main text or in the eMethods. With a mean daily overdose risk of 0.02, the adjusted risk ratio is imprecise (0.70–2.06).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Over four weeks, participants who already used test strips at baseline reported a composite risk-reduction score 0.86 points higher on a 0–15 scale (about 13% above the comparison group's mean) and more of five of the eight behaviours, but less use of non-injection routes; they had also reported more of these behaviours at baseline (median composite score over the past 30 days 8 against 7, eTable 4), a gap of similar size that no model adjusted for (medians against adjusted means; editors' reading), and the raw daily gap neither closed nor widened over the four weeks (eFigure 1). Self-reported nonfatal overdose did not differ after adjustment (RR 1.20, 0.70–2.06), an interval compatible with a 30% reduction or a doubling; unadjusted, it was about twice as high in the strip group, which reported overdoses on more of the 28 days (eFigure 4).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Key Points say the findings demonstrate “the role of FTS as a harm reduction strategy among PWUD” (Key Points › Meaning), and the Discussion that they counter the claim that strips enable fentanyl use (Discussion, 1st paragraph). The abstract's conclusion is more careful: people who use strips may also engage in a broader set of harm-reduction strategies. The design compares people who chose to use strips with people who did not, with self-reported outcomes and baseline differences in the same behaviours, so it shows co-occurrence, not a role of strips. For overdose, “no difference” (abstract) and the suggestion that strips alone may be insufficient to reduce overdose rates (Conclusions) are read from an imprecise null.

timeline.event: Krieger et al. (2018), young adults in the United States, and Karamouzian et al. (2018), a Vancouver supervised injection facility: earlier single-site studies cited by the authors (refs. 8, 51); the latter read in this batch (card sc_karamouzian_2018).
Peiper et al. (2019): strip distribution at a syringe services programme in the southeastern United States (ref. 9); not read.
Green et al. (2020): laboratory sensitivity and specificity of fentanyl strips, cited for the strips' high sensitivity (ref. 11).
Lockwood et al. (2021): high concentrations of stimulants and cutting agents cause false positives on fentanyl strips (ref. 12, cited; not read).
Maghsoudi et al. (2022), systematic review of drug checking services to 2019, not cited here (read in this batch; card sc_maghsoudi_2022).
Recruitment and data collection, May to December 2023.

Kutscher et al. (2024), a scoping review of fentanyl strips, cited for acceptability, associated behaviours and a median uptake of 19% (ref. 14); Zibbell et al. (2024), baseline findings of the South Atlantic Fentanyl Test Strip Study (ref. 52); neither read.
This study published (13 May 2025).

replication.where_it_stands: The largest prospective study of strip use and self-reported behaviour among the papers read. Its behaviour association agrees with the smaller, mostly cross-sectional studies the authors cite (summarized in a scoping review not read), and its null overdose result sits beside the crude association of intended dose reduction with lower overdose odds reported by Karamouzian et al. (2018); neither design can show an effect of strips. The authors' planned analysis of how strip results affect behaviour has not been read.

funding.funder: NIH and the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration through the NIH HEAL Initiative (awards UM1DA049394, UM1DA049406, UM1DA049415, UM1DA049417). what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial, individual or cluster (by site or community), of offering test strips with instruction against usual services among people not yet using strips, measuring behaviours before and after and overdose from emergency, hospital and death records; failing that, a cohort of people starting to use strips (an incident-use design), adjusted for baseline behaviours and analysed by strip result.

domains.note: Adjustment differed by outcome (Table 3, notes d and g, PubMed Central copy): the behaviour models included state, demographics, education, employment, strip instructions, past overdose and daily drug category, but not injecting or the baseline level of the same behaviours; the overdose model included state, demographics and daily drug category but not injecting, past overdose or strip instructions, and it also included strip use and the risk-reduction score during follow-up, which may carry part of any effect. Prior harm-reduction engagement and risk perception were not measured; the strip group already reported more risk reduction at baseline. The crude overdose risk ratio of 2.06 falling to 1.20 after adjustment shows strong confounding by risk, possibly with over-adjustment as well. The supplement confirms both covariate sets (eMethods, p. 6) and shows the strip group's higher baseline level of the same behaviours, which no model included: median composite score 8 against 7, naloxone always nearby 64.5% against 38.8%, never testing the strength of drugs 14.7% against 53.8% (eTable 4).

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Prevalent strip use among clients of strip-distributing sites; the analysed sample (732 of 1156) required at least 2 weekly surveys and a drug-use day, conditions met only after follow-up began. Those not analysed differed in state, race, ethnicity and employment; their strip use and drug use are not compared (eTable 2).

Self-reported past 30-day use, measured once; non-response and 'don't know' classed as no use; frequency of use and results not used. The question asked about using fentanyl test strips to check one's drugs in the past 30 days (eTable 1, note 2).

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Exposure fixed at baseline while strip use during follow-up varied (recorded daily) and harm-reduction messaging varied by site; people in the comparison group may have started using strips during follow-up.

36.7% of enrolled participants were not analysed and up to 7.5% of the analysed sample dropped from the adjusted models (677 of 732); reasons for loss are unknown and may include fatal overdose; a missing-at-random mixed model for the composite score gave negligible differences. Among those analysed, weekly survey completion and loss to follow-up were similar in the two groups (eTable 1), but the 424 not analysed are compared only on demographics, on which they differed (eTable 2); a survey counted as completed when any question was answered; the baseline composite score is missing for 112 of 726 (15.4%, editors' calculation; eTable 4); the missing-at-random check was run for the composite score only, not for overdose (eMethods).

All outcomes self-reported weekly by participants who knew their own strip use, with social desirability and recall bias (authors' limitation); the composite score is unvalidated; testing the strength of drugs is defined in Table 1's note as trying a small amount first, so it does not overlap with strip testing.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No registration; 11 outcomes, unadjusted and adjusted, without correction for multiplicity; the covariates of each model appear only in the table notes and the eMethods; only one of the tested interactions is reported. The eMethods list 13 interaction tests across the two outcomes, one of them reported, and the covariance structures were chosen by best fit (p. 6).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I judges whether the study can estimate the effect of using test strips. It shows co-occurrence rather than an effect: strip use was chosen by people who already reported more risk reduction, outcomes were self-reported, a third of enrolled participants were not analysed, and residual confounding could plausibly explain a difference of 0.86 points on a 0–15 scale. No domain is judged critical, because the design is prospective and the main measured confounders were adjusted for. Citable for: in 2023, among clients of harm-reduction sites in Kentucky, New York and Ohio, people reporting strip use also reported somewhat more risk-reduction behaviours over the next four weeks (adjusted difference 0.86 on 0–15) and less non-injection use, with no clear difference in self-reported nonfatal overdose (adjusted RR 1.20, 0.70–2.06). Not citable for: strips causing behaviour change, strips preventing or failing to prevent overdose, differences by age, or the effect of strip results. The supplement (read 27 October 2026) changes no domain judgment: it confirms the covariate sets, shows a baseline gap in the same behaviours (median composite score 8 against 7) that no model adjusted for and an analysed sample selected from those enrolled, and reports the age modification of the overdose association as one of 13 interaction tests, with bands that overlap at every age.

key_findings.finding: Stay Safe Study, ancillary to the HEALing Communities Study: 1156 people enrolled at 14 strip-distributing harm-reduction organizations in Kentucky, New York and Ohio, May to December 2023; 732 analysed (drug use on at least 1 day and at least 2 weekly surveys), of whom 414 (56.6%) reported strip use in the 30 days before baseline and 318 did not.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Design, Setting, and Participants; Methods › Setting; Results, 1st paragraph; Results › Baseline Characteristics, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: 424 enrolled participants (36.7%) were not analysed (editors' calculation); the flow diagram is an image and was not read; eTable 2 compares them with those analysed (key finding 15).

key_findings.finding: Baseline differences, strip group versus comparison group (Table 2): Ohio 48.6% versus 36.2% and New York 18.1% versus 27.4% (P = .001); White 85.8% versus 75.4% and Black 6.1% versus 12.5% (P = .001); Hispanic 5.6% versus 13.0% (P = .001); past 30-day fentanyl 78.2% versus 59.2%, heroin 76.8% versus 61.8%, methamphetamine 64.5% versus 56.4%, opioids with stimulants 65.7% versus 48.4%, injection 75.1% versus 56.6%; ever received strip instructions 76.2% versus 40.6%; past 30-day overdose 26.0% versus 20.5% (P = .10). Age, sex, education and employment did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Results › Baseline Characteristics, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: At baseline the strip group already had a higher mean composite score and number of risk-reduction behaviours over the past 30 days and a higher prevalence of nearly every behaviour across most drug categories, except non-injection use, which was more common in the comparison group; smoking was more prevalent in the comparison group.
key_findings.locator: Results › Baseline Characteristics, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Values in eTables 3–5 of Supplement 1 (supplement pp. 10–17; key findings 13 and 14). The text calls the baseline composite score and count means; eTable 4 gives medians (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome: adjusted difference in the mean daily composite score 0.86 (95% CI 0.34–1.38; n = 684; P = .001), 7.37 (6.63–8.11) in the strip group versus 6.51 (5.83–7.19); unadjusted 0.89 (0.44–1.35; n = 719). Count of behaviours: adjusted rate ratio 1.11 (1.04–1.19).
key_findings.locator: Results › Overdose Risk Reduction Behaviors › Mean Daily Composite Score; Mean Daily Rate of Behaviors; Table 3
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 0.86 is 5.7% of the 0–15 range and 13% above the comparison group's mean.

key_findings.finding: Individual behaviours, adjusted risk ratios for the strip group: naloxone nearby 1.10 (1.04–1.18); testing the strength of drugs before use 1.41 (1.24–1.61); asking someone to check on them 1.26 (1.10–1.45); throwing out bad or unexpected drugs 1.50 (1.12–2.01; unadjusted 1.27, 0.98–1.66); watching someone use the same drugs first 1.19 (1.04–1.36); someone else present 1.04 (0.99–1.09); using slowly 1.10 (0.99–1.22); smoking, snorting, sniffing, swallowing or anal use 0.86 (0.79–0.94).
key_findings.locator: Results › Overdose Risk Reduction Behaviors › Mean Daily Probability of Each Behavior; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Self-reported nonfatal overdose: unadjusted risk ratio 2.06 (1.09–3.89; n = 710) for the strip group; adjusted 1.20 (0.70–2.06; n = 677), with a mean daily risk of 0.02 (0.01–0.03) in both groups. In adjusted analyses the association was modified by age (P = .02), the ratio decreasing as age increased.
key_findings.locator: Results › Overdose Risk Reduction Behaviors › Mean Daily Risk of Self-Reported Nonfatal Overdose; Table 3
key_findings.note: eFigure 5 (supplement p. 22) plots the modelled risks by age (key finding 19); no age-specific ratios are printed. The raw daily shares are in eFigure 4 (key finding 18).

key_findings.finding: Measures: eight behaviours chosen by the authors from the literature, each rated always, sometimes or never on every drug-use day and summed to a 0–15 daily score (discarding counts 0 or 1); nonfatal overdose = losing consciousness and needing to be revived; exposure = self-reported strip use in the past 30 days at baseline, with non-response and 'don't know' coded as no use.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Variables and Measurement › Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Nonfatal Overdose; Exposure › Baseline FTS Use; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Analysis: population-averaged generalized estimating equations with covariates prespecified for each outcome. The table notes give two sets: for the behaviour outcomes (Table 3, note d), baseline strip use, state, age, race, ethnicity, sex, education, employment, ever having received strip instructions and past 30-day overdose, plus daily drug category, study week and part of the week; for nonfatal overdose (note g), baseline strip use, state, age, race, ethnicity and sex, plus daily drug category, study week, part of the week, the composite risk-reduction score and the number of times strips were used. Injecting entered neither. Models: normal with identity link and compound symmetry for the composite score; Poisson with log link, with compound symmetry or first-order autoregressive structure, for the count, the single behaviours and overdose. A missing-at-random mixed model for the composite score gave negligible differences.
key_findings.page: publisher HTML; PMC HTML; supplement pp. 5–6
key_findings.locator: Methods › Covariates; Sociodemographic and Drug Use Characteristics; Characteristics Varying Over Time; Statistical Analysis; Table 3, notes b and d to g (PubMed Central copy, PMC12076174); eMethods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph (supplement pp. 5–6)
key_findings.note: The table notes are not on the publisher page, which shows only their letters; they were read as text in the PubMed Central copy by the second reader (AI reader 147). The Methods list the covariates without saying which model used which. The eMethods (supplement p. 6) give the same two sets and say which covariates belong to which model.

key_findings.finding: Authors' limitations: harm-reduction clients are not representative; no data on prior harm-reduction engagement; messaging varied across sites; a mostly non-Hispanic White sample; behavioural intent not measured; four-week follow-up; self-reports subject to social desirability and recall bias; anonymity prevented knowing why people were lost, including any fatal overdoses.
key_findings.locator: Strengths and Limitations, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Authors' conclusions: strip use was associated with more risk-reduction behaviours but not with the risk of nonfatal overdose; strips alone may be insufficient to reduce overdose rates, particularly among people with complex, high-risk drug use, and should be integrated with other harm reduction such as naloxone distribution.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions; Abstract › Conclusions and Relevance; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The Introduction states that strips detect fentanyl at approximately 20 to 200 mg/mL in under five minutes, have high sensitivity for fentanyl and analogues, and can be affected by stimulants and cutting agents (refs. 11–13).
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: mg/mL is implausible for an immunoassay threshold; Karamouzian et al. (2018) give a detection limit of 0.13 μg/mL (sc_karamouzian_2018), so the unit is probably ng/mL (editors' reading).

key_findings.finding: The authors hypothesized that people who used strips at baseline would report more risk-reduction behaviours and a lower daily risk of nonfatal overdose during follow-up; the unadjusted overdose estimate went the other way (RR 2.06) and the adjusted one showed no clear difference (1.20).
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 4th paragraph; Results › Mean Daily Risk of Self-Reported Nonfatal Overdose

key_findings.finding: Models (eMethods): population-averaged GEE with a normal or Poisson distribution and identity or log link, the covariance structure chosen by information criteria. Every model included baseline strip use, state, age, race, ethnicity and sex, plus drug category, study week and part of the week for each drug-use day; education, employment, ever having received strip instructions and past 30-day overdose entered the behaviour models only, and the daily composite score and the number of times strips were used the nonfatal-overdose model only. Modification was tested by two-way interactions of baseline strip use with state, age, race, ethnicity, sex and study week (composite score and nonfatal overdose) and daily injection (overdose only). A missing-at-random mixed model was fitted for the composite score only, with negligible differences; all P values are called descriptive.
key_findings.locator: eMethods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph (begins p. 5; the model, covariate and interaction sentences on p. 6)
key_findings.note: The same covariate sets as Table 3, notes d and g (key finding 7). Editors' count: 13 interaction tests, one reported (age, for overdose).

key_findings.finding: Baseline risk-reduction behaviours over the past 30 days, 414 people who had used strips against 312 who had not (the 726 who used drugs in the past 30 days): composite score median 8.0 (quartiles 7.0–10.0) against 7.0 (5.0–8.0) and number of behaviours 6.0 (5.0–7.0) against 5.0 (4.0–6.0) (each P < .001; both missing for 112). Answering always: someone else present 53.4% against 43.3%, naloxone nearby 64.5% against 38.8%, testing the strength of drugs 36.5% against 17.0% (never 14.7% against 53.8%), using slowly 33.1% against 19.9%, asking someone to check 27.3% against 9.3% (each P < .001), watching someone use the same drugs first 15.7% against 9.0% (P = .003); using by routes other than injection 32.4% against 41.5% (only injecting 17.9% against 9.3%; P = .008); throwing out bad drugs sometimes 29.5% against 21.5% (P = .04).
key_findings.locator: eTable 4
key_findings.note: Medians, although the article's text calls them means (reporting issue). No model adjusted for these baseline levels (key finding 12). Editors' calculation: 112 of 726 is 15.4%.

key_findings.finding: Drug categories and routes at baseline (eTable 3) and behaviours by drug category (eTable 5), strip group against comparison group: stimulants only 9.4% against 18.6% and opioids with stimulants (without benzodiazepines) 47.8% against 37.7% (P < .001); past 30-day injection 75.1% against 56.6%, higher in the strip group in four of the five drug categories; smoking 62.6% against 66.4% and snorting or sniffing 53.6% against 62.6%; routes other than injection less common, and testing the strength of drugs more common (overall 85.1% against 45.1%), in the strip group in every drug category.
key_findings.locator: eTable 3; eTable 5
key_findings.note: Confirms Results › Baseline Characteristics, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs. The per-route P values come from Mantel-Haenszel tests stratified by baseline strip use (footnote 11), so they are not used here.

key_findings.finding: Enrolled participants not analysed against those analysed (424 against 732 of 1156): New York 43.2% against 22.1%, Kentucky 17.2% against 34.7%, Ohio 39.6% against 43.2% (P < .001); White 68.3% against 80.2%, other race 17.2% against 9.7%, Black or African American 11.4% against 8.7% (P < .001); Hispanic or Latino 19.5% against 8.7% (P < .001); employed 33.5% against 23.1% and unemployed 39.7% against 53.4% (P < .001); median age 40.0 against 41.0 (P = .03); female 46.0% against 49.6% (P = .01); education P = .27. Strip use, drug use, injecting and past overdose are not compared.
key_findings.locator: eTable 2
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 183 of 345 New York enrollees (53.0%) were not analysed, against 73 of 327 in Kentucky (22.3%) and 168 of 484 in Ohio (34.7%).

key_findings.finding: Weekly survey completion in the analysed sample, strip group against comparison group: 1st survey 343 (82.9%) against 267 (84.0%), 2nd 366 (88.4%) against 286 (89.9%), 3rd 373 (90.1%) against 292 (91.8%), 4th 352 (85.0%) against 274 (86.2%); lost to follow-up between the 2nd and 3rd surveys 11 (2.7%) against 6 (1.9%) and between the 3rd and 4th 40 (9.7%) against 27 (8.5%). A survey counted as completed when it held any data.
key_findings.locator: eTable 1 and its notes
key_findings.note: Note 2 gives the exposure question: use of fentanyl test strips to check one's drugs in the past 30 days.

key_findings.finding: Raw daily values on drug-use days over the 28 days, by baseline strip use: the strip group's mean composite score (about 6.8 to 7.6, against about 5.8 to 7.2) and number of behaviours were higher on every day, with a gap that neither closed nor widened; among single behaviours the gap was widest for testing the strength of drugs (roughly 52 to 62 in 100 against 33 to 45), and the comparison group more often used routes other than injection.
key_findings.locator: eFigures 1, 2 and 3
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of the figures (unadjusted daily values with 95% bands; no numbers are printed).

key_findings.finding: Raw daily share of participants reporting a nonfatal overdose on drug-use days, by baseline strip use: higher in the strip group on 25 of the 28 days, lower on days 1 and 5 and about equal on day 28; the daily values average about 3.4 in 100 in the strip group and 1.6 in 100 in the comparison group, a ratio of about 2.1, close to the unadjusted risk ratio of 2.06; the daily 95% bands overlap on every day.
key_findings.locator: eFigure 4
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of the figure, values measured from the image (no numbers are printed). Unadjusted; after adjustment the mean daily risk was 0.02 in both groups (key finding 5).

key_findings.finding: Adjusted mean daily probability of a self-reported nonfatal overdose by age (19 to 76), by baseline strip use, on a log scale: the strip group's line falls steeply with age while the comparison group's stays nearly flat; they cross at about age 42, so the modelled risk is higher in the strip group among younger and lower among older participants, and the 95% bands overlap at every age. No age-specific ratios or intervals are printed.
key_findings.locator: eFigure 5
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of the figure (crossing age and band overlap measured from the image). The plotted probabilities (about 0.0003 to 0.014 in the strip group, 0.002 to 0.003 in the comparison group) are well below the adjusted mean daily risk of 0.02 in Table 3, and the covariate values behind them are not stated (reporting issue). One of 13 interaction tests (key finding 12); absent in unadjusted analyses (Results › Mean Daily Risk of Self-Reported Nonfatal Overdose).

reporting_issues.issue: Introduction, 2nd paragraph: strips are said to detect fentanyl at approximately 20 to 200 mg/mL; the detection limit reported by Karamouzian et al. (2018) is 0.13 μg/mL, about a million times lower, so the unit is probably ng/mL.
reporting_issues.consequence: Do not cite this sentence for strip sensitivity.

reporting_issues.issue: The Statistical Analysis calls all P values purely descriptive, with no correction for 11 outcomes, but the Key Points describe the strip group as significantly more likely to report more behaviours, and the Results and Discussion read the overdose estimates as tests (no longer statistically significant after adjustment).
reporting_issues.consequence: Four of the five behaviour associations that exclude 1 have lower limits between 1.04 and 1.12; cite them as descriptive estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The exposure is strip use at baseline, but the adjusted nonfatal-overdose model (Table 3, note g) also includes the number of times strips were used and the composite risk-reduction score during follow-up, which come after the exposure and may lie on its path, and it leaves out injecting and past overdose; the behaviour models (note d) include neither follow-up variable. The Discussion attributes the attenuation of the overdose estimate to the strip group's concurrent risk-raising and risk-lowering behaviours, which partly describes the adjustment itself.
reporting_issues.consequence: The adjusted overdose ratio of 1.20 may be pulled towards 1 by this adjustment as well as reflecting confounding by risk; cite it with that caveat. The behaviour estimates are not affected by it, but they were not adjusted for the baseline level of the same behaviours.

reporting_issues.issue: Abstract › Results states there was no difference in nonfatal overdose, from an adjusted risk ratio of 1.20 with a 95% CI of 0.70–2.06.
reporting_issues.consequence: An absence of evidence, not evidence of no effect; claims should give the interval.

reporting_issues.issue: Results › Baseline Characteristics, 3rd paragraph, says the strip group had a higher mean composite score and a greater mean number of behaviours at baseline (eTable 4); eTable 4 gives medians and quartiles (composite 8.0, 7.0–10.0, against 7.0, 5.0–8.0; number 6.0 against 5.0), not means.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the medians; the direction is the same.

reporting_issues.issue: eFigure 5 plots adjusted mean daily probabilities of a nonfatal overdose of about 0.002 to 0.003 in the comparison group at every age, a tenth to a seventh of the adjusted mean daily risk of 0.02 (0.01–0.03) the Results give for that group, and 0.0003 to 0.014 in the strip group (log scale; editors' reading of the figure and calculation); the covariate values at which the figure's estimates were computed are not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Read eFigure 5 for the direction of the age modification only, not for absolute risks or age-specific ratios.

reporting_issues.issue: The Stay Safe Study protocol number is Pro0006830 in the article's Funding/Support statement and Pro00068304, approved on 16 March 2023, in the eMethods.
reporting_issues.consequence: The article's number has one digit fewer; no consequence for the results.

disagreements.first_pass: ROBINS-I judges whether the study can estimate the effect of using test strips. It shows co-occurrence rather than an effect: strip use was chosen by people who already reported more risk reduction, outcomes were self-reported, a third of enrolled participants were not analysed, and residual confounding could plausibly explain a difference of 0.86 points on a 0–15 scale. Not citable for: strips causing behaviour change, strips preventing or failing to prevent overdose, or the effect of strip results.
