design_detail: Analysis of the Stay Safe Study, a prospective observational cohort ancillary to the HEALing Communities Study, May to December 2023, in Kentucky, New York and Ohio. People who use drugs were recruited at community harm-reduction programmes that distributed fentanyl test strips (FTS); the study supplied no strips. After a baseline survey, four weekly surveys over 28 days recorded, for each day of drug use, the drugs used, up to two strip uses, each self-reported result (positive, negative or undetermined) and what participants said they changed because of the result (12 listed changes or none). Analysis of the 541 participants who used a strip at least once during follow-up: population-averaged generalized estimating equations comparing strip uses with a positive and a negative result, adjusted for pre-specified baseline and same-day covariates. Appraised with ROBINS-I, as for the other strip-behaviour cards (sc_vickers_smith_2025, sc_krieger_2018), because the question is whether acting on a strip result changes behaviour; the contrast is positive against negative result among people who chose to test.
can_establish: How often people who use drugs and attend harm-reduction programmes in three US states in 2023 said, in weekly recall, that they changed what they did because of a strip result, and how those reports differed between positive and negative results after adjustment for measured differences.
cannot_establish: Whether a positive result causes people to use less or to use more safely (self-reported, unverified results and behaviours, participants who chose to test and stayed in follow-up, residual confounding by the drug tested and by expectations), whether strip use prevents overdose (not analysed), how accurate the strips were (not examined), or what happens among people outside harm-reduction services.

sample.recruitment: Clients of community harm-reduction programmes, including syringe services programmes, that were distributing strips from buildings or mobile vans in Kentucky, New York and Ohio, May to December 2023; consent and data collection by programme or study staff (Methods › Study design, p. 2). Payment by reloadable cash card: $10 for screening, $50 for the baseline survey and $40 to $55 for each weekly survey (Methods › Surveys, p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 or over; self-assessed proficiency in reading and speaking English; able to consent; living in one of the three states for the 28-day follow-up; non-prescribed use of methamphetamine, cocaine (powder or crack), heroin, fentanyl or prescription opioids, benzodiazepines or stimulants in the past 30 days (Methods › Participants, p. 2). Analysis required the baseline survey, at least two weekly surveys, drug use during follow-up and at least one strip use (Statistical analyses, p. 2).
sample.demographics: FTS sample (Table 1, p. 4): median age 41 years (quartiles 34 to 48); 49.0% female sex at birth; 83.5% white, 7.0% Black or African American, 8.8% Hispanic or Latino; 99.4% urban; 18.3% unsheltered homeless; 88.7% public health insurance; 53.6% unemployed; 65% with a monthly income of $500 or less and over 70% running out of money for necessities every day or weekly (Results, 2nd paragraph, p. 5).
sample.attrition: Of 1156 enrolled, 424 were not in the full sample (371 completed fewer than two weekly surveys, 330 reported no drug use during follow-up; reasons overlap) (Fig. 1, p. 3). In the FTS sample, 454, 477, 486 and 461 completed the four weekly surveys (Fig. 1).
sample.selection_effects: Clients of harm-reduction programmes, whom the authors describe as possibly already inclined to risk reduction (Discussion, p. 7); the analysed 541 are 47% of those enrolled (editors' calculation) and were selected on behaviour after baseline (survey completion, drug use and strip use during follow-up). Compared with the 191 in the full sample who used no strip, they were more often white (83.5% versus 75.3%) and less often Black (7.0% versus 14.2%; p = 0.008) and received food assistance less often (48.6% versus 59.7%; p = 0.008) (Table 1, p. 4).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported strip result for up to two strip uses on each day of drug use, recalled in weekly surveys completed in person on tablets or by web link (Methods › Surveys, p. 2). Results were not verified; strips came from the programmes, not the study, and whether a negative result reflected improper use is unknown (Limitations, p. 7).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable: observational; the study provided no strips (p. 2). Whether participants had ever been instructed in strip use was a baseline covariate. The paper describes study-orientation staff and does not establish that nobody received strip-use instructions during follow-up.
exposure.polysubstance: The drugs tested on each day were grouped as illicit opioids only, illicit stimulants only, illicit opioids and stimulants only, illicit benzodiazepines (with or without opioids or stimulants), and other or unknown; used as a time-varying covariate and as an effect modifier for the amount used (p. 3). Other substance use was not analysed.

comparison.controls: Strip uses with a self-reported negative result in the same sample. The population-averaged models mix comparisons within the same person and between people.
comparison.matching: None; adjustment for state, age, race, ethnicity, sex, education, employment, ever having been instructed in strip use and overdose in the past 30 days, and for study week, weekday or weekend, strip instance (first or second that day), the same-day composite overdose risk-reduction score and the type of drug tested (Methods › Statistical analyses, p. 3; table notes, pp. 6–8).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Whether a person expected or wanted fentanyl in the drug tested, tolerance, injecting, earlier overdoses and overall risk perception; the authors name prior overdoses and risk perception as possible unmeasured confounders (Limitations, p. 7), although overdose in the past 30 days was adjusted for.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Comparison is between results, not people; type of drug tested adjusted for.

outcomes.instruments: Study-developed survey items: after each result, whether behaviour changed because of it, from 12 options (used with someone else; took turns; used near someone with naloxone; tested strength with a smaller amount first; used more; used another drug with it; tested again; did not use; threw drugs away; gave them away; sold them; used less) or no change (Methods › Surveys, p. 2; Table 3, p. 7). Amount used because of the result: less or none, same, or more (Table 4, p. 8).
outcomes.validity_norms: Items written for this study; no validation reported. The primary any-change outcome counts using more and using another drug alongside as changes.
outcomes.operationalization: Primary outcome: daily probability of reporting any of the 12 changes because of a result, modelled as a ratio of probabilities (Poisson GEE, log link). Secondary: each of the 12 changes, and a proportional-odds model of using less or none versus the same versus more (Methods, p. 3; table notes).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None by design: only the any-change association was the primary hypothesis, and the authors call all other p-values descriptive (Statistical analyses, last paragraph, starting p. 3 and continuing p. 5). 14 counts the primary composite, the 12 single changes and the amount model; there were also 6 pre-specified effect-modification tests of the primary outcome and one of the amount model by drug type.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: self-completed surveys by participants who knew their results.

analysis.effect_sizes: Any of 12 changes because of the result: mean daily probability 0.86 (95% CI 0.78 to 0.95) after a positive and 0.76 (0.69 to 0.84) after a negative result; ratio 1.12 (1.04 to 1.21), p = 0.002; modified by age (interaction p = 0.010): ratios 1.06 (0.98 to 1.14), 1.13 (1.05 to 1.22) and 1.23 (1.10 to 1.37) at the first quartile, median and third quartile of age; no modification by state, sex, race, ethnicity or study week (Table 2, p. 6). Single changes, positive versus negative (Table 3, p. 7): took turns 0.24 versus 0.19, ratio 1.29 (1.05 to 1.59); used near someone with naloxone 0.23 versus 0.15, 1.54 (1.16 to 2.05); used less 0.11 versus 0.02, 5.54 (2.52 to 12.19); used more 0.08 versus 0.19, 0.42 (0.26 to 0.68); no clear difference for using with someone else (0.41 versus 0.38), a test amount first (0.12 versus 0.10), testing again (0.05 versus 0.05), not using (0.02 versus 0.02), throwing away (0.01 versus 0.01), giving away (0.01 versus 0.01), selling (0.02 versus 0.01) or using another drug with it (0.02 versus 0.03). Amount (Table 4, p. 8): after a positive result less or none 0.090, same 0.847, more 0.063; after a negative result 0.023, 0.752 and 0.225; printed common cumulative odds ratio for reporting a lower amount category 4.37 (3.45 to 5.55), across both cumulative cut-points. By drug tested: benzodiazepines 19.92 (8.57 to 46.27), stimulants only 10.04 (6.49 to 15.53), opioids and stimulants 4.21 (2.74 to 6.45), opioids only 2.18 (1.44 to 3.28), other or unknown 2.11 (1.14 to 3.92); interaction p < 0.001.
analysis.covariates: Baseline: state, age, race, ethnicity, sex, education, employment, ever instructed in strip use, overdose in past 30 days. Same-day: study week, weekday or weekend, strip instance, composite overdose risk-reduction score, type of drug tested (p. 3). Adjusting for a same-day risk-reduction score whose behaviours overlap the outcomes (for example naloxone nearby) may remove part of what is being estimated.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; covariates and effect modifiers are described as pre-specified (p. 3). Protocol approved by the HEALing Communities Study single IRB (Advarra), protocol numbers printed differently on pp. 2 and 8.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract leads with the secondary amount model and the drug-type subgroups rather than the primary composite. The numbers of strip uses, positive, negative and undetermined results are not reported anywhere, and undetermined results are not analysed. A missing-at-random sensitivity model was fitted only for the primary outcome (negligible difference) (p. 3).
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation reported; 541 participants with repeated daily observations, number of observations not stated.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 541 clients of harm-reduction programmes who tested at least once in 28 days, most uses were followed by no change in amount whatever the result: after a positive result the modelled daily probability of using the same amount was 0.85, of using less or none 0.09 and of using more 0.06; after a negative result 0.75, 0.02 and 0.23. Positive results went with more reports of taking turns (0.24 versus 0.19) and of having someone with naloxone nearby (0.23 versus 0.15), and with fewer reports of using more (0.08 versus 0.19); not using, discarding, giving away or selling drugs were rare (1% to 2%) and no more frequent after a positive result. The any-change composite was high after both results (0.86 and 0.76).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports a four-fold reduction in the amount of drugs used after a positive result, and 20-fold, 10-fold and 2-fold reductions by drug type (p. 1). These are common cumulative odds ratios across both splits of a self-reported ordered amount category, not fold changes in the quantity used, and the contrast is driven as much by more frequent reports of using more after a negative result (0.225) as by using less after a positive one (0.090). The abstract concludes that strips help people immediately reduce their risks (p. 1), and the conclusions call the study compelling evidence for the impact of strips (p. 8), causal language that the limitations paragraph itself rules out (associations, not causal, p. 7). The abstract also merges the opioids-only and other-drugs estimates and omits the opioids-and-stimulants estimate.

timeline.event: Krieger et al. (2018): Rhode Island pilot; behaviour change reported after positive results, unadjusted (card sc_krieger_2018).
Peiper et al. (2019): strip distribution at a southeastern US syringe services programme, cited as finding behaviour change after positive results; not read.
Park et al. (2020): Baltimore pilot among women who sell sex; cited by this paper among studies of behaviour change after results (card sc_park_2020).

Klaire et al. (2022) and Goodman-Meza et al. (2022): cited as other studies of behaviour change directly after results; the authors summarize these earlier studies as finding change in one to two thirds of people with a positive result (p. 2). Klaire et al. on card sc_klaire_2022.
Kutscher et al. (2024): scoping review cited for high acceptability and behaviour change after positive results (card sc_kutscher_2024).

Vickers-Smith et al. (2025): companion analysis of the same Stay Safe cohort on strip use (not results) and risk-reduction behaviours; source of the composite score used here as a covariate (card sc_vickers_smith_2025).
This study: positive versus negative results, 541 participants, three states.

replication.where_it_stands: Earlier smaller, single-site studies report that people often say they act more cautiously after a positive result; this larger multi-state cohort agrees in direction but shows that most uses were followed by no change in amount, and adds that negative results were often followed by reports of using more. All of these studies rest on self-report without verification of results or behaviour, so the consistency may partly reflect shared reporting bias. Whether strip results change overdose risk has not been tested in a randomized or otherwise controlled design in the sources read.

funding.funder: National Institutes of Health and the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration through the NIH HEAL Initiative, awards UM1DA049394, UM1DA049406, UM1DA049415 and UM1DA049417; Drs Villani and Chandler were substantially involved as Scientific Officers; the content is the authors' responsibility (Role of funding source, p. 8).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict declared (p. 9).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from Columbia University, RTI International (data coordinating centre), the Universities of Kentucky and Ohio State, Wake Forest, the National Institute on Drug Abuse, the Kentucky behavioural health department and SAMHSA (p. 1). The study used the infrastructure of the HEALing Communities Study, an intervention to reduce opioid overdose deaths. Recorded as context, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A study that verifies results (for example by laboratory analysis of a portion of the tested sample) and records what people then do by a method less exposed to recall and social desirability (event-level reports soon after testing), in people who test and comparable people who do not, ideally with randomized provision of strips and overdose and amount used as outcomes.

domains.note: Positive and negative results differ systematically by the drug tested and by the person (expectation of fentanyl, preference, tolerance); the drug category and several personal factors are adjusted for, but expectation, injecting and risk perception are not (authors, p. 7). Adjustment for a same-day composite of risk-reduction behaviours that overlap the outcomes may over-adjust.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Clients of strip-distributing programmes; the analysed 541 are 47% of the 1156 enrolled and were selected on follow-up behaviour (surveys, drug use, strip use); people who tested differed from those who did not by race and income measures (Table 1).

Results self-reported up to a week later and not verified; strip accuracy and improper use not examined (p. 7); undetermined results excluded without counts; recall of the result may be influenced by what was done.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: No intervention was assigned; programmes varied in their instructions and harm-reduction messaging, partly captured by the 'ever instructed' covariate and by state.

Weekly completion 84% to 90% in the analysed sample (editors' calculation from Fig. 1); GEE assumes data missing completely at random; a missing-at-random model for the primary outcome changed little (p. 3); the number of observations and of missing items is not reported.

Self-reported, retrospective weekly recall of behaviour attributed by the participant to the result, by people who knew their result; unvalidated items; social desirability and recall bias acknowledged (p. 7). High any-change rates after negative results (0.76) suggest the items also capture routine practices.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Primary hypothesis stated, but no registration; 14 outcomes and several interaction tests without correction (declared descriptive); the abstract highlights secondary estimates and their subgroups.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I asks whether the study can estimate the effect of a positive strip result on what people then do. It shows association in self-report, not effect: results and behaviours are unverified and recalled weekly, the analysed people were selected on post-baseline behaviour, and positive and negative results come from different drugs and different expectations that the adjustment only partly captures. No domain is critical, because the design is prospective, the contrast is between results among the same kind of people, and the covariates were pre-specified. Citable for: what clients of US harm-reduction programmes in 2023 said they did after positive and negative results, as modelled probabilities (for example, same amount after 85% of positive results; using more after about a fifth of negative results; discarding or not using drugs rare after either). Not citable for: strips or positive results reducing the amount used (the abstract's fold reductions), effects on overdose, or strip accuracy.

key_findings.finding: Stay Safe Study, May to December 2023, Kentucky, New York and Ohio: adults recruited at harm-reduction programmes distributing strips completed a baseline survey and four weekly surveys over 28 days recording, for each day of drug use, strip use, up to two results per day and behaviour changes because of each result; the study supplied no strips.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Introduction, last paragraph; Methods › Study design, Participants and Surveys

key_findings.finding: Of 1405 screened, 1201 (85.5%) were eligible; 732 completed the baseline and at least two weekly surveys and reported drug use, and 541 of these (73.9%) used a strip at least once during follow-up and were analysed.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 5); Fig. 1 (p. 3)
key_findings.note: Fig. 1 (an image) gives 1156 enrolled and 424 not in the full sample (371 fewer than two weekly surveys, 330 no drug use during follow-up; reasons overlap).

key_findings.finding: Compared with the 191 people in the full sample who did not test, the 541 who tested were more often white (83.5% versus 75.3%) and less often Black or African American (7.0% versus 14.2%; p = 0.008), and less often received food assistance (48.6% versus 59.7%; p = 0.008); median age 41 in both.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 4); Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome: the modelled daily probability of reporting any of the 12 behaviour changes because of the result was 0.86 (95% CI 0.78 to 0.95) after a positive and 0.76 (0.69 to 0.84) after a negative result; ratio 1.12 (1.04 to 1.21), p = 0.002.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (p. 5); Table 2, Overall row (p. 6)
key_findings.note: The 12 changes include using more of the drug and using another drug with it (Table 3, p. 7).

key_findings.finding: The association with any change was modified by age (interaction p = 0.010): ratios 1.06 (0.98 to 1.14) at the first quartile of age, 1.13 (1.05 to 1.22) at the median and 1.23 (1.10 to 1.37) at the third quartile; there was no modification by state, sex, race, ethnicity or study week.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (p. 5); Table 2 (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: After positive versus negative results, participants more often reported taking turns with someone else (0.24 versus 0.19; ratio 1.29, 1.05 to 1.59), using near someone with naloxone (0.23 versus 0.15; 1.54, 1.16 to 2.05) and using less (0.11 versus 0.02; 5.54, 2.52 to 12.19), and less often using more (0.08 versus 0.19; 0.42, 0.26 to 0.68).
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (p. 5); Table 3 (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Not using the tested drugs (0.02 versus 0.02), throwing them away (0.01 versus 0.01), giving them away (0.01 versus 0.01), selling them (0.02 versus 0.01), testing again (0.05 versus 0.05) and using a smaller test amount first (0.12 versus 0.10) were not clearly more frequent after a positive than after a negative result.
key_findings.locator: Table 3

key_findings.finding: Amount used because of the result: after a positive result the modelled daily probabilities were 0.090 for less or none, 0.847 for the same and 0.063 for more; after a negative result 0.023, 0.752 and 0.225. The printed common cumulative odds ratio for reporting a lower amount category is 4.37 (95% CI 3.45 to 5.55), p < 0.001; the proportional-odds model covers both less or none versus same or more, and less/none/same versus more.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph (p. 5); Table 4, Overall rows (p. 8)

key_findings.finding: The amount association differed by the drug tested (interaction p < 0.001): odds ratios 19.92 (8.57 to 46.27) for illicit benzodiazepines, 10.04 (6.49 to 15.53) for stimulants only, 4.21 (2.74 to 6.45) for opioids and stimulants, 2.18 (1.44 to 3.28) for opioids only and 2.11 (1.14 to 3.92) for other or unknown drugs. After a negative result the modelled probability of using more was 0.373 for opioids only, 0.531 for stimulants only and 0.657 for benzodiazepines.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph (starts p. 5, estimates on p. 6); Table 4 (p. 8)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculations from Table 4's printed category probabilities give cumulative odds ratios of about 3.6 and 5.3 for benzodiazepines, rather than the reported adjusted common odds ratio of 19.92. The printed coefficient and probabilities are retained. These calculations do not re-fit the GEE model and cannot identify which reported quantity or prediction procedure explains the mismatch. Treat this as an unresolved reporting/reproducibility question, not a proven erroneous coefficient or a corrected ranking of drug subgroups.

key_findings.finding: On most days over 100 participants used a strip; the daily share of results reported positive, by state, mostly lay between about half and four fifths.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Fig. 2
key_findings.note: Shares read from Fig. 2 (an image), approximate: about 40% to 90% across days and states, Ohio mostly highest. The total numbers of strip uses and of positive, negative and undetermined results are not reported.

key_findings.finding: False-positive and false-negative results were not examined, and whether a negative result came from improper use is unknown; the authors state the design supports associations, not causal conclusions.
key_findings.locator: Limitations

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes the amount odds ratios as fold reductions in the amount of drugs used (four-fold, 20-fold, 10-fold, 2-fold). They are proportional-odds ratios for reporting a lower ordered amount category, common across less or none versus same or more and less/none/same versus more (Table 4); no quantity of drug used was measured.
reporting_issues.consequence: The amount used was not measured; in absolute terms 9.0% of positive-result uses were followed by using less or none, against 2.3% of negative-result uses, and most of the contrast comes from using more after negative results. Claims must use the probabilities, not the abstract's wording.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives one estimate, OR 2.11 (1.14 to 3.92), for people testing illicit opioids or other drugs; in the Results and Table 4 that estimate belongs to other or unknown drugs, and opioids only have OR 2.18 (1.44 to 3.28); the opioids-and-stimulants estimate (4.21) is omitted from the abstract.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor misreporting in the abstract; the table values should be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The primary outcome, any of the 12 behaviour changes, includes using more of the drug and using another drug with it (Table 3), yet the paper presents its association with a positive result as an association with risk-reduction behaviour.
reporting_issues.consequence: The primary ratio (1.12) mixes protective and risky changes and cannot be read as more risk reduction; the single-item results are more informative.

reporting_issues.issue: The numbers of strip uses and of positive, negative and undetermined results behind the models are not reported; the footnote to Table 4 refers to a number of participants with positive results that the table does not show.
reporting_issues.consequence: The precision and representativeness of the daily probabilities cannot be judged, and readers cannot tell how many observations each subgroup estimate rests on.

reporting_issues.issue: The Stay Safe Study IRB protocol number is printed as Pro00068304 on p. 2 and Pro0006830 on p. 8. Fig. 1 reports weekly survey completions of 454, 477, 486 and 461 and loss-to-follow-up boxes of 16 and 45, but does not show individual patterns of missed and resumed surveys.
reporting_issues.consequence: The protocol number has a minor typographical discrepancy. The diagram cannot reconstruct individual follow-up paths: weekly completion counts can rise when people resume surveys, and an increase alone is not proof of an arithmetic error.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 gives a benzodiazepine odds ratio of 19.918 (95% CI 8.573 to 46.273), but its category probabilities are 0.032, 0.701 and 0.266 after a positive result and 0.009, 0.334 and 0.657 after a negative result. Direct cumulative-odds calculations from those rounded probabilities give about 3.6 and 5.3, not 19.918 (editors' calculations). Ordinary rounding at the displayed precision cannot bridge this numerical gap. The Methods describe balanced marginal predictions from least-square means; the paper does not provide the fitted model or code needed to resolve the discrepancy.
reporting_issues.consequence: Report the paper's odds ratio and probabilities as separate printed results, with this unresolved reconstruction problem. Do not replace the adjusted coefficient with the probability-derived ratios or assert a corrected subgroup ordering without checking the model and prediction procedure. This does not change the independent conclusion that an odds ratio is not a fold reduction in drug quantity.

The paper describes study-orientation staff and does not establish that nobody received strip-use instructions during follow-up. Checked against Methods Study design and Surveys, p. 2; covariates, p. 3.

design_detail: Single-arm pretest–posttest pilot (the Fentanyl Innovative Testing, FIT, study), filed as a prospective cohort, nested in the EMERALD cohort of street-based cis-gender women who sell or trade sex in Baltimore, Maryland. 103 women who had used illegally obtained opioids in the past month were enrolled April 2018 to February 2019; at baseline all received a brief strip training, harm-reduction counselling tailored to their reported risks, an insert card, five fentanyl test strips (BTNX), injection equipment and naloxone, and were re-interviewed after a target of one month (mean 56 days). Outcomes: self-reported strip use, results and actions after results, acceptability, and pre–post changes in drug use, solitary use and overdose by McNemar's test, overall and stratified by strip use. Read from the PubMed Central author manuscript; 'AM p.' is the PDF page. Appraised with ROBINS-I, as for sc_krieger_2018, because strip provision with training is an intervention and the paper infers its effects.
can_establish: How many women in this Baltimore sample of women who sell sex and use opioids used the five strips within about two months, what results they reported, what they said they did after positive and negative results, and how acceptable they found the strips.
cannot_establish: Whether the strips, or the bundle of strips, counselling and naloxone, reduced drug use, solitary use or overdose: there was no comparison group, the women who used no strip changed as much or more, the baseline and follow-up questions on drug use covered different periods, and all outcomes were self-reported to study staff.

sample.recruitment: Targeted sampling with a mobile van in Baltimore neighbourhoods with drug and sex markets for the EMERALD cohort; all women enrolled in EMERALD from April 2018 to February 2019 were invited after their EMERALD visit (Methods 2 and 2.1, AM pp. 3–4). 52 of 175 approached declined screening, mostly for lack of time, childcare or withdrawal (Fig. 2, AM p. 16; Discussion, AM p. 10). Payment: $10 Visa gift card at baseline and $20 at follow-up (AM p. 4).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: EMERALD: aged 18 or over, self-identified cis-gender woman, sold or traded sex in the past 6 months, picked up clients 3 or more times in the past 3 months, willing to give contact details (AM p. 3). FIT: enrolled in EMERALD and used illegally obtained opioids (heroin, fentanyl or street-bought pills) in the past month (AM p. 4). All 20 ineligible women had not used opioids in the past month (Fig. 2, AM p. 16).
sample.demographics: Baseline, n = 103 (Table 1, AM pp. 17–18; Results, AM p. 6): 22.3% aged 18–29 and 54% under 40; 59.2% non-Hispanic White, 34.0% non-Hispanic Black, 6.8% Hispanic; 87.4% actively selling sex; 65.1% homeless in the past 6 months; 48.5% injected heroin and 30.1% injected fentanyl in the past 6 months; 73.8% smoked crack cocaine; 10.7% had ever used a strip; 75.7% concerned about fentanyl in their drugs and 42.7% preferring drugs with fentanyl; 96.1% used drugs alone.
sample.attrition: 68 of 103 (66%) completed follow-up, on average 56 days after baseline and 22.1% within the one-month target (AM p. 6; Fig. 2). Women aged 18–29 (34.3% of those lost versus 16.2% of completers, p = 0.04) and women who injected opioid pills (11.4% versus 1.5%, p = 0.03) were more often lost; no other baseline differences (AM p. 6; Table 1).
sample.selection_effects: A small convenience sample of women already in a cohort study, 70% of those approached agreeing to screening, analysed as completers only. The authors note the low participation rate may have caused selection bias (AM p. 10). Results apply to street-based women who sell sex and use opioids in one city with a fentanyl-dominated market.

exposure.measurement: The FIT bundle was given to everyone at baseline: 5 to 10 minutes of training in collecting a sample, testing and reading results; harm-reduction micro-counselling tailored to the risks reported in the baseline interview (for example on mixing alcohol and opioids, using alone, test doses, naloxone and polysubstance use); an insert card with strip instructions and overdose-prevention messages; five BTNX Rapid Response strips; injection equipment; and two doses of intramuscular naloxone (Methods 2.1, AM p. 4; Fig. 1, AM p. 15). Strip use, timing and results were self-reported at follow-up (Methods 2.2.3, AM p. 5).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to drug doses. Five strips at baseline; more strips, injection equipment and naloxone offered at follow-up and at later cohort visits (AM p. 4).
exposure.polysubstance: Baseline past-6-month use (Table 1): smoked crack cocaine 73.8%, snorted or smoked heroin 62.1%, injected heroin 48.5%, snorted powdered cocaine 34.0%, benzodiazepine pills 21.4%; alcohol in the past month 43.7%. Benzodiazepine and alcohol use were outcomes; no adjustment.

comparison.controls: None: single-arm pretest–posttest. The 68 completers were stratified post hoc into women who used at least one strip (57) and women who used none (11) (Statistical analysis, AM p. 6; Table 3, AM p. 21).
comparison.matching: None; unadjusted McNemar tests within each group.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Without a comparison group, secular trends, regression to the mean after enrolment at a time of heavy use, and the effects of the counselling, naloxone and the cohort visit itself cannot be separated from strip use.

outcomes.instruments: Interviewer-administered computer-assisted surveys of about 10 minutes at baseline and follow-up (AM pp. 4–5): use of each drug by route, frequency dichotomized as daily or less; one AUDIT-C question on drinking frequency; agreement with preferring fentanyl and with concern about fentanyl (5-point scales); solitary use, asking someone to check on you and being near someone with naloxone (any versus never); non-fatal overdose to the point of passing out in the past month; mental health care, needle exchange and medication treatment; at follow-up, strips used, unused, lost or given away, timing of testing, results, surprise (with open-ended reasons), actions after positive and negative results (select all that apply) and likelihood of future use (AM pp. 5–6).
outcomes.validity_norms: Study-specific items; only the drinking question comes from a validated instrument (AUDIT-C).
outcomes.operationalization: Primary prespecified outcome: number of non-fatal overdoses (AM p. 4), analysed as any versus none. Risk behaviours as prevalence or daily use; change as baseline versus follow-up proportions by McNemar's test (AM p. 6).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 15 rows in Table 3 plus any illicit opioid use reported in the text, each tested in the total sample and in two strata (about 45 McNemar tests), at p < 0.05.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: interviews by study staff, and participants and staff knew everyone had received the intervention; whether the interviewers also delivered the training is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Only counts and percentages with significance stars; no odds ratios or confidence intervals are printed although the Methods say McNemar's test produced them (AM p. 6). Total sample, n = 68, baseline to follow-up (Table 3, AM p. 21): daily illicit opioid use 52 (76.5%) to 38 (55.9%), p < 0.01; daily injection 27 (39.7%) to 17 (25.0%), p < 0.01; benzodiazepine use 15 (22.1%) to 5 (7.4%), p < 0.01; daily benzodiazepine use 9 (13.2%) to 2 (2.9%), p < 0.05; solitary use 56 (94.9%) to 40 (67.8%), p < 0.001, among 59 with opioid use at follow-up; asking someone to check 36 (61.0%) to 43 (72.8%), not significant; non-fatal overdose 6 (8.8%) to 1 (1.5%), not significant; any injection 34 (50.0%) to 29 (42.7%), alcohol use 32 (47.1%) to 29 (42.7%) and preferring fentanyl 29 (42.7%) to 26 (38.2%), all not significant. The abstract gives p = 0.003 for daily illicit opioid use, 0.004 for injection frequency, 0.008 for any benzodiazepine use and < 0.001 for solitary use (AM p. 1); it does not give an exact p-value for daily benzodiazepine use. Women who used no strip (n = 11): daily illicit opioid use 9 (81.8%) to 4 (36.4%), daily injection 4 (36.4%) to 2 (18.2%), non-fatal overdose 2 to 0, none significant. Editors' calculation (Wilson 95% CI): used at least one strip 57/68 = 83.8% (73.3 to 90.7); harm-reduction behaviour after a positive result 33/48 = 68.8% (54.7 to 80.1); used the tested drugs after a positive result 30/48 = 62.5% (48.4 to 74.8); likely to use strips again 65/68 = 95.6% (87.8 to 98.5).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; the number of non-fatal overdoses is described as the primary prespecified outcome (AM p. 4). Approved by the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health IRB (AM p. 4).
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract reports significant secondary outcomes and omits the primary outcome, which did not change significantly (6 to 1 women with an overdose). The Discussion calls overdose six times lower at follow-up while noting non-significance (AM p. 8). The text mixes figures from the total sample and from the strip-use stratum (AM p. 7).
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation; the authors say the small sample and suboptimal retention may have left the analysis underpowered (AM p. 10).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In about two months, 57 of 68 followed-up women used at least one of five strips, 49 of them reported a positive result, and 65 of 68 said they were likely to use strips again. After a positive result 30 of 48 used the tested drugs (several to relieve withdrawal) and 33 of 48 reported at least one protective action, most often using a smaller amount (15) or going slower (10); after a negative result 21 of 24 used the drugs as intended. Daily opioid use, daily injection, benzodiazepine use and solitary use were lower at follow-up than at baseline, but the women who used no strip changed as much or more, there was no comparison group, and the baseline drug-use questions covered six months against one month at follow-up.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the study found reductions in drug use frequency and solitary drug use following strip use and that strip-based interventions hold potential for reducing overdose risk (AM p. 2); the Discussion calls the study a documentation of the short-term effectiveness of a brief strip intervention (AM p. 8). These causal readings rest on uncontrolled pre–post changes after a bundle whose counselling and insert card themselves advised against using alone and warned about mixing drugs such as alcohol and benzodiazepines with opioids; the women who used no strip also reduced daily opioid use (81.8% to 36.4%); the drug-use comparisons pair a six-month baseline window with a one-month follow-up window (AM p. 5); and the prespecified primary outcome is not in the abstract. The limitations paragraph acknowledges the lack of a control group, the single follow-up, low participation and social desirability (AM p. 10), and the authors call for a larger longitudinal study (AM p. 8).

timeline.event: Krieger et al. (2018): Rhode Island pilot in young adults, whose one-month follow-up this study copied for comparability (AM p. 4). This paper summarizes it as 87 people with 68% versus 32% behaviour change after positive results (AM p. 3); card sc_krieger_2018 records 81 analysed and 67.7% versus 12.9% (positive versus no positive result).
Karamouzian et al. (2018): low uptake of drug checking among clients of a Vancouver supervised injection facility, cited (card sc_karamouzian_2018).
Peiper et al. (2019): cross-sectional study of people who inject drugs, cited as finding five-fold odds of harm-reduction behaviour after a positive result; not read.
This pilot published (November issue; author manuscript in PubMed Central).

Gelberg et al. (2025): multi-state cohort of 541 people citing this study; most strip uses were followed by no change in amount, and negative results by more reports of using more (card sc_gelberg_2025).

replication.where_it_stands: No controlled replication of the pre–post changes appears in the sources read. The descriptive findings (uptake, frequent positive results, protective actions after positive results reported by a minority to a majority depending on the action, high acceptability) agree with other self-report studies of strips. The authors call for a larger longitudinal study (AM pp. 8, 10).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial among women who sell sex and use opioids (and other people who use drugs) in which both arms receive the same counselling and naloxone and only one receives strips, with the same recall periods at both time points, verified outcomes (urine toxicology, overdose records), and follow-up of several months.

domains.note: No comparison group: pre–post changes may reflect regression to the mean, secular change or the co-delivered counselling and insert card (which advised against using alone and warned about mixing drugs such as alcohol and benzodiazepines with opioids) and naloxone. The post hoc comparison of women who used strips with those who did not is unadjusted, and the 11 who used none changed as much or more.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: 70% of women approached agreed to screening; a cohort-based convenience sample; analysis restricted to the 66% who completed follow-up, with younger women and those injecting pills lost more often.
Everyone received the bundle; whether and how strips were used, and the results, were self-reported and unverified; 18% gave strips to others.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Follow-up took on average 56 days instead of one month (22.1% within the target), so exposure time varied; additional strips and naloxone were available at later cohort visits.
34% lost to follow-up, complete-case analysis; item non-response (for example 5 of 29 women with a negative result lacked answers on actions; 3 missing on surprise).

Self-reported to study staff who knew everyone had received the intervention (social desirability, recall; acknowledged, AM p. 10); unvalidated items; drug use at baseline asked for the past 6 months and at follow-up for the past month (AM p. 5), which by itself tends to produce apparent reductions.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: The prespecified primary outcome (number of non-fatal overdoses) was analysed only as any versus none and omitted from the abstract; about 45 unadjusted tests; odds ratios and intervals described in the Methods are not shown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I judges whether the study can estimate the effect of providing strips with training. It cannot: there is no comparison group, the intervention was a bundle with counselling that targeted the same behaviours, the women who used no strip changed as much or more, and the drug-use questions covered different periods before and after. Citable for: uptake (57 of 68 used at least one strip), self-reported results (49 of 57 with at least one positive), what women said they did after positive and negative results (for example 15 of 48 used a smaller amount after a positive result; 30 of 48 used the tested drugs; 21 of 24 used drugs as intended after a negative result), surprise at results, sharing of strips and acceptability, all as self-reports from 68 women in Baltimore in 2018–2019. Not citable for: strips reducing drug use, benzodiazepine use, solitary use or overdose.

key_findings.finding: Of 175 women approached, 123 were screened, 103 were eligible and enrolled (all ineligible women had not used opioids in the past month), and 68 (66%) completed follow-up, on average 56 days after baseline and 22.1% within the one-month target.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (AM p. 6); Fig. 2 (AM p. 16)
key_findings.note: The counts are in Fig. 2, an image, and were read from the rendered page; 103 enrolled and 68 followed up are also in the abstract (AM p. 1).

key_findings.finding: At baseline every woman received 5 to 10 minutes of strip training, harm-reduction micro-counselling tailored to the risks she reported, an insert card, five BTNX strips, injection equipment and two doses of intramuscular naloxone.
key_findings.locator: Methods 2.1, 2nd paragraph (AM p. 4); Fig. 1 (AM p. 15)

key_findings.finding: Baseline (n = 103): 22.3% aged 18–29, 59.2% non-Hispanic White, 87.4% actively selling sex, 48.5% injected heroin and 30.1% fentanyl in the past 6 months, 73.8% smoked crack cocaine, 10.7% had ever used a strip, 75.7% were concerned about fentanyl in their drugs, 42.7% preferred drugs with fentanyl and 96.1% used drugs alone.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (AM p. 6); Table 1 (AM pp. 17–18)

key_findings.finding: At follow-up 57 of 68 (83.8%) had used at least one strip: 33 (57.9%) only before using drugs, 17 (29.8%) before and after, 7 (12.3%) only after. Of the 57, 49 (86.0%) had at least one positive result, 29 (50.9%) at least one negative and 8 (14.0%) an unclear result; 34 still had unused strips and 12 (17.7%) had given strips to others.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (AM p. 6); Table 2 (AM p. 19)

key_findings.finding: After a positive result (48 women with answers), 33 (68.8%) reported at least one harm-reduction behaviour and 30 (62.5%) used the tested drugs; 15 (31.3%) used a smaller amount than intended, 10 (20.8%) went slower when injecting, 5 (10.4%) did a tester shot, 3 (6.3%) asked someone to check on them, 3 (6.3%) threw the drugs out, 3 (6.3%) sold them, 6 (12.5%) told others and 2 (4.2%) stopped going to that dealer; none stopped using drugs or entered treatment.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph (AM p. 7); Table 2 (AM p. 19)

key_findings.finding: Of the 30 women who used drugs as intended despite a positive result, 12 cited withdrawal (some also a missed or insufficient methadone dose); others said they enjoyed or wanted fentanyl, had a fentanyl habit, or doubted the result.
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph (AM p. 7)
key_findings.note: The denominators printed for these reasons (5/12, 2/12, 4/12) do not fit the 30; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: After a negative result (24 women with answers), 21 (87.5%) used their drugs as intended, 2 reported a harm-reduction behaviour and 2 sold the drugs.
key_findings.locator: Results, 6th paragraph (AM p. 7); Table 2 (AM p. 19)

key_findings.finding: 31 women (57.4%) were surprised by their results: 26 of 48 (54.2%) with a positive and 17 of 24 (70.8%) with a negative result; all 5 women with only negative results had assumed fentanyl was in all drugs.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (starts AM p. 6, ends AM p. 7); Table 2 (AM p. 19)

key_findings.finding: 49 of 68 women (72.1%) said they were extremely likely and 16 (23.5%) likely to use strips in future; by the editors' sum, 65 of 68 (95.6%).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, last rows

key_findings.finding: Total sample (n = 68), baseline to follow-up: daily illicit opioid use 76.5% to 55.9%, daily injection 39.7% to 25.0% and benzodiazepine use 22.1% to 7.4% (each p < 0.01); solitary use 94.9% to 67.8% (p < 0.001; n = 59 with opioid use at follow-up); asking someone to check on you 61.0% to 72.8% and non-fatal overdose 8.8% to 1.5% (6 to 1 women), not significant; preference for fentanyl 42.7% to 38.2%, not significant.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (AM p. 1); Table 3, Total columns (AM p. 21)
key_findings.note: The baseline drug-use questions covered the past 6 months and the follow-up questions the past month (Methods 2.2.2, AM p. 5); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Women who used no strip (n = 11) changed in the same direction, some by more: daily illicit opioid use 81.8% to 36.4%, daily injection 36.4% to 18.2%, non-fatal overdose 2 to 0 women; none significant, which the authors attribute to the small group.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.1, end (AM p. 8); Table 3, Did not use any FTS columns (AM p. 21)

key_findings.finding: The primary prespecified outcome was the number of non-fatal overdoses; it was analysed as any overdose in the past month (6 of 68 women at baseline, 1 at follow-up) and did not change significantly.
key_findings.locator: Methods 2, last sentence (AM p. 4); Results 3.1 (AM p. 8); Table 3 (AM p. 21)

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods state that drug use was asked for the past 6 months at baseline and the past month at follow-up, while Table 3 labels all drug-use rows as past month; the baseline values in Table 3 (benzodiazepine use 22.1%, any injection 50.0%) equal the past-6-month values for completers in Table 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: The drug-use comparisons have unequal recall windows, which can by itself produce an apparent reduction. They do not establish a behavioural change caused by the intervention. Solitary use and overdose were asked about the past month at both visits and are not affected by this particular window mismatch.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives solitary drug use as 96% versus 68%; Table 3 gives 94.9% versus 67.8% among 59 women reporting opioid use at follow-up. The rounded 96% matches both all 103 women at baseline (96.1%) and the 68 completers at baseline (95.6%), rather than the paired baseline of 94.9%. The abstract's 24% who had overdosed in the past year appears nowhere in the body, where Table 1 gives 9.7% with a non-fatal overdose in the past month.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract mixes denominators and contains a figure that cannot be checked; cite the tables.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text gives benzodiazepine use among women who used strips as 22.8% to 7.40%; Table 3 gives 22.8% to 7.0% for that group, and 7.4% is the total sample's follow-up value. Non-significant changes are referred to Table 2 instead of Table 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; figures from different groups are combined in one sentence.

reporting_issues.issue: Denominators in the Results text do not match Table 2: 25 women with a negative result in the text against 24 with answers (29 with a negative result, 5 missing) in Table 2, with percentages (87.5%, 8.3%) that fit 24; reasons for using drugs despite a positive result given as 5/12, 2/12 and 4/12 for a group of 30; and 24/25 (96%) likely to use strips again against 49 extremely likely and 16 likely out of 68 in Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: The percentages are usable from Table 2, but the open-ended reasons cannot be quantified reliably.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 30 of 48 women used their drugs as originally intended, without behavioural modifications, after a positive result, while Table 2 shows 33 of 48 engaged in a harm-reduction behaviour; in a select-all question at least 15 women must have done both.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text's gloss of used the tested drugs as no behavioural modification is not consistent with the table; the categories overlap and should not be added.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say McNemar's test produced odds ratios and confidence intervals, and the Results say these show the precision of the estimates, but no table or text reports them.
reporting_issues.consequence: The precision of the pre–post changes cannot be judged from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The strip validation figures of 98% sensitivity and 94% specificity are attributed to Sherman et al. (2018) in the Introduction and to Krieger et al. (2018) in the Discussion; baseline concern about fentanyl among completers is 80.9% in Table 1 but 83.8% in Table 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor citation and transcription inconsistencies.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods and Table 2 describe the reactions-to-results item as allowing multiple selected answers, but the Results describe it as an open-ended question.
reporting_issues.consequence: The response format is reported inconsistently. Describe the recorded responses without inferring that every action was volunteered without prompting, and do not add overlapping categories.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 places non-fatal overdose in a block marked as restricted to 59 women who used opioids at follow-up, but the printed overdose percentages use all 68 completers: 6/68 = 8.8% and 1/68 = 1.5%. The strip-use columns themselves print 4 to 1 women and the no-strip columns 2 to 0. No exact McNemar statistic, p-value or paired interval is reported for overdose.
reporting_issues.consequence: Keep the printed counts and denominator, identify the ambiguous footnote, and retain the paper's statement that the change was not statistically significant. The 4-to-1 counts are printed figures, not an editors' subtraction. A paired interval cannot be recovered from marginal counts alone.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract, hypothesis, Methods, flow diagram and Table 2 frame follow-up as one month, while the Results report a mean of 56 days and only 22.1% within the one-month goal. Table 2 also labels strip use as occurring in the past month.
reporting_issues.consequence: Separate the planned follow-up from the observed average. The one-month wording is in the primary paper itself, so a review repeating it is not the sole source of this discrepancy. The table does not establish that the whole variable follow-up interval was covered by its recall window.

reporting_issues.issue: The needle-exchange row of Table 3 reports totals of 29 at baseline and 22 at follow-up, while its strip-use strata sum to 17 + 2 = 19 and 13 + 1 = 14. The subgroup percentages also imply denominators different from the column headings.
reporting_issues.consequence: This service-access row cannot be reconstructed from the printed counts and denominators. Do not use it to quantify a change without clarification.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods dichotomize alcohol frequency as at least weekly versus less than weekly, while Table 3 labels the frequency categories as at least daily versus less than daily.
reporting_issues.consequence: The alcohol-frequency threshold is uncertain from this report. It is not used in the current group's claims.

design_detail: Descriptive monitoring report pooling 2008–2013 results from seven European consumer drug-checking services in the Trans European Drug Information (TEDI) project: DIMS (Netherlands, 28,613 samples), Energy Control (Spain, Catalonia, 8,305), Ailaket (Basque country, 1,629), Saferparty (Switzerland, 3,290), Checkit! (Austria, 3,078), Modus Fiesta (Belgium, 244, from 2011) and Check!n (Portugal, 700, from three editions of one biennial festival): 45,859 samples in all (Figure 1, PDF p. 4). People handed in drugs voluntarily at stationary or mobile services; laboratory methods differed by service (GC-MS and LC-DAD at DIMS; thin-layer chromatography with GC-MS confirmation and UV spectrophotometry at Energy Control; thin-layer chromatography at Ailaket and Check!n; mobile HPLC at Checkit! and Saferparty) (PDF pp. 2–3). At DIMS, a tablet matching a batch already analysed by GC-MS at least three times was identified from its colour-test result and recorded physical features (logo, diameter, thickness, weight, colour, groove) without a new laboratory analysis, and the person who brought it was given the batch's average content and range (PDF p. 2). Results are shares of samples containing the expected drug, purity or MDMA content, adulterants and new psychoactive substances (NPS) by service and year, almost all shown in figures without sample sizes. Filed as cross-sectional and appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for drug-checking data. The online-first PDF was read (see verification).
can_establish: What seven European drug-checking services found in the cocaine, amphetamine and ecstasy samples people brought them in 2008–2013, including, for ecstasy tablets, the share containing MDMA and the average MDMA content per tablet by service and year, and which NPS turned up in ecstasy.
cannot_establish: How much tablets with the same logo or look vary in content (no such data are reported; tablet recognition by logo is described as a method and its reliability is cited, not shown), how representative the samples are of each country's market, precise yearly values (no sample sizes or intervals), or any effect of drug checking on behaviour or on the market.

sample.recruitment: Samples handed in voluntarily, face to face, by people who use drugs at stationary or mobile drug-checking services (PDF p. 2, Materials and methods › Participants). Check!n data come from three editions (2008, 2010, 2012) of one biennial electronic music festival (PDF p. 3, Results, 1st paragraph); Modus Fiesta data start in 2011 (Figure 1 note, PDF p. 4).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated beyond the services' 2008–2013 data. How tablets identified by logo and colour test at DIMS were counted (with the batch average, separately, or not at all) is not stated. Figure 1 shows only four sample types (cocaine, amphetamine, ecstasy pills, MDMA crystals) summing to 100% for each service, so whether the 45,859 include other drugs is unclear.
sample.demographics: Not collected in this analysis. Earlier studies are cited: 386 people testing at the Amsterdam facility in 2008–2011 were 73% male, relatively highly educated and mostly of Dutch ethnicity; 1,376 visitors to the Swiss service in 2003–2010 were 78.1% male, mean age 27.8, and 81.1% reported using several drugs on a typical party night (PDF p. 2, Participants).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected people who want their drugs analysed; services differ greatly in reach (DIMS supplied 62% of samples, editors' calculation; Belgium 244 and Portugal 700), and some test at festivals while others are stationary. The authors state that people using the services did not necessarily represent all people who use drugs and that an unknown proportion are not interested in testing (PDF p. 9, Discussion, 9th paragraph). Similarity of people who test and people who do not is asserted from earlier studies, not measured here.

exposure.measurement: Laboratory analysis by service: DIMS used LC-DAD and GC-MS (GC-MS suitable for analytes at 1% w/w or more; ten common analytes calibrated for quantification); Energy Control thin-layer chromatography confirmed by GC-MS, with UV spectrophotometry for purity; Ailaket and Check!n thin-layer chromatography; Checkit! and Saferparty mobile HPLC with diode-array detection (PDF pp. 2–3, Colourimetric drug tests; Instrumentation). Laboratories differed in sensitivity and in reporting purity as salt or base (PDF p. 9, Discussion, 10th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (samples). Purity or content was quantified by some services only: cocaine and amphetamine purity by four services (Figures 3 and 5), MDMA per tablet by four (Figure 8), MDMA crystal purity by five (Figure 10).
exposure.polysubstance: Adulterants reported for cocaine (Table 1, PDF p. 5) and amphetamine (caffeine and 4-methylamphetamine, Figure 6, PDF p. 6); NPS found in ecstasy tablets and powders (Table 2, PDF p. 8).

comparison.controls: None; comparisons are between services, between years and with what the sample was sold as.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not reported: the number of samples per service, year and drug type; how tablets identified without laboratory analysis were treated; content variation within a logo or batch; prices; and what people did after receiving results.

outcomes.instruments: Percentage of samples sold as a drug that contained it (the rest called 'misrepresented'), average purity (%) or MDMA per tablet (mg), percentage of samples containing each adulterant, and counts and types of NPS (PDF p. 3, Statistics; Figures 2–12; Tables 1–2).
outcomes.validity_norms: Techniques and detection limits differed between laboratories; the authors say this limits comparability and may have led to underreporting of NPS and adulterants (PDF p. 9, Discussion, 10th paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Misrepresented' means a sample not containing the main labelled psychoactive compound (PDF p. 3, Statistics).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: descriptive means and percentages only, no statistical tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; analysts knew what each sample was sold as.

analysis.effect_sizes: No sample sizes per year or service, no intervals, no tests. Read from the figures (approximate): ecstasy tablets containing MDMA in 2009, Austria about 18%, Spain about 31%, Switzerland about 47%, Netherlands about 64%; in 2013, Netherlands about 92%, Switzerland about 95%, Belgium about 100%, Austria about 78%, Spain about 62% (Figure 7, PDF p. 7). Average MDMA per tablet in 2009 about 62–74 mg across four services, and about 104–114 mg in 2013 (Figure 8, PDF p. 7); the text gives 60–70 mg in 2009 and 107–114 mg in 2013 (PDF p. 4). Cocaine: average purity 42% in Austria across 2008–2013 and around 60% in the Basque country, the Netherlands and Switzerland in 2013 (PDF p. 3); levamisole was found in 66.7% of Dutch cocaine samples in 2013 (Table 1) and averaged 7.5% (2010) and 8.7% (2013) of their content (PDF p. 3). MDMA crystal powders averaged 73.5% purity across countries (PDF p. 4). Amphetamine purity averaged 39% across countries in 2013 (PDF p. 4).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Detailed results only for cocaine, amphetamine and ecstasy; the numbers behind the percentages are not given and figure values are not tabulated; the logo-recognition procedure is described without its own data, its reliability cited from earlier DIMS publications (refs 17 and 28).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across seven services, the share of ecstasy tablets containing MDMA fell sharply around 2009 and recovered by 2013 in most services but not all (about 62% in Spain and 78% in Austria in 2013); average MDMA per tablet rose from about 62–74 mg in 2009 to about 104–114 mg in 2013 in the four services that measured it; many NPS appeared in ecstasy, some in one country only. No data on how content varies among tablets with the same logo are reported.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says drug testing can generate a global picture of drug markets (PDF p. 1), which the authors themselves qualify by self-selected samples and non-comparable laboratory methods (PDF p. 9, Discussion, 9th and 10th paragraphs). The Conclusion asserts that dealers and manufacturers will be less inclined to trade dangerous substances if consumers can test, and that traders withdraw products after warnings (PDF p. 9), with no data in the paper. The Methods state that tablet recognition from logo, physical features and a colour test has been proven very reliable in the Netherlands, citing earlier DIMS work (refs 17 and 28) without data here (PDF p. 2). The text's summary of Figure 8 (a low of 60–70 mg in 2009, doubling to 107–114 mg by 2013) does not match the figure for Austria and Spain (reporting issues).

timeline.event: Parrott (2004), review of the proportion of ecstasy tablets containing MDMA and their dosage levels, cited for concern about misrepresentation and unexpected contents (ref. 14).
Vogels et al. (2009), content of ecstasy in the Netherlands 1993–2008, cited with Brunt and Niesink (2011) as showing that DIMS tablet recognition is very reliable (refs 28 and 17). Neither read.
This study, published online in 2016 (print issue 2017).
Palamar et al. (2022) cite this study as an example of European drug checking to which people can bring or send samples (card sc_palamar_2022).

replication.where_it_stands: A descriptive monitoring report, so replication is not the question; it documents large swings in what ecstasy tablets contained in 2008–2013 and differences between countries. It does not test whether a logo predicts content: the reliability of identifying tablets by logo and physical features rests on earlier DIMS publications cited here (Vogels et al., 2009; Brunt and Niesink, 2011), which need their own reading before any claim about logos.

funding.funder: TEDI and this study were supported by grants of the European Commission (Grant Agreement Number 2010 12 07, Nightlife Empowerment & Well-being Implementation Project) (PDF p. 9, Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the version read.
funding.affiliations_note: All seven authors work for the drug-checking services whose data are reported (DIMS at the Trimbos Institute, Checkit!, Safer Nightlife Switzerland, APDES, Ai Laket, Modus Vivendi, Energy Control) (PDF p. 1), and the Conclusion argues for these services. A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A study in which every tablet submitted with a given logo and set of physical features over a defined period is analysed in the laboratory (rather than inferred from earlier batches), reporting the spread of MDMA content and the share containing other substances within each logo, across services and years.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Consumer drug-checking services: a frame for what people using the services submit, not for national markets; reach differs greatly between services.
Self-selected voluntary submissions; Portuguese data from one festival; stationary and festival services mixed.
45,859 samples in all, but the yearly service-level estimates that make up the results have unreported sample sizes, some from small services (Belgium 244 over three years).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Services and laboratory methods are described; sample numbers by year and drug type are not, and the description of people testing comes from earlier studies.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Whether tablets identified by logo without laboratory analysis were included, and what the 45,859 contain beyond the four drug types analysed, is not stated.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: GC-MS and HPLC are valid for identification and quantification, but some services used thin-layer chromatography, and repeat tablets at DIMS were identified from logo, features and a colour test.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Different laboratories, techniques, detection limits and salt or base reporting (authors' limitation).
Descriptive means and percentages suit monitoring, but without denominators or intervals, and several text summaries do not match the figures.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Samples, not respondents.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Large multi-country drug-checking data, but self-selected samples, non-comparable laboratory methods, unreported denominators and an unclear treatment of logo-identified tablets put the yearly estimates at high risk of bias as measures of national markets. Citable for: in 2008–2013, tablets sold as ecstasy at these services often did not contain MDMA around 2009 (as low as about one in five in Austria), and their average MDMA content rose markedly by 2013; MDMA crystals mostly contained MDMA; NPS appeared in ecstasy, some only in one country; services identified repeat tablets partly by logo. Not citable for: how reliably a logo predicts content, content variation within a logo, precise national prevalence, or effects of drug checking on sellers or on people who use drugs.

key_findings.finding: Between 2008 and 2013 the seven TEDI services analysed 45,859 samples: DIMS (Netherlands) 28,613, Energy Control (Spain) 8,305, Saferparty (Switzerland) 3,290, Checkit! (Austria) 3,078, Ailaket (Basque country) 1,629, Check!n (Portugal) 700 and Modus Fiesta (Belgium) 244.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 3); Figure 1 labels (PDF p. 4)
key_findings.note: The text says DIMS received approximately 30 000 samples; Figure 1 gives 28,613.

key_findings.finding: Logo-based identification: for each tablet, services recorded logo, diameter, thickness, weight, colour and presence of a groove; if a tablet from a batch had been analysed by GC-MS at least three times, the colour-test result and these features were taken as sufficient identification, and the person who brought it was given the batch's average content and range. The authors state this recognition has proven very reliable in the Netherlands (citing refs 17 and 28); new tablets, powders, liquids and capsules were analysed instrumentally.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Colourimetric drug tests, single paragraph
key_findings.note: No data are given on agreement between logo-based identification and laboratory results, or on how much content varies among tablets with the same logo.

key_findings.finding: The share of tablets sold as ecstasy that contained MDMA dropped sharply around 2009 and rose again from 2010; read from Figure 7 (approximate), in 2009 about 18% (Austria), 31% (Spain), 47% (Switzerland) and 64% (Netherlands), and in 2013 about 92% (Netherlands), 95% (Switzerland), 100% (Belgium), 78% (Austria) and 62% (Spain).
key_findings.locator: Results › Ecstasy pills and MDMA crystal powders, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 4); Figure 7 (PDF p. 7)
key_findings.note: Values read from a 300-dpi crop of Figure 7; approximate; sample sizes per year and service are not reported.

key_findings.finding: Average MDMA content per ecstasy tablet rose after 2009: read from Figure 8 (approximate), about 62–74 mg in 2009 across the four services that quantified it and about 104–114 mg in 2013; Austria's lowest value (about 43 mg) was in 2010. The text gives an average of 60–70 mg in 2009 and 107–114 mg in 2013, described as approximately doubled.
key_findings.locator: Results › Ecstasy pills and MDMA crystal powders, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 4); Figure 8 (PDF p. 7)
key_findings.note: Figure values read from a 300-dpi crop; approximate. The text and figure disagree for Austria and Spain (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Types of samples differed by service (Figure 1, approximate readings): the text says the Netherlands mostly received ecstasy pills, which are its largest sample type at about 45% of DIMS samples; the Basque country and Portugal received no ecstasy pills in 2008–2013; Spain (Energy Control) and Austria received more MDMA crystals than ecstasy pills (about 34% against 16%, and 27% against 25%), the opposite of the Netherlands, Belgium and Switzerland.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 3); Figure 1 (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Most MDMA crystal powders contained MDMA, with relatively little adulteration; the text gives an average purity across countries of 73.5%. Read from Figure 10 (approximate), average purity was about 70–78% in most services and years, lower in Belgium (about 46–52%) and in Austria in 2008 and 2010 (about 55% and 52%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Ecstasy pills and MDMA crystal powders, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 4); Figures 9–10 (PDF p. 7)
key_findings.note: Figure values approximate.

key_findings.finding: NPS found in tablets sold as ecstasy or powders sold as MDMA (Table 2): mCPP was listed by all five services in 2008; 4-FA and its analogues, 4-APB, 5-APB, 6-APB, PMMA and PMA appeared only in the Netherlands; 4-MEC appeared in Switzerland, Spain and Austria but not in the Netherlands; the range of substances found in ecstasy grew over the years.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adulterants of the ecstasy market (PDF p. 5); Table 2 (PDF p. 8)

key_findings.finding: The number of samples containing NPS, and the number of different NPS, increased over 2008–2013, especially from 2011; many NPS were found in samples not sold as NPS.
key_findings.locator: Results › New psychoactive substances (NPS) (PDF p. 5); Figure 11 (PDF p. 8); Figure 12 (PDF p. 9)

key_findings.finding: Cocaine: most samples sold as cocaine contained it, with Austria showing the most misrepresented powders; average purity was lowest in Austria (42% across 2008–2013) and around 60% in the Basque country, the Netherlands and Switzerland in 2013; levamisole was the commonest adulterant in 2013 (in 66.7% of Dutch samples), and its average content in Dutch cocaine rose from 7.5% in 2010 to 8.7% in 2013.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cocaine, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (PDF p. 3); Table 1 (PDF p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Amphetamine: 82–99% of samples sold as amphetamine contained it in most services, Austria showing about 10% more misrepresented samples; Austria had the lowest purity (around 15%) and the Netherlands the highest; average purity across countries was 39% in 2013; most amphetamine powders also contained caffeine.
key_findings.locator: Results › Amphetamine, single paragraph; Figures 4–6 (PDF p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: people using the services do not necessarily represent all people who use drugs; services differed greatly in scale; an unknown proportion of people are not interested in testing; laboratories used different techniques, sensitivities and salt or base reporting, and may have missed new substances.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 9th and 10th paragraphs (on representativeness and on laboratory comparability)

reporting_issues.issue: The text says MDMA per tablet was at a low in 2009 (an average of 60–70 mg for four countries), rose rapidly from 2010 and roughly doubled to 107–114 mg by 2013. Figure 8 shows Austria at about 74 mg in 2009 with its low (about 43 mg) in 2010, Spain at about 104 mg in 2013, and 2009-to-2013 increases of about 1.4- to 1.8-fold (editors' reading of a 300-dpi crop).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite approximate figure values with care; 'doubled' holds roughly for the Netherlands only.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the Netherlands and Switzerland were far exceeding 90% of ecstasy tablets containing MDMA in 2013; Figure 7 shows about 92% for the Netherlands and about 95% for Switzerland.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says MDMA crystal powders containing MDMA ranged between 75% and 97% across all countries; this fits neither Figure 9 (lowest value about 53%, Spain 2009) nor Figure 10 (lowest about 46%, Belgium 2012), and what the range refers to is unclear.
reporting_issues.consequence: Do not cite the 75–97% range.

reporting_issues.issue: Sample sizes are given only per service for the whole period (Figure 1 labels); Figure 1 shows each service's mix of four drug types only as percentage bars summing to 100%, so it is unclear whether the 45,859 samples include other drugs; no numbers are given by year or by drug type, and there are no intervals.
reporting_issues.consequence: Yearly percentages from small services (for example Belgium) may rest on few samples; their precision cannot be judged.

reporting_issues.issue: Whether tablets identified by logo, physical features and colour test, without new laboratory analysis, were counted in the results, and with what values (the batch average given to the person who brought the tablet), is not stated; the paper describes the procedure for the testing facilities in general, without saying which services used it, and claims its reliability for the Netherlands (PDF p. 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: If included, such tablets would repeat earlier batch results and hide any variation within a logo; the paper gives no basis for claims about logos.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says amphetamine purity was high in Spain and the Netherlands; Figure 5 shows the Basque service (the only Spanish service quantifying amphetamine) at about 17–35%, below the Netherlands in 2009–2013 and similar to Switzerland.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the abstract's statement holds for the Netherlands, not clearly for Spain.

reporting_issues.issue: 4-Methylamphetamine is described as increasingly prevalent across all countries between 2008 and 2013, but Figure 6 shows it absent in several services and years and lower at DIMS in 2013 (about 5%) than in 2012 (about 12%), after the 2012 ban mentioned in the Discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; describe 4-MA as appearing from 2009 and peaking in 2012.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 12 stacks each service's count of different NPS, so a substance found by several services is counted several times; the totals are not numbers of distinct NPS.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the rise over time is visible, but the totals should not be cited as numbers of distinct substances.
